🍼 Baby safety rules, always

Never move a baby before placing a matching band on the baby, the mom, and the dad.

  • Security bands are removed only by the discharge nurse.
  • Keep babies in the rolling bassinet. No carrying babies down the hall.

🧠 Clinical Reasoning

Every question in this guide is built on clinical reasoning and clinical thinking tied to evidence-based practice. Maslow, ADPIE, and SBAR are the lenses. This is NCLEX preparation.

🧭 The thinking frame

Evidence-based practice sits under everything. Then Maslow tells you WHICH need comes first, ADPIE tells you WHICH STEP you are in, and SBAR tells you HOW to report it.

ToolThe question it answersHow to use it on an OB question
Evidence-based practiceWhat do research and standards of care say?When two actions look right, pick the one with evidence: early prenatal care, left side lying, folic acid, private IPV screening
MaslowWhich need is threatened first?Rank options: physiological, then safety and security, then love and belonging, then esteem, then self-actualization
ADPIEWhich step of the nursing process is this?Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation. Assess before you act unless the client is unstable
SBARHow do I tell the provider?Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Fix a quick danger first, then call

🔁 ADPIE with OB examples

StepWhat it isOB example
AssessmentCollect dataBP, fundal height, fetal heart rate, danger signs, privately asking about safety at home
DiagnosisName the client problem as a risk or problem related to a causeRisk for injury related to an abusive relationship
PlanningMeasurable client-centered goal with a time frame, in priority orderClient will state three danger signs before leaving today
ImplementationCarry out the planTurn her left, teach danger signs, offer a safety plan
EvaluationCheck whether the goal was metTeach-back, repeat BP after turning, review the safety plan with her
🧠 Teaching trap
Teaching is Implementation. Asking her to repeat it back is Evaluation.

⛰️ Maslow in mother baby care

LevelOB meaningWeek 1 examples
1. PhysiologicalOxygen, circulation, fluid, nutrition, bleeding, fetal oxygenationSupine hypotension, bleeding with pain, no fetal movement, severe preeclampsia signs
2. Safety and securityProtection from harmIPV and trafficking screening, teratogen exposure, infection, baby security bands, hot tubs
3. Love and belongingFamily and supportFamily-centered care, partner and sibling involvement, support types
4. EsteemRespect and confidenceConfidentiality, culturally respectful care, appraisal support
5. Self-actualizationReaching potentialChildbirth classes, birth plan, parenting preparation
⭐ RuleThe lower level wins. A physiological threat is addressed before a safety, belonging, esteem, or learning need.

📞 SBAR script

PartSayExample
SituationWho you are, who the client is, the problem nowI am calling about Ms. J, 36 weeks, with new bright red bleeding and abdominal pain for 20 minutes
BackgroundHistory that mattersG2 P1, history of placenta previa, no allergies
AssessmentWhat you foundBP 98/60, pulse 118, FHR 100, constant abdominal pain, I am concerned about abruption or previa
RecommendationWhat you need and how soonPlease come evaluate her now and prepare for urgent delivery
⚠️ TrapCurrent vital signs are Assessment, not Background. A request is Recommendation, not Situation.

🧪 Putting it together

  1. Read the stem word: first, best, priority, or most likely
  2. Rank every option by Maslow level
  3. Name the ADPIE step in the stem. Assess before you act unless she is unstable
  4. Choose the evidence-based action that protects the highest-level need
  5. If you must call the provider, organize it with SBAR

🧩 Example walkthrough

Stem: A client at 29 weeks on the exam table is pale, dizzy, and sweaty. BP is 84/50.

  • Maslow: physiological (circulation).
  • ADPIE: she is unstable, so Implementation first (turn her left), then Evaluation (recheck BP), then Assessment of the fetus.
  • EBP: left side lying frees the vena cava.
  • SBAR: after she is stable, call with Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.

🧩 Clinical judgment model (NCLEX Next Generation)

Clinical judgment is the thinking that connects the evidence, Maslow, ADPIE, and SBAR. The NCLEX tests six cognitive steps. They run alongside ADPIE.

StepQuestion to askOB example: late decelerations on oxytocin
1. Recognize cuesWhat matters in this data?Late decelerations with each contraction, BP 90/50, oxytocin running
2. Analyze cuesWhat do the cues mean together?Poor uteroplacental blood flow made worse by oxytocin and low BP
3. Prioritize hypothesesWhich problem is most urgent?Fetal hypoxia first (physiological need)
4. Generate solutionsWhat can I do, based on evidence?Stop oxytocin, left side, fluids, oxygen, notify with SBAR
5. Take actionsDo the highest priority actionsPerform the steps and call the provider
6. Evaluate outcomesDid it work?Recheck the tracing and BP. If not improved, escalate by chain of command
⭐ Why it matters in OBClinical judgment and evidence-based practice are central to OB nursing. Poor recognition or delayed action is also where most OB claims begin. See the FHR Monitoring tab.

🔎 How to Answer

General nursing exam habits. These come from the class slide questions and standard test strategy, not from any known style of your instructor.

1. Start with Maslow

Rank every option by need level: physiological (airway, breathing, circulation, bleeding, fetal oxygenation), then safety and security, then love and belonging, then esteem, then self-actualization. The lower level wins.

2. Find the ADPIE step

Ask which step the stem describes. Collecting data is Assessment. Naming the problem is Diagnosis. Setting a goal is Planning. Doing something is Implementation. Checking the result, like teach-back or a repeat BP, is Evaluation. Unless the client is unstable, assess before you act.

3. SBAR when you call

Situation (who and what now), Background (history), Assessment (findings), Recommendation (what you need). If one quick action fixes a danger, do it first, then call.

4. EBP is the tie-breaker

When two actions seem right, choose the one backed by evidence and standards of care, such as early prenatal care, left side lying, folic acid, and private IPV screening.

5. Say the question in your own words first

Cover the choices. Ask: what is this really asking? Then find the choice that matches your answer, instead of being pulled by a choice that sounds familiar.

6. Hunt for the word that changes the answer

NOT, EXCEPT, FIRST, BEST, MOST, and numbers like 20 weeks or 28 days turn a right idea into a wrong answer. Circle them.

7. True or false with a near twin

These swap one word: primigravida for multipara, posterior for anterior, probable for positive, hydramnios for oligohydramnios. Say the true version out loud.

8. Clinical judgment steps

Recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take actions, evaluate outcomes. Stems that give findings want you to name what they mean before you pick an action.

9. Priority questions: safety first

Danger to the mother or fetus beats comfort. Bleeding with pain, a gush of fluid, severe headache, or imminent abuse come before routine labs and teaching.

10. Prevention questions: broadest and earliest

If every choice sounds helpful, pick the one that reaches the most people soonest, like early prenatal care.

11. Select all that apply

Judge every choice on its own as true or false. Do not look for a pattern, and do not stop after you find two.

12. Therapeutic communication

Pick the choice that listens, believes, and respects choice. Avoid blame, warnings, and advice given before understanding.

13. Culture and consent

Educate and respect. Never coerce, threaten, or hold a client. Check who is legally allowed to consent.

14. When two answers look right

Ask which one the nurse does first, or which one addresses the cause. Use the Why Engine tab to practice cause and effect.

15. After every miss

Read the rationale for the right answer AND the wrong ones. Your Vault keeps the miss until you answer it right.

🧠 Why Engine

Facts stick when you know the cause. Read each chain out loud.

Why do physiological needs come first?

Without oxygen, circulation, and blood volume, nothing else matters.
→ A threat to airway, breathing, circulation, or fetal oxygenation can kill in minutes.
→ Maslow puts physiological first, then safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualization.

Why assess before you act?

Actions based on guesses can harm.
→ Assessment gives data for the diagnosis and plan.
→ Exception: if the client is unstable, fix the threat first, then assess (turn her left, then recheck her BP).

Why does the fetus skip the lungs?

The placenta supplies the oxygen. The lungs are filled with fluid.
→ The fetal lungs are not working yet, so blood is routed around them.
→ Three shunts do the rerouting: ductus venosus (skips the liver), foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus (skip the lungs). They close after birth when the lungs take over.

Why does hemoglobin drop in a healthy pregnancy?

Plasma volume rises about 1200 to 1600 mL.
→ Red cells rise less than plasma, so blood gets diluted.
→ This is physiologic anemia. It becomes true anemia when hemoglobin is under 11 g/dL (1st and 3rd trimester) or under 10.5 g/dL (2nd).

Why does lying flat make a pregnant woman faint?

The heavy uterus sits on the inferior vena cava.
→ Less blood returns to the heart, so cardiac output and BP fall.
→ Turn her to the left side. That frees the vena cava.

Why is a positive pregnancy test only probable?

The test detects hCG.
→ hCG can be raised by conditions other than pregnancy.
→ Only the baby itself proves it: seen, heard, or felt by a clinician.

Why do nurses push early prenatal care?

Most pregnancy complications are preventable.
→ Visits catch hypertension, diabetes, and infection while they can be treated.
→ That is why it is the best single answer to lowering maternal and infant death.

Why is abuse more dangerous in pregnancy?

Abuse is about control. Pregnancy changes the power balance and adds stress.
→ Risk of violence rises during pregnancy and threatens the mother and fetus.
→ So every woman is screened, alone, and safety is assessed first.

Why are hot tubs and saunas avoided?

They raise the core body temperature.
→ Overheating, especially early, can harm the developing fetus.
→ Showers are fine. Avoid saunas and hot tubs.

Why are live vaccines not given in pregnancy?

Live vaccines contain weakened live virus.
→ The virus could cross the placenta and infect the fetus.
→ MMR and varicella wait until after birth. Tdap and inactivated flu vaccine are safe and recommended.

Why does an Rh negative mother get Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks?

Fetal Rh positive cells can leak into her blood.
→ Her body would make antibodies against them (sensitization).
→ The shot stops that, protecting future Rh positive babies. It is given at 28 weeks and again within 72 hours after birth if the baby is Rh positive.

Why take folic acid before conception?

The neural tube forms in the first weeks, often before she knows she is pregnant.
→ Low folic acid causes neural tube defects.
→ So it starts before conception: 400 mcg daily, then 600 mcg in pregnancy.

Why does the first pregnancy with triplets count as Para 1?

Parity asks how many pregnancies reached 20 weeks.
→ One pregnancy happened, no matter how many babies.
→ Only L counts the children. G1 T1 P0 A0 L3 for term triplets.

Why is failure to communicate the top malpractice cause?

Maternity involves many handoffs between nurses and providers.
→ Missed or unclear information delays care.
→ Document, escalate, and use clear handoffs.

🪝 Memory Hooks

Short hooks for the facts that trip people up.

Top causes of maternal death
H.I.P.C.A.
Hemorrhage, Infection, Preeclampsia and eclampsia, Cardiovascular disease, Abortion complications.
Pregnancy history
GTPAL
G is every pregnancy. Then T, P, A, L: Term, Preterm, Abortions, Living. Only L counts babies.
Trisomies
Down 21, Edwards 18, Patau 13
D, E, P in alphabetical order, with the numbers counting down 21, 18, 13.
Teratogenic infections
TORCH
Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, Zika), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes.
Four types of support
I.E.A.I.
Informational, Emotional, Appraisal (esteem), Instrumental.
Sexual violence care
S.E.P.P.
Support, Evidence, Pregnancy prevention, PTSD screen (plus STI check).
Umbilical cord
2 A, 1 V
Two arteries, one vein. The vein is the oxygen-rich one.
Positive signs
Seen, Heard, Felt
Ultrasound (seen), Doppler heart tones (heard), movement felt by a clinician. Everything else is probable or presumptive.
Nagele's rule
Minus 3, plus 7
First day of last period, minus 3 months, plus 7 days.
Prenatal visits
4 / 2 / 1
Every 4 weeks to 28, every 2 weeks 28 to 36, weekly after 36.
Do no harm
Non-MAL-eficence
Mal means bad. Do not do bad. Bene means good.
AWHONN core values
C.A.R.I.N.G.
Commitment, Accountability, Respect, Integrity, Nursing excellence, Generation of knowledge.
Amniotic fluid
Hydra = water
Hydramnios is too much (over 2000 mL). Oligohydramnios is too little (under 500 mL).
Mortality windows
Neo 28, Infant 12
Neonatal mortality is the death of an infant in the first 28 days of life. Infant mortality is the death of an infant in the first 12 months of life.
Mess with fetus development
Teratogens
Teratogens mess with fetal development: alcohol, ACE inhibitors, warfarin, anticonvulsants, cocaine, and the TORCH infections.
Clinical reasoning
Maslow, ADPIE, SBAR
Maslow ranks the need (physiological first). ADPIE is the nursing process (assess first). SBAR is how you report. EBP is the base under all three.
Evidence-based answer
Best way to lower mortality
Early and adequate prenatal care. It finds treatable problems early.
FHR decelerations
VEAL CHOP
Variable = Cord compression. Early = Head compression. Acceleration = OK. Late = Placental insufficiency.
Normal FHR baseline
110 to 160
Below 110 is bradycardia and above 160 is tachycardia, each for 10 minutes or more. Moderate variability is 6 to 25 bpm.
Late deceleration actions
Late = left, fluids, oxygen, stop Pitocin
Reposition to the left, IV bolus, oxygen, stop oxytocin, notify the provider, and prepare for birth.
Clinical judgment model
Recognize, Analyze, Prioritize, Generate, Act, Evaluate
The six NCLEX clinical judgment steps. They run alongside ADPIE.
Prevention
Primary, Secondary, Tertiary
Before disease, find it early (screen), limit the damage.
Position
Left is best
Left side lying relieves supine hypotension and improves blood flow to the uterus.
Kick counts
5 in 1, or 10 in 2
At least 5 kicks in 1 hour, or 10 kicks in 2 hours, is reassuring. Less: cold drink and recount, then call.
Biophysical profile score
8 to 10 good, 4 to 6 bad, under 4 awful
Normal 8 to 10. Abnormal 4 to 6 (suspect asphyxia). Under 4 strongly abnormal. Five parts: movement, tone, breathing, fluid, NST.
Alpha-fetoprotein
Low is Down, high is the tube
Low AFP points to Down syndrome. High AFP points to a neural tube defect. Many false positives.
Contraction stress test
No contractions, no test
It needs contractions (oxytocin or nipple stimulation) and a place where a baby can be delivered.
Cervix versus lower segment
Goodell = cervix, Hegar = lower uterus
Goodell sign: cervix softens (about 8 weeks). Hegar sign: lower uterine segment softens (about 6 weeks). Chadwick: bluish cervix (6 to 8 weeks).
Cord vessels
AVA
Artery, Vein, Artery: two arteries and one vein.

📖 Vocabulary by chapter

352 terms. Tap a chapter to filter, then drill them in Flash Study Game or Match Games.

Clinical Reasoning: EBP, ADPIE, SBAR, Maslow (22)

TermMeaning
Clinical reasoningThinking through a client situation to decide what matters most and what to do, using evidence, the nursing process, priorities, and communication.
Evidence-based practice (EBP)Using the best research, clinical expertise, and client preferences to make decisions. The gold standard behind every nursing action. Also called: EBP.
ADPIEThe nursing process: Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation.
AssessmentCollecting data: history, vital signs, physical exam, screening questions, and what the client says. Usually the first step.
Nursing diagnosisA client problem the nurse can treat, written as a risk or problem related to a cause. Not a medical diagnosis.
PlanningSetting measurable, client-centered goals and choosing interventions, in order of priority.
ImplementationCarrying out the plan: teaching, positioning, medications, referrals, safety actions.
EvaluationChecking whether the goal was met, for example with teach-back or a repeat vital sign.
SBARA communication tool: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
Situation (SBAR)Who you are, who the client is, and the problem right now.
Background (SBAR)Relevant history: gestational age, G and P, diagnoses, allergies, medications.
Assessment (SBAR)What you found: vital signs, fetal heart rate, symptoms, and what you think the problem is.
Recommendation (SBAR)What you want: come to the bedside, an order, a test, or a change in the plan.
Maslow's hierarchyNeeds ranked from the base up: physiological, safety and security, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualization. Meet lower needs first.
Physiological needsAirway, breathing, circulation, fluid, nutrition, bleeding, and fetal oxygenation. Highest priority.
Safety and securityProtection from harm: abuse, falls, infection, teratogens, and baby security bands.
Love and belongingFamily, partner, and support systems.
EsteemRespect, confidentiality, and confidence.
Self-actualizationReaching potential, such as childbirth classes, birth plans, and parenting preparation.
PriorityWhat the nurse does first. Rank by Maslow and ABCs: what threatens life fastest comes first.
Teach-backAsking the client to explain or show what she learned. A way to evaluate teaching.
Clinical judgment modelNCSBN model with six steps: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take actions, evaluate outcomes. Used in NCLEX NGN.

FHR Monitoring (21)

TermMeaning
Baseline FHRAverage fetal heart rate over 10 minutes, excluding accelerations and decelerations. Normal is 110 to 160 bpm.
Fetal tachycardiaBaseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more.
Fetal bradycardiaBaseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more.
VariabilityFluctuation in the baseline. Absent undetectable, minimal 5 or less, moderate 6 to 25 (normal), marked over 25.
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more for 15 seconds or more. Reassuring.
Early decelerationGradual drop that mirrors the contraction. Caused by fetal head compression. Benign.
Variable decelerationAbrupt drop of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes. Caused by umbilical cord compression.
Late decelerationGradual drop with the lowest point after the peak of the contraction. Caused by uteroplacental insufficiency. Ominous when recurrent.
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes.
Sinusoidal patternSmooth wave-like FHR pattern. Ominous. Category III.
TachysystoleMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes.
Category INormal tracing: baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations.
Category IIIndeterminate tracing. Anything not Category I or III. Needs evaluation and surveillance.
Category IIIAbnormal tracing. Absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia, or sinusoidal. Immediate action.
Intrauterine resuscitationBedside measures to improve fetal oxygenation: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus, oxygen, check for cord prolapse, notify the provider.
Leopold maneuversFour abdominal palpation steps to find fetal lie, presentation, and position, used to place the Doppler over the fetal back.
Tocodynamometer (toco)External belt device over the fundus that records contraction frequency and duration but not intensity. Also called: Toco.
IUPCIntrauterine pressure catheter. Measures contraction pressure in mm Hg. Requires ruptured membranes.
Fetal scalp electrodeInternal electrode that reads the FHR directly. Needs ruptured membranes, dilation, and an accessible presenting part. Also called: FSE, internal fetal monitor.
Chain of commandThe steps for escalating a safety concern when a provider does not respond: charge nurse, supervisor, then department chair.
VEAL CHOPVariable = Cord compression, Early = Head compression, Acceleration = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency.

GTPAL & OB Basics (15)

TermMeaning
GravidaA woman who is pregnant. Counts every pregnancy, including the current one.
GravidityThe number of pregnancies a woman has had, no matter how they ended. Also called: Gravida.
NulligravidaA woman who has never been pregnant.
PrimigravidaA woman who is pregnant for the first time.
MultigravidaA woman who has had two or more pregnancies.
ParityThe number of pregnancies that reached 20 weeks or more. It is NOT the number of babies. Twins or triplets from one pregnancy count as 1. Live birth or stillbirth does not change it. Also called: Para.
NulliparaA woman who has not completed a pregnancy to 20 weeks or beyond.
PrimiparaA woman who has completed one pregnancy to 20 weeks or beyond.
MultiparaA woman who has completed two or more pregnancies to 20 weeks or beyond. (The first-time pregnant woman is a primigravida, never a multipara.)
TermA pregnancy from the beginning of week 37 through the end of week 42. A birth at exactly 37 weeks counts as term.
PretermA pregnancy that has reached 20 weeks but has not completed 37 weeks. Also called: Premature.
Abortion (in GTPAL)Any pregnancy loss before 20 weeks. Includes miscarriage (spontaneous), elective, and ectopic.
GTPALG = gravidity. Para is broken down into T = term, P = preterm, A = abortions (losses before 20 weeks), L = living children. Everything counts pregnancies except L, which counts children. Short form: G and Para, where Para = T + P.
EDB (EDD)Expected date of birth, also called expected date of delivery. Found with Nagele's rule.
LMPLast menstrual period. Counted from the first day of the last period.

Ch 1: Perspectives (59)

TermMeaning
Family-centered careCare that treats childbirth as a normal, healthy family event, is individualized and respectful, keeps mother and baby together, and shares decisions between the woman and her providers.
Evidence-based practice (EBP)Using research and problem solving to set the plan of care and make clinical decisions. It is the gold standard. Also called: EBP.
Case-managed careCare built around care coordination, utilization management, and client advocacy.
Utilization managementMaking sure services used are necessary, appropriate, and cost-effective.
Client advocacyThe nurse speaks up for the client's rights, needs, and choices.
AWHONNAssociation of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses. Its core values spell CARING.
ACOGAmerican College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Maternal mortalityDeaths of women related to pregnancy, birth, or the postpartum period.
Fetal mortalityIntrauterine demise. Also called stillbirth, fetal demise, or stillborn.
Neonatal mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 28 days of life. About 4 per 1000.
Infant mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 12 months of life. About 5.8 per 1000.
MorbidityA disease state or condition (illness), as opposed to death.
Healthy People 2030National health objectives. For mother and baby it aims to cut maternal deaths, severe complications, and preterm births, and to increase early prenatal care, vaccination in pregnancy, folic acid, and effective birth control.
Low birth weight (LBW)Newborn weight under 2500 g (5 lb 8 oz).
IUGRIntrauterine growth restriction. The fetus is smaller than expected for gestational age.
MacrosomiaAn overly large newborn, usually over 4000 g. Linked to maternal obesity and diabetes.
CultureShared beliefs and practices about health and illness, language, religion and spirituality, birth and postpartum, and family and gender roles.
Health literacyThe ability to read, understand, and use health information to make decisions and navigate the system.
Informed consentVoluntary agreement after the client has been told the risks, benefits, and alternatives. A minor generally needs a parent or guardian to consent.
Emancipated minorA minor who is legally treated as an adult, for example by marriage or court order. Can consent for self.
MoralityPersonal beliefs about right and wrong. Adaptable over time.
EthicsThe disciplined study of morality, expressed through systematic norms such as the ANA Code of Ethics.
BeneficenceDoing good. Acting for the client's benefit. Also called: Do good, be of benefit.
NonmaleficenceThe duty to do no harm to the woman or the fetus. Also called: Do no harm.
FidelityEthical duty of loyalty and continuity of care, such as a complete shift handoff.
VeracityEthical duty to be truthful, including honest disclosure of risks and benefits.
AutonomyThe client's right to self-determination and to make her own decisions.
JusticeFairness. Equal and fair distribution of care and resources.
UtilitarianismThe right action gives the greatest good to the greatest number of people.
LibertarianismIndividual liberty and freedom of choice come first.
EgalitarianismResources should be shared equally.
Ethical dilemmaA choice between equally good or equally bad alternatives, or a conflict between a patient's rights and the professional's obligations.
Moral distressDistress when a nurse's beliefs conflict with what care requires. Manage with education and by telling leadership in writing ahead of time.
Negligence elementsDuty, breach, causation, damages. All four must be proven.
Statute of limitationsState-specific deadline for filing a malpractice claim.
Affordable Care Act (ACA)Federal law that expanded access to insurance and required added preventive services for women. Nurses should understand it so clients get the care they need.
Certified nurse midwife (CNM)A nurse with postgraduate training in normal pregnancy and birth, certified by the American College of Nurse Midwives.
DoulaA birth assistant who gives emotional, physical, and educational support during birth and postpartum. Not a clinician.
Cultural humilityA lifelong commitment to self-evaluation, correcting power imbalances between patient and provider, and partnership that is not paternalistic.
EnculturationThe process of learning the knowledge and values of your culture, first in the family, then school and community.
Family-centered maternity careSafe, satisfying, high-quality care that adapts to the physical and psychosocial needs of the whole family, built on trust and partnership.
Case managementAn interdisciplinary process of assessment, planning, coordination, referral, and evaluation to meet a person's needs cost-effectively.
Maternal mortality ratioDeaths from causes related to or worsened by pregnancy (not accidents), during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end, per 100,000 live births.
Perinatal mortality rateLate fetal deaths plus early neonatal deaths.
Health disparityA health difference closely linked to social, economic, and environmental disadvantage affecting groups that have faced greater obstacles to health.
Social determinants of healthConditions where people live, work, learn, and play: education, economic stability, neighborhood, health care access, and social and community context.
Managed careA system that controls cost by monitoring use of services, set fees, and emphasizing prevention.
Utilization reviewChecking whether care is medically necessary.
Continuum of careAn integrated system that follows patients over time through levels of care from hospital to home.
RADARAbuse screening: Routinely screen, Ask direct questions, Document, Assess safety, Review options and refer.
Neonatal abstinence syndromeWithdrawal in a newborn after prenatal exposure to drugs such as opioids.
Maternal-fetal conflictWhen what benefits one of the two patients may harm the other, as in a refusal of fetal therapy. Counsel, use the ethics committee, and avoid coercion.
Binuclear familyA child belongs to two families because of joint custody.
Commuter familyAdults live and work apart for job or financial reasons.
Public cord blood bankNonprofit bank that stores donated cord blood free for anyone who needs it. Preferred by ACOG and the AAP.
Utilitarian frameworkHealth care ethics that maximize collective welfare.
Libertarian frameworkHealth care ethics that emphasize individual autonomy and free markets.
Egalitarian frameworkHealth care ethics that prioritize equal access, with lifestyle taxation.
StillbirthFetal death at 20 weeks or later. Antenatal testing aims to reduce preventable stillbirths.

Ch 2: Family and Community (33)

TermMeaning
Family-centered care (Ch 2)A partnership among the individual, family, and caregivers to set goals, share information, offer support, and plan care. The family is the constant.
Informational supportGiving facts and advice.
Emotional supportCaring, empathy, trust, and listening.
Appraisal (esteem) supportFeedback and affirmation that builds self-worth.
Instrumental supportConcrete help, such as transportation, money, or child care.
CommunityPeople in a defined area who share interests, interact, and function together in a social structure. The community is the unit of service.
Community-based nursingNursing care in nontraditional settings in the community, focused on health promotion, disease prevention, and primary care. Community health and public health nursing are a subset.
Health promotionKeeping communities healthy by engaging people to choose healthy behaviors and reduce the risk of chronic disease.
Primary preventionPreventing disease before it happens: immunizations, education, environmental protection.
Secondary preventionEarly identification of people who already have disease: screening.
Tertiary preventionLimiting disease progression or disability after injury or illness: rehabilitation.
CAMComplementary and alternative medicine. Prayer is the most common form.
TelemedicineDelivering care at a distance by phone or video.
Birthing centerA home-like setting for low-risk women, close to a hospital, with midwives as the usual providers.
Case managerCoordinates referrals, services, and follow-up for the client.
Discharge planningPreparing the client and family for the transition home, including follow-up and resources.
Community health nursingNursing that prevents illness and improves the health of populations and communities, regardless of age or diagnosis. Public health nursing is a specialized area.
PopulationA group of people who share personal or environmental characteristics, most often location.
EpidemiologyThe study of the causes, distribution, and control of disease in populations.
5 As modelBehavior counseling: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange follow-up.
Complementary medicineCAM used together with conventional medicine.
Alternative medicineCAM used in place of conventional medicine.
Integrative medicineCombines mainstream medical therapies and CAM therapies that have some evidence of safety and effectiveness.
TelehealthA provider uses real-time audio and video to assess, diagnose, and treat a patient at a distance. Also called: Telemedicine.
Regionalized perinatal careA system of care levels with level III regional centers for high-risk mothers and newborns, which improves outcomes.
Birth centerA home-like facility for healthy, low-risk patients with midwives as the usual providers and obstetricians as backup. Also called: Birthing center, freestanding birth center.
MenarcheFirst menstrual period
Gestational wheelPregnancy wheel
CouvadeCouvade syndrome, sympathetic pregnancy
Fourth trimesterThe immediate postpartum period
WICFederal program run by each state that gives food, nutrition counseling, and access to health services to pregnant, postpartum, and young children from lower-income families.
Active listeningGiving full attention and showing you hear the patient. Builds trust and uncovers concerns questions can miss.
Medicaid waiverState-run program using federal and state money to pay for care for people with certain medical conditions.
CARTCommunication Access Real-time Translation. Live captioning that a Deaf patient can read on a tablet, laptop, or phone.
Competency-based educationTeaching built around identified skills, the best teaching method, how to evaluate achievement, and documented proof that learning occurred.
Teach-backAsking the patient to repeat instructions or demonstrate the skill to confirm understanding.
Social determinants of health (Ch 2)Economic, social, cultural, and political conditions in which people are born, grow, and live that affect health.

Ch 9: Violence and Abuse (26)

TermMeaning
Intimate partner violence (IPV)Actual or threatened physical or sexual violence, or psychological or emotional abuse, used to control a person. Also called: Domestic violence, domestic abuse, spouse abuse.
Cycle of violencePhase 1 tension-building, Phase 2 physically abusive (acute battering), Phase 3 reconciliation or honeymoon. It repeats and gets worse over time. Also called: Power and control wheel (as your textbook uses it).
Battered woman syndromeA pattern in which the victim rarely calls herself abused, often withdraws, and has low self-esteem.
Emotional abuseInsults, threats, humiliation, and isolation.
Physical abuseHitting, kicking, choking, or any bodily harm.
Financial abuseControlling money or access to money.
Sexual abuseForced or coerced sexual contact.
Sexual violenceAny sexual act without consent. Needs early counseling, evidence collection, STI assessment, pregnancy prevention, and PTSD assessment.
Elder abusePhysical, sexual, or emotional abuse, financial exploitation, neglect, abandonment, or self-neglect of a vulnerable elder. Healthcare workers have state reporting duties.
Human traffickingRecruitment, transport, or harboring of people by force, fraud, or coercion for exploitation. The 3 Ps: protection, prevention, prosecution.
Safety planA written plan for leaving safely: bag packed, documents, money, and a safe place to go.
PTSDPost-traumatic stress disorder. Flashbacks, sleep problems, fear, and withdrawal after trauma.
Mandatory reportingLegal duty to report certain abuse. Rules vary by state and by victim type.
Danger AssessmentA 20-item tool by Campbell that estimates risk of homicide in an abusive relationship. Used for every patient who screens positive for IPV.
SAVE modelSexual violence screening: Screen, Ask, Validate, Evaluate-Educate-Refer.
EMPOWERFramework for caring for abuse survivors: Empathetic listening, Make time to document, Provide information, Offer choices, Work with specialists, Encourage safety planning, Refer.
RADAR (Ch 9)Routinely screen, Ask direct questions, Document, Assess safety, Review options and refer.
SANESexual assault nurse examiner. A registered nurse trained to collect forensic evidence and provide crisis care after sexual assault.
Statutory rapeSexual activity between an adult and a person under 18, even if the minor was willing.
IncestSexual activity between people so closely related that marriage is prohibited. Nurses are mandated reporters when a child is involved.
RohypnolA date rape drug that dissolves without taste or color. Effects within 30 minutes with memory loss up to 8 hours. Also called: "Roofies" (street name).
GHBLiquid depressant rape drug. Acts in about 15 minutes and lasts 3 to 4 hours. Also called: "Liquid ecstasy" (street name).
FGM/CFemale genital mutilation or cutting. Any injury to external female genitalia for nonmedical reasons. WHO describes four types.
InfibulationType III FGM/C. Removal of external genitalia with stitching that narrows the vaginal opening.
Trauma-informed careTreating every patient as a possible trauma survivor. Creates safety, empowers, avoids retraumatization, and asks permission before touching.
GaslightingManipulating someone to doubt their own perceptions so the abuser regains control.

Ch 10: Fetal Development and Genetics (86)

TermMeaning
ChromosomeA strand of DNA. Humans have 46 (23 pairs).
GeneA segment of DNA.
AutosomeOne of the 22 pairs of non-sex chromosomes.
Sex chromosomesThe 23rd pair: XX is female and XY is male. The sperm decides the sex.
TrisomyThree copies of a chromosome instead of two. The most common survivable chromosomal anomaly.
Trisomy 21Down syndrome. The most prevalent trisomy.
Trisomy 18Edwards syndrome.
Trisomy 13Patau syndrome.
Turner syndromeA female with a missing or incomplete X chromosome (45,X). Also called: Monosomy X, 45,X.
Dominant traitShows up with two dominant genes, or one dominant plus one recessive.
Recessive traitShows up only with two recessive genes. A carrier has one and passes it on.
Autosomal recessiveBoth parents carry the gene. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, PKU, Tay-Sachs.
X-linkedGene on the X chromosome. Examples: hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Huntington diseaseAutosomal dominant. A single defective gene causes it. Also called: Huntington chorea.
TeratogenAnything that messes with fetal development: a substance, organism, physical agent, or deficiency that can cause abnormal structure or function during gestation.
PharmacogenomicsHow a person's genes affect the effects and side effects of drugs.
Genetic counselingThe process of advising clients about the nature and probability of an inherited disorder and the options open to them. Ideal time is before conception.
ZygoteThe fertilized egg.
MorulaThe solid ball of cells after the zygote divides.
BlastocystThe hollow ball that implants in the endometrium. Implants about day 5 to 6, with attachment completed 7 to 10 days after conception.
ImplantationAttachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium and the start of placenta formation.
Preembryonic stageFertilization through week 2.
Embryonic stageWeek 3 (15 days after conception) through week 8. All major organs form.
Fetal stageEnd of week 8 until birth.
PlacentaExchanges nutrients, gases, and wastes by diffusion, and makes hormones.
hCGHuman chorionic gonadotropin. Keeps the corpus luteum making estrogen and progesterone. What pregnancy tests detect.
hPL (hCS)Human placental lactogen. Raises maternal glucose availability for the fetus.
RelaxinRelaxes smooth muscle, ligaments, and the cervix.
Umbilical cordOne large vein and two arteries, cushioned by Wharton jelly.
Wharton jellyThe gelatinous tissue that protects the cord vessels.
Amniotic fluidCushions, warms, allows movement, and supports lung development. Made from maternal blood and fetal urine.
OligohydramniosToo little amniotic fluid. Under 500 mL at term.
Hydramnios (polyhydramnios)Too much amniotic fluid. Over 2000 mL at term. Also called: Polyhydramnios.
Ductus venosusFetal shunt from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava. Closes when the umbilical cord is clamped.
Ductus arteriosusFetal shunt from the main pulmonary artery to the aorta. Initial closure within 72 hours after birth in a term infant. Permanent closure at 3 to 4 weeks.
Foramen ovaleOpening between the right and left atria. Closes within 1 to 2 hours after birth. Permanent closure by about 6 months.
OogenesisDevelopment of the ovum in the ovary.
MittelschmerzOne-sided mid-cycle pain at ovulation. Also called: Mid-cycle ovulation pain.
FSHFollicle-stimulating hormone. Stimulates spermatogenesis in males and follicle growth in females.
LHLuteinizing hormone. Stimulates testosterone in males and triggers ovulation in females.
TestosteroneDevelops male secondary sex characteristics and supports spermatogenesis.
InfertilityInability to conceive. Causes include ovulatory dysfunction, tubal and pelvic problems, cervical mucus factors, and male factors.
ARTAssisted reproductive technology, such as IVF and donor sperm or eggs.
AlleleOne of two or more versions of a gene at a locus. One comes from each parent.
GenotypeThe specific genetic makeup, usually the DNA code a person inherits.
PhenotypeThe observed characteristics, set by genotype plus environment.
HomozygousTwo matching alleles for a trait.
HeterozygousTwo different alleles for a trait. The dominant one is usually expressed.
KaryotypeA picture of the number, form, and size of a person's chromosomes. 46,XX is a typical female and 46,XY a typical male.
GenomicsThe study of all of a person's genes and how they interact with each other and the environment.
TrophoblastOuter layer of the blastocyst that forms the chorion and helps form the placenta.
Inner cell massPart of the blastocyst that forms the embryo and amnion.
EctodermGerm layer that forms the nervous system, special senses, skin, and glands.
MesodermGerm layer that forms skeletal, urinary, circulatory, and reproductive organs.
EndodermGerm layer that forms the respiratory system, liver, pancreas, and digestive system.
Placental barrierLayers of fetal tissue that keep maternal and fetal blood from mixing. Exchange is by diffusion, and many substances pass through.
NondisjunctionFailure of a chromosome pair to separate in cell division. A cause of monosomy and trisomy.
MosaicismOnly some cells carry a chromosomal abnormality. Symptoms are usually milder.
TranslocationA piece of one chromosome moves to another. A balanced translocation carrier is usually normal but has higher miscarriage risk.
Genomic imprintingOnly the maternal or paternal allele is expressed, so the effect depends on which parent it came from.
Mitochondrial inheritancePassed from the mother to all of her children through mitochondrial DNA.
Multifactorial inheritanceCaused by many genes plus environmental factors, such as cleft lip and spina bifida.
PedigreeA family tree diagram of relationships and health information, ideally three generations. Also called: Family tree diagram.
ConsanguinityHaving a common ancestor. Raises the chance that two parents carry the same recessive gene.
GINAGenetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008. Protects against discrimination by health insurers and employers, not life, disability, or long-term care insurers.
NexplanonEtonogestrel contraceptive implant placed in the upper inner arm. Lasts 3 years. Replaced Implanon.
Depo-ProveraMedroxyprogesterone acetate contraceptive injection given every 12 to 13 weeks. Can reduce bone density.
ParaGardCopper T 380A IUD with no hormone. Lasts up to 10 years. Also the most effective emergency contraception.
MirenaLevonorgestrel IUD. Lasts up to 8 years. Liletta and Kyleena are other levonorgestrel IUDs.
NuvaRingVaginal ring with etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol. In for 3 weeks, out for 1.
Plan B One-StepLevonorgestrel 1.5 mg emergency contraception, best within 72 hours. Over the counter.
ellaUlipristal acetate emergency contraception. Effective up to 120 hours. Prescription.
Yaz and YasminCombined oral contraceptives containing drospirenone with ethinyl estradiol.
SlyndDrospirenone progestin-only pill with a 24 hour missed-pill window.
PhexxiPrescription vaginal gel that changes vaginal pH to prevent pregnancy.
CayaSilicone diaphragm used with spermicide.
Ductus arteriosus closureFunctional closure within 72 hours in a term infant and permanent closure at 3 to 4 weeks. Becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
Foramen ovale closureFunctional closure within 1 to 2 hours and permanent closure by the 6th month. Becomes the fossa ovalis.
Ductus venosus closureCloses when the cord is clamped. Becomes the ligamentum venosum.
Triple X syndrome47,XXX in females. Often mild and found incidentally. Also called trisomy X.
Jacob syndrome47,XYY in males. Also called XYY syndrome.
MenarcheA girl's first menstrual period.
Klinefelter syndrome47,XXY in males. Low testosterone and usually infertility. Also called: 47,XXY.
Corpus luteumThe ovarian structure that makes progesterone early in pregnancy until the placenta takes over. hCG keeps it working.
TORCH infectionsInfections that can cross the placenta and harm the fetus: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, Zika), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes.
AVA (cord vessels)Artery, vein, artery: the three umbilical cord vessels. The two arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus and the one vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus.

Ch 11: Maternal Adaptation (46)

TermMeaning
Presumptive signsSubjective signs the pregnant person feels or notices, such as amenorrhea, nausea, breast tenderness, fatigue, urinary frequency, and quickening. They could have other causes.
Probable signsObjective signs found on exam or by test, such as Goodell, Chadwick, and Hegar signs, ballottement, Braxton Hicks, abdominal enlargement, and a positive pregnancy test. Most likely a fetus, but they could have other causes.
Positive signsSigns that can only come from a fetus: fetal heart tones by Doppler or ultrasound, the fetus seen on ultrasound, and fetal movement felt by a trained examiner. Only these are 100% certain.
AmenorrheaAbsence of menstruation.
QuickeningThe mother first feels fetal movement. A presumptive sign at 16 to 25 weeks, often earlier in later pregnancies.
Chadwick signBluish-purple color of the cervix, vagina, and vulva from increased blood flow. Probable sign.
Goodell signSoftening of the cervix. Probable sign.
Hegar signSoftening of the lower uterine segment (isthmus). Probable sign.
BallottementThe examiner taps the cervix on pelvic exam and feels the floating fetus bounce and rebound. Probable sign at about 16 to 18 weeks.
Braxton Hicks contractionsPainless irregular contractions that tighten the uterus. Probable sign. Also called: False labor, practice contractions.
DopplerUltrasound device that picks up fetal heart tones at 10 to 12 weeks. Positive sign. Also called: Doppler ultrasound.
Linea nigraA dark vertical line from the umbilicus to the pubis caused by hormones.
Striae gravidarumStretch marks from tears in the subcutaneous tissue over areas of growth, such as the abdomen, breasts, and hips. They fade but do not fully go away. Most noticeable at 6 to 7 months. Also called: Stretch marks.
Spider neviSpider angiomas (called spider veins in class)
DyspareuniaPainful intercourse
Melasma (chloasma)The mask of pregnancy. Brown pigmentation over the cheeks and forehead, more common in darker skin and with sun exposure. Also called: Chloasma, mask of pregnancy.
LeukorrheaThin white vaginal discharge from increased estrogen. Normal.
OperculumThe mucus plug that seals the cervix.
Physiologic anemia of pregnancyHemodilution because plasma volume rises more than red cell mass. A normal adaptation that lowers hemoglobin and hematocrit.
Supine hypotension syndromeLying flat lets the uterus compress the vena cava, lowering venous return and BP. Causes dizziness. Fix with left side lying. Also called: Supine hypotension, vena cava syndrome.
PicaCraving and eating nonfood items for at least a month, such as soil or clay, ice, and laundry starch. Often linked to iron deficiency anemia, so check iron.
PtyalismExcessive saliva, up to 2 liters a day. Often resolves in the second trimester. Also called: Sialorrhea, excessive salivation.
CouvadeThe partner has pregnancy symptoms such as weight gain, nausea, and indigestion. Also called: Couvade syndrome, sympathetic pregnancy.
AmbivalenceMixed feelings about the pregnancy. Normal in the first trimester.
Rubin's maternal tasksEnsuring safe passage, securing acceptance, binding-in to the child, and learning to give of oneself.
Gestational weight gainRecommended gain depends on prepregnancy BMI. Normal BMI: 25 to 35 lb total.
LighteningThe fetal head descends and engages about 2 weeks before labor in a first pregnancy, and at labor onset in later pregnancies. Breathing eases but bladder pressure returns. Also called: Dropping.
Dietary reference intakes (DRIs)Nutrient intake goals that go beyond preventing deficiency disease.
ListeriosisInfection from Listeria in contaminated food. Pregnant women are about 10 times more likely to get it. Can cause miscarriage, preterm labor, and neonatal sepsis.
Binding inRubin's task of attaching to the baby (maternal-fetal attachment), which includes accepting herself as a parent.
ProgesteroneMaintains the pregnancy and relaxes smooth muscle and ligaments. Slows the gut, causing heartburn, bloating, and constipation.
EstrogenEnlarges the breasts, nipples, and areola, softens the vagina, and causes nasal and sinus congestion.
ProlactinStarts lactation (milk production).
OxytocinStimulates uterine contractions and helps with breastfeeding.
LordosisExaggerated inward curve of the lower spine (anterior curve of the lumbar spine). Compensates for the shifting center of gravity and raises fall risk.
Diastasis rectiSeparation of the rectus abdominis muscles from the growing uterus. Usually benign and heals on its own in about 3 to 6 months. Physical therapy, and rarely surgery, only if it does not.
Round ligament painSpasms or sharp lower abdominal pain from the round ligaments stretching and loosening as the uterus grows. Common and adds to fall risk.
Spider nevi (spider angiomas)Tiny red spider-shaped vessels on the skin from high estrogen. Shown as "spider veins" in class.
Palmar erythemaRed palms from high estrogen.
VaricositiesSwollen leg or vulvar veins from higher venous pressure. Raises the risk of edema and hemorrhoids too.
Hypercoagulable statePregnancy raises fibrinogen and clotting factors. It protects against bleeding at birth but raises the risk of blood clots.
NestingA burst of energy and an urge to prepare the home for the baby, caused by an adrenaline rush.
DyspareuniaPainful intercourse. A common first trimester discomfort.
Bloody showPink-tinged mucus or spotting as the cervix changes. A sign labor is coming soon.
Fourth trimesterThe immediate postpartum period after delivery.
TrimestersFirst: weeks 1 to 12. Second: weeks 13 to 27. Third: week 28 to birth.
True laborRegular, consistent contractions that get longer and stronger, do not ease with walking or a position change, start in the back and move forward, and change the cervix (dilation and effacement).
Pelvic precautionsNothing in the vagina, including sex, for clients at risk of preterm labor.

Ch 12: Nursing Management (44)

TermMeaning
Preconception careCare to promote health before pregnancy and to find and change risks to the woman or the pregnancy outcome.
Folic acidVitamin B9. Prevents neural tube defects. Start before conception.
Nagele's ruleEstimates the due date: first day of the LMP, minus 3 months, plus 7 days, plus 1 year. Less reliable with irregular or long cycles or an unsure LMP, so use ultrasound then.
Fundal heightMeasured from the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterus in cm. Matches weeks of gestation from 20 to 36 weeks, give or take 2 cm.
Fetal kick countsThe mother counts fetal movements. At least 5 kicks in 1 hour (or 10 in 2 hours) is reassuring. If not reached, try a cold drink and recount, then call the provider. Also called: Count to 10.
PelvimetryMeasurement of the bony pelvis to judge if the fetus can pass.
Quad screenMaternal blood test at 15 to 22 weeks that checks hormone levels, mainly AFP, to screen for neural tube defects and chromosomal anomalies. Also called: Multiple marker screen.
Glucose challenge testScreens for gestational diabetes at 24 to 28 weeks.
GBS cultureGroup B strep vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks for all pregnant women. It is not an STI. If positive, penicillin in labor protects the newborn from sepsis.
TdapTetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine. Given each pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks.
Live vaccinesMMR and varicella. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
Childbirth educationClasses such as Lamaze or Bradley that prepare the woman and partner for labor.
DoulaA layperson who gives continuous emotional and physical support in labor. Does no clinical procedures.
Certified nurse-midwifeAn advanced practice nurse who can care for low-risk pregnancy and birth.
Danger signs of pregnancyVaginal bleeding, severe headache, visual changes, severe abdominal pain, gush of fluid, decreased fetal movement, persistent vomiting, fever, burning with urination, sudden facial or hand swelling, calf pain.
Interconception careCare between pregnancies to improve health, especially after a poor outcome.
Reproductive life planA personal plan for whether and when to have children.
Gravida and paraGravida is the number of pregnancies. Para is the number of births at 20 weeks or more.
CenteringPregnancyGroup prenatal care for about 12 people at the same stage of pregnancy over 10 sessions.
McDonald methodMeasuring fundal height in centimeters from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the fundus.
Nonstress test (NST)Noninvasive test from 32 weeks. Reactive means two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Also called: NST.
Biophysical profile (BPP)Ultrasound scoring of five parts, 0 or 2 points each: body movement (3 or more), tone, breathing movement, amniotic fluid, and a reactive NST. 8 to 10 normal, 4 to 6 abnormal, under 4 strongly abnormal. Also called: BPP.
AmniocentesisInvasive diagnostic test at 15 to 20 weeks. Rh negative clients get anti-D immune globulin.
Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)Invasive placental biopsy at 10 to 13 weeks.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)Maternal serum screen at 16 to 18 weeks. High with neural tube defects, low with trisomy 21 or 18. Also called: AFP. In maternal blood: MSAFP.
Nuchal translucencyUltrasound at 11 to 14 weeks. Increased fluid at the neck suggests trisomies and heart defects. Also called: NT scan.
Quad screenMultiple marker screen
Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS)Cordocentesis, percutaneous umbilical cord blood sampling
Contraction stress testCST
Amniotic fluid indexAFI
Lamaze methodPsychoprophylactic method using breathing and relaxation.
Bradley methodPartner-coached childbirth with slow abdominal breathing.
Dick-Read methodNatural childbirth that breaks the fear-tension-pain cycle.
HypnoBirthingDick-Read plus self-hypnosis.
Screening testIdentifies those who are not affected by a disease. Many are offered to all pregnant women. Example: ultrasound.
Diagnostic testIdentifies a disease or problem and helps make the diagnosis. Often invasive and reserved for high risk pregnancies. Examples: amniocentesis, MRI.
Genetic testsDetect health problems and help parents make fully informed decisions about the pregnancy.
UltrasoundNoninvasive imaging with very little risk. First trimester: confirms pregnancy and gestational age, often transvaginal. Second trimester: anatomy scan. An abdominal scan early on needs a full bladder.
Doppler flow studiesMeasure the speed of red blood cells moving to the uterus. Useful for growth restriction and placental perfusion. Not the best test for fetal compromise.
MRIUsed to see the placenta, brain anomalies, and complicated defects. No known harm. No metal, and use a left lateral tilt so she does not lie flat.
Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS)Blood is removed from the umbilical cord at about 18 weeks or later to look for metabolic and hematologic disorders. Highest fetal loss rate of the three biochemical procedures. Also called: Cordocentesis.
Maternal assay (cell-free fetal DNA)The mother's blood is tested for fetal DNA. It can show fetal sex as early as 9 to 10 weeks and screen for some anomalies.
Contraction stress test (CST)Checks how the fetus handles contractions, for about 20 minutes. It needs contractions and must be done where a baby can be delivered.
Nipple stimulation testStimulating the nipples releases oxytocin and can start the contractions needed for a contraction stress test. Not always successful.
Vibroacoustic stimulationVibration and sound used to wake the fetus during a nonstress test.
Amniotic fluid index (AFI)Ultrasound measure of amniotic fluid volume.
Antenatal fetal surveillanceTesting while the mother is still pregnant to check fetal well-being: kick counts, NST, CST, and BPP. It aims to reduce preventable stillbirths and avoid unneeded interventions.
Gestational wheelA wheel that gives the due date: line up the first day of the last menstrual period and read the EDB. Also called: Pregnancy wheel.

🧮 OB Basics: G, Para, GTPAL

The language every OB chart, history, and exam uses. Learn it once, use it everywhere.

🧠 The big idea

Count pregnancies, then sort how each one ended.
Each pregnancy adds 1 to G → Reached 20 weeks? → Yes: T or P (this is Para) → No: A → L counts living children

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Twins or triplets are ONE pregnancy. Only L counts babies.
  2. 20 weeks is the line. Reached it: Para (T or P). Did not: A.
  3. A stillbirth after 20 weeks still counts under Para, and L stays 0.
  4. Short form: G and Para, where Para = T + P.
  5. Always count the CURRENT pregnancy in G.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Baby count vs pregnancy countTriplets in her first pregnancy is G1 Para 1, not Para 3. The only letter that counts babies is L.
⚠️ Ectopic pregnancyIt is a pregnancy loss before 20 weeks, so it counts in A, not in Para.
🩺 Think like a nurseRead the history one PREGNANCY at a time. For each one write down: weeks reached, how it ended, and how many children are alive now.

This was covered first in class. It shows up again in every chart, history, and exam.

🧮 The words

TermMeaning
GravidaA woman who is pregnant
GravidityThe number of pregnancies, including the current one
NulligravidaNever pregnant
PrimigravidaPregnant for the first time
MultigravidaTwo or more pregnancies
NulliparaPregnant but never carried a fetus past 20 weeks
PrimiparaCompleted one pregnancy to 20 weeks or more
MultiparaCompleted two or more pregnancies to 20 weeks or more
🧠 Memory anchor
GRAVID means "heavy with pregnancy" so it counts pregnancies. PARA means "to bear" so it counts deliveries past 20 weeks.
⚠️ TrapParity counts pregnancies, not babies. Twins or triplets from one pregnancy are still parity 1. Live birth or stillbirth does not change it.

🧮 GTPAL: everything under Para

G is gravidity. Para is broken down into T, P, A, and L. Gravidity counts pregnancies. Everything under Para is about how those pregnancies ended and who is living.

LetterStands forWhat it countsTwins or triplets
GGravidityAll pregnancies, including the current oneOne pregnancy, so G adds 1
ParaParityPregnancies that reached 20 weeks or more, whether the baby was born alive or notOne pregnancy, so Para adds 1
TTermPregnancies delivered at term (see the warning below)One pregnancy, so T adds 1
PPretermPregnancies delivered from 20 weeks to before 37 weeksOne pregnancy, so P adds 1
AAbortionsPregnancies lost before 20 weeks: miscarriage (spontaneous), elective, and ectopicOne pregnancy, so A adds 1
LLivingThe number of living CHILDREN right nowCounts each baby, so twins add 2 and triplets add 3
⭐ High yieldOnly L counts babies. G, Para, T, P, and A all count pregnancies. Triplets from a first pregnancy are still G1 Para 1.
⚠️ TrapTwo ways to write it. The short form is two numbers: G and Para, for example G3 P2. In the short form Para equals T plus P (the pregnancies that reached 20 weeks). The long form GTPAL spells out the breakdown, for example G3 T1 P1 A1 L2. Abortions are pregnancies under 20 weeks, so they are not added into the Para number in the short form.
⚠️ TrapTerm and preterm. Term runs from the beginning of week 37 through the end of week 42. Preterm is 20 weeks to before 37 weeks complete. A birth at exactly 37 weeks counts as term (T). A birth at 36 weeks 6 days counts as preterm (P).
🧠 Memory anchor
G is every pregnancy. Then T, P, A, L: Term, Preterm, Abortions, Living. T and P are pregnancies past 20 weeks, A is losses under 20 weeks, and L is the children alive right now.
🔍 Go deeper: Pregnancy timing labels and risk

Trimesters: first is conception to the end of week 13, second is week 14 to the end of week 27, third is week 28 to birth.

LabelGestational age
Preterm20 weeks to before 37 weeks
Term37 weeks through 42 weeks
PosttermAfter 42 weeks
  • Viability: roughly 23 to 24 weeks with intensive support. Parity still uses 20 weeks.
  • Grand multipara: five or more births past 20 weeks. Higher risk of hemorrhage from uterine atony, precipitous labor, and malpresentation.
  • Adolescent and advanced maternal age (35 or older) are risk categories you will see on a history.
  • Documenting: some charts write G P with a TPAL in parentheses, for example G3 P2 (1-1-1-2).

✏️ Examples, built step by step

SituationShort formGTPAL
Pregnant for the first time, nothing delivered yetG1 P0G1 T0 P0 A0 L0
First pregnancy delivered a healthy baby at 39 weeksG1 P1G1 T1 P0 A0 L1
First pregnancy, healthy premature baby at 33 weeks, baby aliveG1 P1G1 T0 P1 A0 L1
Triplets delivered at 38 weeks in her first pregnancy, all livingG1 P1G1 T1 P0 A0 L3
Twins at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy, both livingG1 P1G1 T0 P1 A0 L2
Miscarriage at 8 weeks, not pregnant nowG1 P0G1 T0 P0 A1 L0
Stillbirth at 28 weeks (it reached 20 weeks, so it counts as preterm)G1 P1G1 T0 P1 A0 L0
Currently pregnant with her 2nd pregnancy. First was a term baby, livingG2 P1G2 T1 P0 A0 L1
⭐ High yieldStillbirth still counts under Para. Parity does not care if the baby was born alive. It only asks whether the pregnancy reached 20 weeks. L is what drops.

📚 Class practice problem, worked

A 28 year old is at her first prenatal visit. One full-term vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. Twins delivered at 34 weeks. One miscarriage at 10 weeks. One ectopic pregnancy at 8 weeks. Two living children. She is now pregnant.

StepWork
GTerm pregnancy + twin pregnancy + miscarriage + ectopic + current pregnancy = 5
T1 (the 39 week delivery)
P1 (the twin pregnancy at 34 weeks is ONE pregnancy)
A2 (miscarriage and ectopic)
L2, as the stem states. That history produced three babies, so one child is not living. Use the number the question gives
⭐ High yieldAnswer: G5 T1 P1 A2 L2, with Para (short form) = 2. Check yourself: T plus P = 1 + 1 = 2.
💡 Good to knowQuick check for any problem: (1) Count every pregnancy for G. (2) Sort each past pregnancy into T, P, or A by weeks. (3) Add T + P to get the short form Para. (4) L is the living children, counted one by one.

🎯 Instructor practice: GTPAL activity (10 cases)

Her activity sheet. Try each case in your head, then tap to check. Remember: current pregnancy counts in G only, twins are one pregnancy and one birth, L counts each living child, and any loss before 20 weeks is an A.

Case 1: Maria, 24, first pregnancy, now 10 weeks. No miscarriage or births.

G1 T0 P0 A0 L0

The current pregnancy counts in G. Nothing has been delivered or lost yet, so T, P, A and L are all 0.

Case 2: 27-year-old. One earlier pregnancy: daughter born at 39 weeks, living. Not pregnant now.

G1 T1 P0 A0 L1

39 weeks is term. She is not pregnant now, so only the past pregnancy is counted.

Case 3: 30-year-old. Two pregnancies: boy at 40 weeks (living) and a miscarriage at 9 weeks. Not pregnant now.

G2 T1 P0 A1 L1

A loss before 20 weeks is an abortion (A), including a spontaneous miscarriage.

Case 4: 32-year-old. Three pregnancies: 38 weeks (living), 34 weeks (living), miscarriage at 11 weeks. Not pregnant now.

G3 T1 P1 A1 L2

38 weeks is term. 34 weeks is preterm. The 11-week loss is an A.

Case 5: 29-year-old, 16 weeks pregnant now. Earlier: daughter at 39 weeks (living) and a miscarriage at 10 weeks. This is her third pregnancy.

G3 T1 P0 A1 L1

The current pregnancy adds to G only. It is not a T, P or A until the outcome is known.

Case 6: 35-year-old. Four pregnancies: 38 weeks, 32 weeks, 36 weeks (all living) and a miscarriage at 8 weeks. Not pregnant now.

G4 T1 P2 A1 L3

Only the 38-week birth is term. Both 32 and 36 weeks are before 37 weeks, so they are preterm.

Case 7: 31-year-old. Three pregnancies: twins at 38 weeks (both living), miscarriage at 12 weeks, one baby at 39 weeks (living). Not pregnant now.

G3 T2 P0 A1 L3

Twins are one pregnancy and one term birth, so G and T count once. L counts each living child, so 3.

Case 8: 36-year-old. Three pregnancies: 39 weeks (living), 38 weeks (died shortly after birth), miscarriage at 14 weeks. Not pregnant now.

G3 T2 P0 A1 L1

A baby born alive at term still counts as a T birth even if the baby later dies. Only L drops, to 1.

Case 9: 33-year-old, currently pregnant for the 6th time. Earlier: miscarriage at 9 weeks, girl at 38 weeks, twins at 36 weeks, boy at 39 weeks, miscarriage at 14 weeks. All babies living.

G6 T2 P1 A2 L4

G counts the current pregnancy. Term births: 38 and 39 weeks. The twin birth at 36 weeks is one P. Living children: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.

Case 10: 35-year-old, currently pregnant for the 7th time. Earlier: 41 weeks, miscarriage at 10 weeks, twins at 35 weeks, 39 weeks, miscarriage at 16 weeks, 33 weeks. All babies living.

G7 T2 P2 A2 L5

41 weeks is still term (through week 42). The twins at 35 weeks and the baby at 33 weeks are two preterm births. Living children: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5.

📅 Instructor practice: Naegele's rule (5 cases)

Naegele's rule (also spelled Nagele's): first day of the LMP, minus 3 months, plus 7 days, plus 1 year. It is an estimate, and less accurate with irregular cycles or cycles longer than 28 days. Ultrasound in the first trimester is the most accurate dating tool.

Case 1: LMP January 12, 2026

EDD: October 19, 2026

Jan 12, 2026 minus 3 months = Oct 12, 2025. Add 7 days = Oct 19, 2025. Add 1 year.

Case 2: LMP March 5, 2026

EDD: December 12, 2026

Mar 5 minus 3 months = Dec 5, 2025. Add 7 days = Dec 12, 2025. Add 1 year.

Case 3: LMP June 18, 2026

EDD: March 25, 2027

Jun 18 minus 3 months = Mar 18. Add 7 days = Mar 25. Add 1 year.

Case 4: LMP December 20, 2026

EDD: September 27, 2027

Dec 20 minus 3 months = Sep 20. Add 7 days = Sep 27. Add 1 year.

Case 5: LMP August 25, 2026

EDD: June 1, 2027

Aug 25 minus 3 months = May 25. Add 7 days = Jun 1 (May has 31 days, so the 7 days cross into June). Add 1 year.

LMPEDD
January 12, 2026October 19, 2026
March 5, 2026December 12, 2026
June 18, 2026March 25, 2027
December 20, 2026September 27, 2027
August 25, 2026June 1, 2027

🔗 Related terms

  • EDB (EDD): expected date of birth, found in Ch 12 with Nagele's rule.
  • Viability: the point the fetus can survive outside the womb, roughly 23 to 24 weeks with support.
