📈 Ch 1: Perspectives on Maternal, Newborn, and Women's Health Care

Why mothers and babies die, what nurses can do about it, and the ethics and law behind care.

🧠 The big idea

Most pregnancy deaths are preventable, so nurses push care EARLY.
Early prenatal care → Problems found while treatable → Fewer maternal and infant deaths

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Top causes of maternal death: H.I.P.C.A. (Hemorrhage, Infection, Preeclampsia and eclampsia, Cardiovascular disease, Abortion complications).
  2. Neonatal death is the first 28 days. Infant death is the first 12 months.
  3. Best single action to lower mortality: early and adequate prenatal care.
  4. Nonmaleficence means do no harm. Beneficence means do good. Veracity means tell the truth.
  5. Failure to communicate causes most malpractice suits against nurses.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Which prevention answer?When a question lists several good ideas, pick the broadest and earliest one. Prenatal care beats a diet class or a shelter referral.
⚠️ Culture conflictNever coerce, threaten, or hold a client. Explain, respect, and document.
⚠️ Who consents?Married, emancipated, and adult clients consent for themselves. A 15 year old high school student does not.
🩺 Think like a nurseWhen a question feels like an ethics puzzle, name the principle first (do good, do no harm, truth, promise, choice, fairness), then pick the action that protects the client without forcing her.

🧩 1. Three core concepts

ConceptWhat to know
Family-centered careChildbirth is a normal, healthy family event. Care is individualized and respectful. Birth changes relationships for the whole family. Mothers and newborns stay together. Decisions are shared between the woman and her providers.
Evidence-based practiceUse research to set and carry out the plan of care. Use a problem-solving approach for clinical decisions. Use resources to collect, interpret, integrate, and validate research evidence. It is the gold standard.
Case-managed careThree parts: care coordination, utilization management, client advocacy.

Case manager example: connects a pregnant or postpartum client with WIC, transportation, a home visit nurse, insurance help, and mental health follow-up.

Professional organizations in OB: ANA (American Nurses Association), NLN (National League for Nursing), AWHONN (Association of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses), ACOG (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists).

🔍 Go deeper: Family-centered care, case management, and EBP steps
Family-centered maternity care in practiceWhat the nurse does
Mother and baby stay togetherRooming-in, skin-to-skin, couplet care
Support persons welcomePartner, doula, siblings, grandparents per policy
Choices respectedReview the birth plan, offer options, explain risks
Teaching starts earlyFeeding, safe sleep, newborn care, danger signs for mother and baby

Case manager resources: WIC, Medicaid, Healthy Start, home visiting programs such as Nurse-Family Partnership, lactation support, transportation, and mental health referral.

EBP stepOB example
Ask a focused question (PICOT)In pregnant women, does left side lying versus supine improve fetal oxygenation?
Acquire the best evidenceSearch guidelines, systematic reviews, ACOG, AWHONN
Appraise itIs it valid, important, and applicable to this client?
Apply it with clinical judgment and client preferenceTeach left side lying
Assess the outcomeDid she tolerate it? Did the outcome improve?

Strongest evidence to weakest: systematic review of randomized trials, randomized trial, cohort study, case series, expert opinion. Barriers: time, lack of skill finding research, resistance to change. Strategies: journal clubs, unit champions, protocols, and leadership support.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: family-centered care, EBP, and case management

Textbook principles of family-centered maternity care:

  • Childbirth is a normal, healthy event that affects the whole family.
  • Care is individualized and respectful.
  • Continuous support during labor benefits the patient and family.
  • Decisions are made together by the patient and providers.
  • Education is based on current, evidence-based knowledge.
  • Birthing parents and newborns stay together with skin-to-skin contact.
  • Family is the constant. Nurses shift from an authoritarian role to an empowering one, honor the birth plan, and build on family strengths.
  • Models of care: LDR (labor, delivery, recovery) and LDRP (adds postpartum) rooms keep families together and protect breastfeeding.
  • Inclusive care: care must also respect LGBTQ+ families. Transgender patients often face discrimination, so support them without judgment.

Evidence-based practice (textbook): a problem-solving approach to clinical decisions based on the most current research, internal evidence from outcome and process improvement data, and patient preferences. It involves collecting, interpreting, and integrating validated evidence. It reduces variation in care and raises quality. AWHONN, ANA, and NLN publish evidence-based guidelines.

Evidence example (Box 1.1)A study of continuous labor support found that people with a birth companion reported lower pain. Nursing use: teach clients the value of a support person and advocate for support persons in the unit.

Case management (textbook): an interdisciplinary, collaborative process of assessment, planning, coordination of services, referral, and evaluation of options in a cost-effective way. Results: fewer complications, better outcomes, lower costs, higher patient and family satisfaction, and less fragmented care. The nurse helps families navigate the system.

📉 2. Mortality and morbidity numbers

MeasureKey facts from your slides
Maternal mortality2 to 3 US women die every day from pregnancy complications. 700 to 900 per year. More than 30% of pregnant women have some illness or injury during childbirth. US ranks 47th. 60% of pregnancy-related complications are preventable.
Fetal mortalityIntrauterine demise: stillbirth, fetal demise, stillborn. Much is still unknown.
Neonatal mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 28 days of life. About 4 per 1000.
Infant mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 12 months of life. About 5.8 per 1000.
MorbidityA disease state or condition, not death.

Top five causes of pregnancy-related maternal death (slide)

  1. Postpartum hemorrhage
  2. Postpartum infection
  3. Preeclampsia and eclampsia
  4. Cardiovascular diseases
  5. Abortion complications
🧠 Memory anchor: H.I.P.C.A.
Hemorrhage, Infection, Preeclampsia and eclampsia, Cardiovascular disease, Abortion complications.
🔍 Go deeper: Definitions, causes, and disparities
TermMeaning
Maternal mortality ratioMaternal deaths per 100,000 live births
Pregnancy-related deathDeath during pregnancy or within 1 year of the end of pregnancy from a cause related to pregnancy
Severe maternal morbidityUnexpected outcomes of labor and birth that cause serious short or long term harm
Stillbirth (fetal death)Death of a fetus at 20 weeks or more before birth
Neonatal mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 28 days of life
Infant mortalityDeath of an infant in the first 12 months of life

Leading causes of infant death (CDC list): birth defects, preterm birth and low birth weight, SIDS, unintentional injury, and maternal pregnancy complications.

Disparities: Black women have maternal death rates more than double those of White women, and Black infants have higher infant death rates. Contributors include access to care, insurance, chronic disease, bias in care, and social conditions. Nurses reduce this by listening, taking symptoms seriously, and escalating early.

Why the US ranks low: uneven access to prenatal care, gaps in insurance coverage, rising chronic disease in pregnancy, disparities, and limited preventive focus (your slide list above).

🔍 Go deeper: Definitions, risk factors, and causes
TermTextbook definition
MortalityNumber of deaths over a period, reported as rates per 100,000. Used as an indicator of national health
Maternal mortality ratioFemale deaths from any cause related to or worsened by pregnancy or its management (not accidents or incidental causes) during pregnancy and birth or within 42 days of ending the pregnancy, per 100,000 live births
Fetal mortality (fetal death, demise, stillbirth)Intrauterine death with no signs of life. After 20 weeks it is a stillbirth. Before 20 weeks it is a spontaneous abortion
Neonatal mortality rateInfant deaths in the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births
Perinatal mortality rateLate fetal deaths plus early neonatal deaths
Infant mortality rateDeaths in the first 12 months per 1,000 live births. Includes neonatal and post-neonatal (the remaining 11 months)
MorbidityAny physical or mental diseased state or condition. The prevalence of an illness in a population, in rates per 1,000
  • Risk factors for higher maternal mortality: Black race (more than double the rate of non-Hispanic White and Hispanic people, linked to social and structural factors and not biology), older maternal age, high BMI, and comorbidities. Lack of prenatal care is a major factor.
  • Perinatal and neonatal risk factors: prematurity, postterm, congenital malformations, multiple gestation, and Black ethnicity.
  • Other contributors to maternal death: mental health conditions, thromboembolism, and cardiomyopathy, in addition to H.I.P.C.A. (hemorrhage, infection, preeclampsia and eclampsia, cardiovascular disease, abortion complications).
  • Main causes of early infant death: congenital malformations, short gestation, low birth weight, sudden unexplained infant death (SUID), unintentional injuries, and maternal complications of pregnancy.
  • Ways to lower infant death: breastfeeding (fewer infections), back to sleep and no bed sharing to lower SUID, and support groups for postpartum depression and parenting.
  • Preterm birth: peaked in 2006, declined, then rose again, hitting an all-time high in 2021.

📉 3. Best ways to lower maternal and fetal mortality

⭐ High yieldThe best way to reduce maternal and fetal mortality: early and adequate prenatal care. It is the evidence-based answer because it finds hypertension, diabetes, infection, and growth problems while they can still be treated. The other measures below support it.
  • Early and adequate prenatal care (the answer to the class slide question)
  • Prevent smoking and alcohol use
  • Prevent drug use and unnecessary prescriptions
  • Adequate nutrition and exercise

Gaps that raise morbidity (slide)

  • No state has focused enough on preventive measures.
  • Too many people lack health insurance.
  • No state has adequately addressed reproductive health and violence against females.
  • Little research on conditions that mainly affect females or affect them differently.

🌍 4. Factors that affect health

Genetics, sex, race, society, socioeconomic status and poverty (it does affect health: TRUE on the class slide), media and social media, homelessness, violence.

Healthy People 2030 maternal and infant goals

  • Lower maternal deaths, severe complications, and preterm births
  • More early and adequate prenatal care and vaccination during pregnancy
  • Lower mother-to-child transmission of disease
  • Address substance use in pregnancy and promote effective birth control to cut unintended pregnancy
  • Support prepregnancy weight management and folic acid in women of reproductive age
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: family structures and changing roles (Table 1.1)
Family typeDescriptionNursing point
NuclearHusband, wife, and children in one household, natural or adoptedOnce the traditional norm, now less common
BinuclearA child belongs to two families because of joint custodyWorks best when the child's interests come first
Single-parentOne parent cares for the children. Divorce, death, desertion, birth outside marriage, or adoptionEconomic, social, and personal strain
CommuterAdults live and work apart for job or money reasonsSimilar to single-parent
Step or blendedAdults with children from earlier or new marriagesConflict over expectations and child care views
ExtendedNuclear family plus grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousinsIdentify the decision maker and main caregiver. Common in some cultures
LGBTQ+Same-sex adults with or without childrenMay face negative attitudes. Children often show resilience
CommunalUnrelated people raising children togetherFind the decision maker and caregiver
FosterTemporary family for children placed away from parentsHigher unmet health needs and chronic problems
Grandparents as parentsGrandparents raise grandchildrenPhysical, financial, and emotional strain on older adults
AdolescentYoung parents still doing their own developmental tasksHigher risk of problems in pregnancy and preterm infants. Need family support
  • Definition (US Census): a group of two or more people related by birth, marriage, or adoption and living together. Some say family is whatever the child says it is.
  • Roles have changed: both parents are often providers and nurturers. About 27% of children live with one parent.
  • Nursing practice: stay open-minded, invite both parents, learn their names, direct questions to them, and offer support to nonbirthing parents too.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: genetics, sex, and race
  • Sex is set when the sex chromosomes join. XX is female, XY is male. Premature females have higher survival than premature males.
  • Intersex means natural variation in chromosomes, reproductive organs, or sex traits that do not fit typical male or female. Any treatment is the person's own choice.
  • Race refers to physical features. A normal finding in one group can look like a disorder in another. Example: epicanthic folds are normal in children of Asian descent but may signal Down syndrome or renal agenesis in other children.
  • Disease patterns: sickle cell anemia is more common in Black and Mediterranean groups. Tay-Sachs is more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish or French-Canadian descent. Either can occur in any group.
  • Preconception genetic counseling can include preimplantation genetic diagnosis, which uses IVF to test embryos before transfer (for example, BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations).
  • Precision health uses a patient's genomic information to guide care.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: social determinants, poverty, homelessness, and global health
Social determinants of health (Healthy People 2030)Examples
Education access and qualityLiteracy, school completion
Economic stabilityIncome, employment, poverty
Neighborhood and built environmentHousing, safe streets, clean water, lead paint
Health care access and qualityInsurance, providers, transportation
Social and community contextSupport, discrimination, violence
  • Low socioeconomic status can mean no insurance, irregular meals, crowded or unsafe housing, missed preventive care, and more depression, behavior problems, substance misuse, and injuries in children. Poverty is preventable.
  • Poverty and women: women lag behind men in cash, credit, and collateral. Nurses help by teaching, advocating for equal pay, and supporting community participation.
  • Homelessness: linked to mental health problems, chronic illness, injury, premature death, poorer birth outcomes, nutritional deficiency affecting fetal growth, limited prenatal care, and violence.
  • Global women's health: a woman dies about every 2 minutes from pregnancy or childbirth, mostly in developing countries. Major direct causes there: hemorrhage, sepsis, gestational hypertension, delivery complications, and unsafe abortion. In the US: mental health conditions, hemorrhage, cardiac conditions, thrombotic embolism, and cardiomyopathy.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: violence against women, RADAR, and the other factors
  • UN definition: any act of gender-based violence that results in physical, sexual, or mental harm, including threats, coercion, or arbitrary deprivation of liberty. One in three women worldwide reports physical or sexual violence. A woman is killed by a partner or family member about every 11 minutes.
  • Pregnancy is often when abuse starts or escalates. Nurses are often the first health care provider an injured victim sees. Support her strengths. Do not try to rescue her.
RADARMeaning
RRoutinely screen every patient for abuse
AAsk direct questions
DDocument your findings
AAssess safety before she leaves
RReview options and make referrals
  • Lifestyle: eating, exercise, tobacco, drugs, alcohol, and coping. Most health problems today relate to lifestyle.
  • Environmental exposure: air pollution, smoking, and toxins harm the developing fetus. Agents that harm development are teratogens.
  • Stress: disasters, violence, finances, and weak support can lead to low birth weight, preterm birth, and hypertension.
  • Nutrition: iron deficiency anemia and obesity are common. Folic acid prevents neural tube defects.

📈 4b. Healthy People 2030 as it relates to mother and baby

Healthy People 2030 is the national set of health objectives. For mother and baby it aims to improve maternal and infant health. Nurses use it as evidence for setting goals in the Planning step of ADPIE, and community-based nursing uses it as the national guide.

Goal area (from your slides)What it targetsWhat the nurse does
Fewer deaths and complicationsReduce maternal deaths, severe complications, and preterm birthsScreen at every visit and report danger signs early
Prenatal careIncrease early and adequate prenatal careGet every client into care in the first trimester
Vaccination and infectionMore vaccination during pregnancy. Less mother-to-child transmission of diseaseTeach inactivated flu and Tdap, screen for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis
Substance useAddress substance use during pregnancyScreen without judgment, refer, teach teratogens
Family planningPromote effective birth control to reduce unintended pregnancyContraception teaching and preconception counseling
Weight and folic acidPre-pregnancy weight management and folic acid in women of reproductive ageTeach folic acid 400 mcg before conception and healthy weight goals
⭐ High yieldLink it to your framework. Healthy People 2030 is the evidence behind the goals you write in Planning. Early prenatal care, folic acid, and vaccination are the answers it keeps pointing to.

⚠️ 5. Special issues, with the numbers

IssueFacts
Teen pregnancyUS rate fell from 1990 to 2016 (about 21 births per 1000 ages 15 to 19). Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black rates are almost double the non-Hispanic White rate. Poverty is linked. Risks: STIs, hypertension, preterm infants, LBW. About 50% of teen mothers graduate high school and few finish college.
Tobacco and e-cigarettesSmoking causes LBW, IUGR, miscarriage, abruptio placentae, preterm birth, SIDS, and respiratory illness. Nicotine impairs fetal brain and lung development. E-cigarettes are unregulated and contain carcinogens.
Alcohol14% report use during pregnancy.
Illegal drugs5% report use during pregnancy.
Prescription and OTC drugs9 out of 10 pregnant women use one.
Overweight and obesityMother: higher risk of diabetes and cesarean birth. Infant: higher risk of fetal death and macrosomia.
Violence1 in 6 pregnant women has IPV before or during pregnancy. 1 in 5 adolescents has dating violence. 1 in 10 older women has elder abuse. 83% of women with disabilities are sexually assaulted in their lifetime. Screen ALL women for IPV.
Perinatal mood disorders1 in 7 women has postpartum depression. 13 to 21% have perinatal anxiety. 20% of postpartum deaths are from suicide.
STIsReportable STIs rose 30% from 2015 to 2019. Congenital syphilis quadrupled. HPV may raise the risk of preterm birth.
🔍 Go deeper: Counseling frameworks and infections in pregnancy
TopicFramework or key detail
TobaccoThe 5 A's: Ask, Advise, Assess readiness, Assist, Arrange follow-up. Quitting at any point helps
AlcoholNo known safe amount. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders cause growth restriction, facial changes, and learning and behavior problems
Substance use screeningSBIRT: Screening, Brief intervention, Referral to treatment. 4Ps for pregnancy (Parents, Partner, Past, Present). CRAFFT for teens. Nonjudgmental and universal
Opioid useMedication-assisted treatment is preferred over detox in pregnancy. The newborn may have withdrawal (neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome)
Perinatal mood disordersScreen with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or PHQ-9. Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm. 988 is the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
ObesityAlso raises risk of preeclampsia, neural tube defects, and difficult birth. Counsel on weight goals before and during pregnancy
Infection in pregnancyNewborn risk and nursing point
SyphilisCongenital syphilis. Screen at the first visit. Penicillin treats it
ChlamydiaNeonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia. Screen and treat
GonorrheaOphthalmia neonatorum. Newborn eye prophylaxis
HIVAntiretrovirals in pregnancy sharply lower transmission. Screen every pregnancy
Hepatitis BNewborn gets hepatitis B vaccine, and immune globulin if the mother is positive
Group B strepSwab at 35 to 37 weeks. Antibiotics in labor protect the newborn

🌎 6. Culture and barriers

Culture covers: health and illness beliefs, communication and language, religion and spirituality, birth and postpartum beliefs, and family and gender roles.

Barriers: finances, transportation, language and culture, the healthcare delivery system, and health literacy.

⭐ High yieldCultural conflict rule. Client refuses treatment for cultural reasons: explain why the treatment is important and respect her. Never coerce, threaten arrest for neglect, or refuse to let her leave.
Case: Cherokee in labor

Her culture shows in: a sixth child, no insurance, home birth is usual, family dance to scare away evil spirits, refuses an epidural, 20 family members present, discards colostrum, and a family celebration after birth.

Culturally sensitive nursing: ask about her wishes, make space for family within safety limits, offer pain options without pressure, explain the benefit of colostrum without judgment, treat the high blood pressure with her beliefs in mind, and involve the family.

Case: the 17 year old migrant worker

The receptionist focused on insurance and the Social Security number, asked personal questions, and ignored her for an hour. She left without care. Barriers shown: language, finances, stigma, health system. Nurses fix this with interpreters, welcoming first contact, and early prenatal care for everyone.

🔍 Go deeper: Cultural humility, interpreters, and teaching
  • Cultural humility means staying curious and learning from each client. It goes beyond memorizing facts about groups.
  • LEARN model: Listen, Explain your view, Acknowledge differences, Recommend, Negotiate a plan.
  • Interpreters: use a qualified medical interpreter, in person, by phone, or by video. Do not use children or family. Face and speak to the client, not the interpreter. Use short sentences.
  • Examples of beliefs to ask about: hot and cold foods after birth, rest or confinement periods, placenta and cord customs, modesty, and who may be present. Accommodate unless it harms mother or baby.
  • Health literacy: plain language, small chunks, pictures, and teach-back.
Nursing processAssess beliefs (Assessment), name the conflict (Diagnosis), set goals with her (Planning), adapt care (Implementation), ask if it worked for her (Evaluation).
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: culture, cultural humility, and Table 1.2
  • Culture: a view of the world and set of traditions shared by a group and passed to the next generation. It includes beliefs, values, language, time, personal space, and worldview. People learn it through enculturation, first in the family, then school and community.
  • Cultural humility: a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation, to correcting power imbalances between patient and provider, and to partnerships that are not paternalistic. Combine cultural respect with humility, self-reflection on bias, and willingness to learn from the patient.
  • Goal: see culture as a point of congruence, not conflict. Diversity exists within every culture. Assess each person.
  • Complementary practices are fine if they do no harm and do not delay needed treatment.
AreaExamples to assess
Health and illness beliefsIllness as fate or God's will, preference for folk healing or prayer, distrust of the system, refusal of blood products or certain medications
Communication and languageUse a medical interpreter, never a family member. Ask how to address the patient. Note eye contact, voice, and body language
Religious and spiritualFasting, kosher or halal diets, prayer time, refusal of certain products
Birth and postpartumModesty, who may be present, eating non-food items such as clay for nausea, beliefs about photographing or buying baby clothes early, staying home after birth, views on contraception
Family and gender rolesMatriarchal or patriarchal, extended family role, decision making by a male partner, stigma about pregnancy outside marriage
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: health disparities and barriers to care
  • Health disparity (Healthy People 2030): a health difference closely linked to social, economic, and environmental disadvantage that affects groups who have faced greater obstacles because of race or ethnicity, religion, income, sex, age, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity, location, or other traits linked to discrimination. It is ultimately a quality-of-care problem.
  • Finances: childbirth is the leading reason for hospitalization in the US. Medicaid covers more than 40% of births and about 65% of births to Black parents. Paperwork can stop people from enrolling.
  • Transportation: hard to attend visits without a car or with small children.
  • Language and culture: no interpreter means misread complaints.
  • Health literacy: the ability to read, understand, and use health information. Low health literacy raises emergency visits and poor outcomes. Assess with screening tools and use teach-back and return demonstration.
  • Delivery system: limited clinic hours, referral gatekeeping, and staff attitudes. Long waits, rushed visits, and rude comments make patients leave.
Think it through: clinic no-showsBarriers (transport, child care, hours, language, past mistreatment) drive missed visits. Strategies: evening or weekend hours, reminder calls and texts, transportation help, child-friendly waiting areas, interpreters, welcoming staff, and teaching why each visit matters.

⚖️ 7. Legal and ethical issues

Issues list

Abortion, substance abuse, intrauterine therapy, maternal-fetal conflict, stem cell research, umbilical cord banking, informed consent.

Consent for minors (class slide question)

ClientConsents for self?
17 year old who is marriedYes
14 year old who is an emancipated minorYes
15 year old high school studentNo. Needs parent or legal guardian. This is the answer to the class slide question.
20 year old college studentYes. An adult.
Discussion: 15 year old wants birth control and says "don't tell my parents"

Legal care: in most states a minor can consent to contraception and STI care. Laws differ by state, so follow your state law and facility policy.

Issues to address: confidentiality and its limits, STI protection (condoms plus the pill), screening for coercion, abuse, or an older partner, correct pill use and what to do if she misses one, and encouraging a trusted adult in her life.

Most important: confidentiality plus safety. She will only keep coming back if she feels safe, and the nurse must rule out abuse.

🔍 Go deeper: Consent, confidentiality, EMTALA, and documentation
TopicKey points
Informed consent needsCapacity, voluntary choice, full disclosure of risks, benefits, and alternatives, and understanding
Who does whatThe provider explains and obtains consent. The nurse witnesses the signature, checks that she understands, and tells the provider if she does not
MinorsParent or guardian consents unless the minor is married, emancipated, or covered by a state law for specific care such as contraception or STI treatment
Confidentiality (HIPAA)Share only what is needed for care. Be careful about discussing a teen's care with parents or a partner in earshot
EMTALAA woman in labor or with an emergency who comes to a hospital must be screened and stabilized regardless of ability to pay
NegligenceDuty, breach, causation, damages
  • Documentation: factual, timely, complete, and signed. Quote the client. Never alter or erase. Late entries are labeled. Do not mention the incident report in the chart.
  • Standard of care: what a reasonable nurse with the same training would do.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: abortion, substance misuse, fetal therapy, and maternal-fetal conflict
  • Abortion: Roe v. Wade (1973) protected the right before viability. A June 2022 decision overturned it, so states set their own laws. The ANA Code of Ethics lets a nurse refuse to assist if ethically opposed. Nurses must notify the employer in writing ahead of time and still give nonjudgmental care to every patient. Clarify your own values first.
  • Substance misuse in pregnancy: can cause preterm birth, abruption, low birth weight, stillbirth, miscarriage, and behavior and learning problems. Regular use can cause neonatal abstinence syndrome (diagnosed about every 25 minutes in the US). Punitive laws and the threat of jail deter women from prenatal care. Screen every pregnant woman and woman of childbearing age. Counsel calmly without judgment and refer to recovery services.
  • Fetal therapy: treatment of the fetus in the womb, such as intrauterine transfusion, spina bifida repair, and treatment of obstructive uropathy. Risks fall on the pregnant person with no direct benefit to her, which creates ethical tension.
  • Maternal-fetal conflict: beneficence and nonmaleficence can clash. Counsel and educate. ACOG opposes coercion and court orders. If disagreement continues, use the institutional ethics committee. Going to court is almost never justified.
  • Confidentiality and informed consent apply in every one of these situations.
🔍 Go deeper: Why OB and GYN are among the most sued specialties, and how nurses lower the risk
Why claims happenWhat the nurse does about it
Fetal heart rate misread or not acted onAssess correctly, use standard NICHD terms, act on Category II and III patterns, escalate
Delay in recognizing deterioration (bleeding, preeclampsia, nonreassuring tracing)Clinical judgment: recognize cues early, prioritize, and call with SBAR
Poor communication or handoffSBAR, read-back, closed-loop communication. "Failure to communicate" drives most nursing malpractice claims
Not using the chain of command when a provider does not respondFollow the policy: charge nurse, then supervisor, then department chair
Poor or missing documentationTimely, objective, complete notes. Chart what you saw, what you did, who you told, and when
Not following evidence-based protocols and unit policyKnow the guideline (for example oxytocin and FHR protocols) and follow it
  • Why the stakes are high: birth injuries, especially neonatal encephalopathy, affect a child for life, so claims can be large and are brought years later. States set the statute of limitations and it can be extended for minors.
  • What must be proved: duty, breach of the standard of care, causation, and damages.
  • Evidence-based practice is the gold standard and the best defense of care. Patient safety comes before convenience, productivity, and cost.
  • Nurses are legally liable for fetal monitoring and assessment. See the FHR Monitoring tab.

🧭 8. Ethics

TermMeaningOB example
MoralityPersonal beliefs. Adaptable over time.A nurse's own view on abortion
EthicsDisciplined study of morality written as systematic normsANA Code of Ethics, binding for conduct
BeneficenceDo goodTeach warning signs of preeclampsia
NonmaleficenceDo no harm to woman or fetusHold oxytocin for tachysystole
FidelityKeep promisesReturn to the call light as you said you would
VeracityTell the truthHonest information to parents of a sick neonate
AutonomySelf-determinationClient declines an epidural
JusticeFairnessSame quality of care no matter insurance
ApproachIdea
UtilitarianismGreatest good for the greatest number
LibertarianismIndividual liberty first
EgalitarianismEqual sharing of resources

Ethical dilemma: a choice between equally good or equally bad options, or a conflict between a patient's rights and the professional's duties. In OB the duties to mother and fetus can conflict.

Moral distress: your core beliefs conflict with the care you must give.

Neonatal ethics: counterbalance to do no harm, be truthful with parents, respect parental decisions, and support communication and teamwork.

🧠 Memory anchor
Non-MAL-eficence: "mal" is bad. Do NOT do bad. Bene-ficence: "bene" is good.
🔍 Go deeper: Principles at work and maternal-fetal conflict
PrincipleWhen it clashes
Autonomy vs nonmaleficenceA competent client refuses a recommended cesarean or transfusion. She has the right to refuse. The nurse informs, supports, documents, and involves the ethics committee
Beneficence vs autonomyThe care team believes treatment helps but the client declines
Justice vs resourcesLimited NICU beds or staffing
Veracity vs fidelityKeeping a promise of confidentiality when safety is at risk
  • Steps for a dilemma: identify the conflict, gather the facts, name the principles, consider options and consequences, act, and evaluate.
  • Cord blood banking: parents choose public donation or private storage. Give accurate information without pressure.
  • Extremely preterm infants: parents and the team share decisions. Be truthful and support the family.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: stem cells and cord blood banking
  • Stem cells can become many cell types. Adult stem cells (such as in bone marrow) replace old cells. Embryonic stem cells come from the inner cell mass of an early embryo, and the controversy is about their source because obtaining them destroys the embryo.
  • Umbilical cord blood (UCB) is a source of blood-forming stem cells for bone marrow transplant and some genetic, blood, and malignant disorders.
  • Private (for-profit) banks store cord blood for a fee for the same child or family. Public (nonprofit) banks store it free for anyone who needs it.
  • Cord blood cannot treat the same child's own genetic disease or leukemia because it carries the same problem.
  • ACOG and the American Academy of Pediatrics oppose for-profit banking and its marketing and recommend donating to public banks.
  • Evidence-based practice: delayed cord clamping is best, so collection must not change clamping time.
  • Nurse role: give accurate, unbiased, evidence-based information about options.

⚖️ 9. Nurses' rights, responsibilities, and legal issues

  • AWHONN supports a nurse's right to refuse to assist. Federal law also protects the right to refuse.
  • BUT access to healthcare is a basic human right. A nurse must not abandon a patient, must give high-quality care in an emergency regardless of beliefs, and must tell the employer about any belief that could interfere with essential duties.
  • Follow your state's Nurse Practice Act. Nurses are legally liable for fetal monitoring and assessment.

AWHONN core values, CARING: Commitment, Accountability, Respect, Integrity, Nursing excellence, Generation of knowledge.

  • Maternity is the most litigious practice area. OBs and gynecologists are among the most sued.
  • Problem areas: clinical judgment, communication, collaboration. "Failure to communicate" causes most malpractice suits against nurses.
  • Cases often involve neonatal encephalopathy. A plaintiff must prove duty, breach, causation, and damages.
  • States set the statute of limitations and burden of proof (your slide gave 2 to 4 years in Florida as an example).
  • Fetal heart rate monitoring is legally important: failure to assess correctly is a major risk.
  • Risk management: use EBP as the foundation and put patient safety ahead of convenience, productivity, and cost.

Abortion and reproductive rights (your slides)

  • After Roe v. Wade was overturned, each state sets its own abortion laws, including bans, mandatory counseling, and parental consent for minors.
  • Birth control and prenatal care remain protected under the ACA.
Virginia (as shown on your slide)
May be performed up to 26 weeks and 6 days
Informed consent is required. No waiting period. Telehealth is permitted.
Prohibited in the 3rd trimester unless 3 doctors certify the pregnancy threatens the woman's life
Parental consent for minors, with an exception through judicial bypass
Encouraging or promoting abortion is prohibited

Abortion law changes often. Treat this as what your slide said on class day and confirm anything state-specific with your instructor before the exam.

Slides list: use of research in critical practice, research utilization challenges, barriers to EBP, and strategies to improve EBP. Summary topics: ethical standards, nurses' rights and responsibilities, legal issues, evidence-based practice.

🔍 Textbook: history of childbirth in the United States

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: history of childbirth in the United States
EraWhat happened
1700sWomen cared for women. Female midwives attended home births. Childbirth was feared because death was common
1800sShift from midwives to doctors among the middle class. Puerperal (childbed) fever occurred in epidemics. Pasteur showed streptococci caused it. First cesarean in Boston in 1894. X-ray introduced in 1895 to assess the pelvis
Early 1900sFewer than 5% gave birth in hospitals. Twilight sleep (heavy narcotics and amnesiacs) was used. Hospital births 50% by 1940 and 97% by 1960. Nurseries separated babies from mothers
1933Dick-Read wrote Childbirth Without Fear to break the fear, tension, and pain cycle
1950Sister Mary Stella introduced family-centered maternity care
LamazeDistraction and relaxation breathing. Book Painless Childbirth: The Lamaze Method
1960sBirth control pill. Consumer movement brought back birth centers, prepared childbirth, partner involvement, and nurse midwives
1970s to 1990sReturn to nonmedicated, low-intervention care. Freestanding birth centers. Home births rise. Rooming-in and breastfeeding support
2000sAbout one in three births is a surgical birth. CNMs and doulas in demand again
  • Certified nurse midwife (CNM): postgraduate training in normal pregnancy and birth, certified by the American College of Nurse Midwives.
  • Doula: a birth assistant who gives emotional, physical, and educational support during birth and postpartum. Not a clinician.
  • Trend: after WWII nurses shifted from tasks to teaching parents and promoting bonding and breastfeeding.

🔍 Textbook: major female health issues and pregnancy

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: major female health issues and pregnancy
  • Cardiovascular disease is the number one cause of death in females. Women are more likely than men to have an MI without chest pain, with symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, or nausea, and it is more likely to go unrecognized. Risks in women include menopause, history of preeclampsia or gestational hypertension, diabetes, smoking, polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity, and older maternal age. Pregnancy raises heart workload, so women with heart disease need preconception counseling.
  • Cancer is the second leading cause of death. Lung cancer is the most fatal in women. Breast cancer affects about 1 in 8 women. Early detection and reducing avoidable risks are best.
  • Obesity in pregnancy raises risk of blood clots, cesarean birth, long labor, preterm birth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, stillbirth, gestational diabetes, congenital defects, preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, sleep apnea, and postpartum infection.
  • Many start pregnancy with chronic conditions: hypertension, diabetes, autoimmune disease, anemia, asthma, STIs, depression, or cancer.

🔍 Textbook: health care system trends and cost containment

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: health care system trends and cost containment
ConceptMeaning
Managed careControls cost by monitoring use of services, set fees, and an emphasis on prevention. Often uses a primary provider as gatekeeper
Utilization reviewChecks whether care is medically necessary
Access to careSeeing a provider within a reasonable time. Health insurance is a major factor. Women are more likely than men to be uninsured
Preventive care focusMammograms, cervical screening, prenatal care, smoking cessation, immunizations. The ACA added preventive services for women
Continuum of careAn integrated system that follows patients over time from hospital to clinic, home, and long-term care. Nurses ease transitions
Consumer empowermentFamilies want information and a voice. Nurses respect views, include the family, and involve them in decisions

Better diagnosis and treatment means nurses care for people who survive what was once fatal, such as women with repaired congenital heart disease who become pregnant, and premature infants who may have long-term respiratory or developmental problems. Fetal treatment now exists for some conditions.

🔍 Case: Sophia (clinical reasoning walkthrough)

🔍 Go deeper: Case: Sophia (clinical reasoning walkthrough)

Sophia is 38, pregnant with her third child, and has two children aged 4 and 9. Her husband is out of town, so her mother Betty came. She works part-time as a lunch aide. She plans natural childbirth with her children present. She says she does most of the running around during the week.

LensApplication
Factors affecting healthAge 38 (advanced maternal age), third pregnancy, role strain from work and children, limited partner support on weekdays, family structure, stress, and likely time pressure on nutrition and rest
StrengthsSupport from her mother, a birth plan, engaged family, and stable employment
MaslowCheck physiological needs first (nutrition, sleep, vital signs). Then safety (home, transportation), belonging (support), esteem, and self-actualization (birth plan)
ADPIEAssess BP, weight, fetal checks, stress, support. Diagnose a nursing problem such as role strain related to caring for two children and limited support. Plan goals together. Implement teaching, referral to community supports, and sibling preparation. Evaluate with teach-back and follow-up
Family-centered careHonor the birth plan, prepare the children, and include her husband and mother

How things changed since Betty's time: continuous support, partners and siblings welcome, birth centers and doulas, rooming-in, skin-to-skin contact, and evidence-based practice.

🔍 Roe v. Wade overturned: how it affects OB care, and Virginia law

🔍 Go deeper: Roe v. Wade overturned: how it affects OB care, and Virginia law
⚠️ Laws are changing right nowVirginia is in the middle of a ballot measure and court challenges. This card has two parts: the class slide version (use this for your exam) and a current-status snapshot checked on October 5, 2026. Confirm the latest with your instructor and Virginia sources before relying on anything.
TopicWhat to know
Roe v. Wade (1973)The Supreme Court ruled the government cannot excessively restrict abortion. A person had a constitutionally protected right to abortion before viability, in consultation with a provider
Dobbs decision (June 2022)Overturned Roe, so each state now sets its own abortion laws. Some states ban or restrict abortion, add mandatory counseling or waiting periods, or require parental consent for minors. Other states protect access
What did NOT changePer your slide, reproductive health services such as birth control and prenatal care remain protected under the ACA

How the overturning affects OB care and nursing practice:

  • Care depends on the state. Rules differ on when abortion is allowed, what exceptions apply, who must consent, and what counseling is required, so the nurse must know the law where she works.
  • Emergency and complicated pregnancies: professional groups such as ACOG have raised concern that unclear exceptions can delay care for conditions like miscarriage with bleeding or infection, ectopic pregnancy, premature rupture of membranes, and severe preeclampsia. The nurse's tools are early recognition, SBAR, the chain of command, and documentation.
  • EMTALA still requires screening and stabilizing emergency conditions, including labor. How it fits with state bans is being litigated.
  • Access and equity: travel for care, cost, and telehealth rules create barriers. This links to health disparities and maternal morbidity.
  • Conscience and duty: the ANA Code lets a nurse refuse to assist if ethically opposed, but she must notify her employer in writing ahead of time, never abandon a patient, and always give emergency care without bias.
  • Nurse role: give accurate, nonjudgmental information, support informed consent, keep confidentiality, document carefully, and escalate concerns. Clarify your own values before you care for someone considering abortion.
  • Contraception, prenatal, and postpartum care remain central to prevention.
Virginia (as on your class slide)Detail
Gestational limitMay be performed up to 26 weeks and 6 days
Third trimesterProhibited unless 3 doctors certify that the pregnancy threatens the woman's life
Informed consentRequired
Waiting period and telehealthNo waiting period, and telehealth is permitted
MinorsParental consent required, with an exception through judicial bypass
PromotionEncouraging or promoting abortion is prohibited (as listed on your slide)
Virginia current-status snapshot (checked Oct 5, 2026)Detail
Where Virginia standsVirginia is described as the most protective of abortion access among the former Confederate states, and the House rejected a near-total abortion ban in February 2024
Ballot measureQuestion 1, the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment, is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Governor Spanberger signed the enabling bill on February 6, 2026 after the General Assembly passed it in two sessions
What it would doAdd to the Virginia Constitution a fundamental right to reproductive freedom, including decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility care. It would allow the state to restrict third-trimester abortion but requires exceptions to protect the life and health of the pregnant person or when the fetus is not viable. The ballot text also says it would protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions
Legal challengesOne lawsuit (Bansley v. Nardo) claims the amendment process was not followed. A circuit court dismissed it in July 2026, it was appealed, and the Court of Appeals heard arguments on September 12, 2026. A separate case challenges the ballot wording. Opponents say they would try to overturn the amendment in court if it passes
ImportantUntil voters decide and any court rulings are final, the existing statutes are what govern practice. Check for updates after November 3
Clinical judgment and EBP linkWhen the law, the plan of care, and the patient's safety seem to conflict, the nurse still acts on assessment and evidence, communicates with SBAR, uses the chain of command, and documents.

👪 Ch 2: Family-Centered, Community-Based Care

Care that treats the family as the constant and the community as the unit of service.

🧠 The big idea

The family is the constant, so care includes the whole family.
Family health → Affects the client → Plan care with the family

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Four supports: Informational, Emotional, Appraisal (esteem), Instrumental.
  2. Community is the unit of service in community-based nursing.
  3. Primary prevention is before disease, secondary is screening, tertiary limits damage.
  4. Hospital 60%, community 18%, long-term care 7% of RNs.
  5. Teach with plain language, small chunks, survival skills first, and show-and-do.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Which prevention level?Immunization = primary. Glucose screening = secondary. Managing a disease already present = tertiary.
⚠️ CAM answersAsk without judgment, give facts, and discourage only what is harmful. Never lecture or ignore it.
🩺 Think like a nurseAsk yourself: who else is affected, where can this be handled outside the hospital, and what is the simplest survival skill she must learn first?

👪 1. Family-centered care

A collaborative partnership among the individual, family, and caregivers to set goals, share information, offer support, and plan care. The family is the constant: the health and abilities of every family member affect the client and everyone else.

Core concepts: dignity and respect, sharing healthcare information, letting patients and families take part in care, and collaborative care for the client and family.

Type of supportWhat it looks like
InformationalFacts, advice, answers
EmotionalCaring, empathy, listening
Appraisal (esteem)Affirmation, feedback that builds confidence
InstrumentalPractical help: rides, money, child care
🧠 Memory anchor: I.E.A.I.
Information, Emotion, Appraisal, Instrument.

  • Ecomap: a diagram of the family and its connections to community supports.
  • Assess: who lives at home, who helps, finances, transportation, culture, and how the family copes.

Nursing support to families means a supportive relationship, ongoing information, encouragement and affirming comments, emotional support, and competent nursing care. Good family-centered care needs adequate resources, education, and support from managers and other disciplines.

🏘️ 2. Community-based care

  • Community: a group in a defined geographic area who share interests, interact, and function together in a social structure to address common concerns.
  • A person belongs to many communities.
  • The community is the unit of service.
  • Concern covers current clients and the larger group of potential or at-risk clients.

Community-based nursing

  • Focus: health promotion, disease prevention, and primary health care.
  • Settings include ambulatory care, home health, occupational health, school health, and hospice.
  • Practice includes case management, research, quality improvement, and discharge planning.
  • Uses Healthy People 2030 as the national guide.
  • Roles include staff development, program development, and community education.
  • Includes geographically and culturally diverse settings.

Where RNs work

SettingPercent of RNs
Hospital60%
Community-based (offices, home health, community centers, schools, public health, ambulatory clinics)18%
Nursing and long-term residential care7%

Challenges: earlier discharge, more complications after discharge, more time needed for concerns, nursing shortages, fewer resources.

Interventions: health education programs, health screening, medication administration, telephone consultation, health system referral, instruction, nutritional counseling, risk identification.

🔍 Go deeper: Community nursing and the focus of care
  • Community-based nursing cares for individuals and families where they live and work. Public health nursing focuses on the health of whole populations.
  • Community assessment: who lives there, resources, risks, and strengths.
  • Challenges listed on your slide (earlier discharge, more complications at home, more time needed, shortages, fewer resources) all mean teaching must be clear and follow-up must be planned before the client leaves.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: definitions, population, and why care moved to the community
  • Community: a specific group of people, often in a defined area, who share common interests, interact, and function together in a social structure to address common concerns. A person belongs to many communities (home, work, language, culture, worship, clubs).
  • Population: a group that shares personal or environmental characteristics, most often location. Examples: night shift nurses, first-time pregnant women, high-risk infants. The goal of community-based nursing is the betterment of populations.
  • The community is the unit of service. Care covers current patients and the larger group at risk.
  • Community health nursing: prevents illness and improves health of populations. Public health nursing is a specialized area of it.
  • Epidemiology: the study of the causes, distribution, and control of disease in populations. It helps plan services. Healthy People 2030 was built with the epidemiologic process.
  • Community-based nursing: care in nontraditional settings. Community health and public health nursing are now a subset of it.

Why care moved to the community: Medicare's prospective payment system (1983) replaced cost reimbursement with fixed rates and rewarded cost control. Hospital stays shortened. Care shifted from reactive treatment to proactive health promotion and prevention. Technology allows home care such as IV antibiotics and dialysis. More people live with chronic illness, and the population is aging.

  • Challenges: earlier discharge means more complex needs at home. Example: after a cesarean, a woman with infection, pelvic abscess, and a leg DVT now gets IV heparin and antibiotics at home, so nursing time goes to procedures instead of teaching. Nurses work with fewer resources and often decide alone, so strong assessment and communication skills are essential.
  • Requirements: many positions want a baccalaureate degree. Home health agencies usually require prior medical-surgical experience because the nurse works independently.
  • Mission: treat every person with dignity and compassion. Use interpreters. Individualize care to cultural, social, and economic diversity.

🛡️ 3. Levels of prevention

LevelGoalOB example
Health promotionKeep communities healthy and empower healthy behaviorsNutrition class for pregnant teens
PrimaryPrevent disease before it occurs: education, immunization, environmental protectionRubella vaccine, folic acid before pregnancy
SecondaryEarly identification of disease already present: screeningGlucose screening for gestational diabetes, GBS swab
TertiaryLimit progression or disability after disease or injuryInsulin management after gestational diabetes is found
🔍 Go deeper: Telling the levels apart
LevelTest questionMore OB examples
Health promotionDoes it build healthy habits for everyone?Prenatal exercise class, breastfeeding education
PrimaryDoes it stop the disease before it exists?Folic acid, rubella and Tdap vaccines, safe sex teaching, seat belt use
SecondaryDoes it find disease early?Pap smear, STI screening, glucose test, GBS swab, newborn screening
TertiaryDoes it limit damage from an existing disease?Diabetes management after diagnosis, physical therapy, rehabilitation, support groups
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: examples, the 5 As, and folic acid
  • Primary: prevents disease before it occurs through health promotion, environmental protection, and specific protection. Examples: nutrition, hygiene, sanitation, immunizations, sunscreen, genetic counseling, bicycle helmets, bathtub handrails, school drug education, shelter, smoking cessation, family planning, seat belts. Prevention is more cost-effective than treatment. Health begins at home.
  • Secondary: early identification of disease through screening. Examples: pregnancy testing, blood pressure checks, cholesterol, fecal occult blood testing, breast exams, mammography, hearing and vision exams, Pap smears. Osteoporosis is a silent disease, so screen those at risk.
  • Tertiary: limits progression and restores function in permanent or irreversible disease. Examples: managing effects of cerebrovascular disease or chronic STIs (herpes, HIV, untreated syphilis), and helping people with long-term effects of violence. Education is the cornerstone.

5 As behavior counseling: Ask about the behavior, Advise briefly about risks, Assess the behavior, Assist in overcoming barriers, Arrange follow-up.

Folic acid as primary preventionAbout 300,000 babies a year worldwide are born with neural tube defects, the second most common major congenital anomaly (heart defects are first). Folic acid daily for 3 months before and 3 months after conception reduces the risk of a first occurrence. The USPSTF recommends 0.4 to 0.8 mg daily for anyone who plans pregnancy or may be pregnant, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first trimester. 58 countries fortify food.
Healthy People 2030 objectiveNursing significance
More community-based organizations offering primary preventionPrograms in schools, worksites, and agencies reach people outside traditional care
More adults whose provider checked their understandingUse teach-back and support shared decision making
Fewer adults reporting poor communication with their providerGood communication leads to better prevention and disease management

Nurse role: health promotion often involves social determinants of health (economic, social, cultural, and political conditions of life). Modifiable risk behaviors include smoking, poor diet, obesity, insufficient sleep, and inactivity. Nurses provide care at all three levels and advocate for services.

🌿 4. CAM in maternity nursing

  • 38% of adults and 12% of children use CAM. Prayer is the most common form.
  • Midwives use CAM more and more for childbirth.

Nursing implications

  • Show cultural sensitivity. Respect different beliefs, attitudes, and lifestyles.
  • Accept CAM and work it into care if it comforts and does no harm.
  • Give accurate information, not opinions.
  • Teach how the client can monitor her condition while using CAM.
  • Discourage a practice only if it is harmful.
  • Avoid confrontation when asking. Be reflective, nonjudgmental, and open minded.
🔍 Go deeper: CAM categories and safety in pregnancy

Natural products: herbs, vitamins, probiotics. Mind and body: yoga, meditation, hypnosis, acupuncture, massage. Other: traditional healers and spiritual practices.

PracticePregnancy considerations
GingerCommonly used for nausea. Tell the provider
Acupuncture and acupressureUsed for nausea and pain. Use a trained practitioner and tell the provider
Yoga, meditation, massageUsually acceptable with provider approval. Avoid hot yoga and lying flat late in pregnancy
Blue cohosh and black cohoshCan stimulate the uterus. Avoid unless the provider approves
High-dose vitamin ATeratogenic in high doses
St. John's wortInteracts with many medications

Always ask about every herb, tea, and supplement. Products are not tested the way medications are.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: types, therapies, and teaching
TypeMeaningExample
ComplementaryUsed together with conventional medicineAromatherapy to reduce pain in early labor or after surgery
AlternativeUsed in place of conventional medicineA special diet instead of recommended chemotherapy
IntegrativeCombines mainstream medicine with CAM that has some evidence of safety and effectivenessAcupuncture alongside standard care
TherapyDescription
AromatherapyEssential oils to stimulate smell and balance mind, body, and spirit
Homeopathy"Like treats like" to restore balance
AcupressurePressing points to restore balance
Feng shuiPlacing objects to create harmony
Guided imageryHealing images with deep relaxation
ReflexologyDeep massage of points on the foot or hand
Therapeutic touchBalancing energy by moving hands over the body
Herbal medicineTherapeutic use of plants
Spiritual healingPrayer, chanting, laying on of hands, meditation
ChiropracticSpinal manipulation for musculoskeletal complaints
MassageStroking or kneading to relieve pain and improve circulation
  • Use is common: 38% of adults, more often women, and common in pregnancy and birth. Many patients do not tell providers, so ask specifically about vitamins, minerals, herbs, and anything not ordered.
  • Nausea in early pregnancy: ginger lollipops or tea, Sea-Bands, peppermint, acupuncture or acupressure, and vitamin B6. They may cause no harm, but most substances cross the placenta, so discuss every remedy with the provider.
  • Other uses: soy isoflavones and red clover for osteoporosis, and various products for hot flashes. Many are untested.
  • Teach: natural does not mean safe. Tell your provider about everything you take. Check the label for all ingredients and amounts. Avoid frequent or large doses. Mixing can cause harm, for example vitamin E, garlic, and aspirin all have anticoagulant effects.
  • Nurse actions: be culturally sensitive, give accurate information, accept CAM that brings comfort without harm, discourage only what is harmful, help the patient weigh risks and benefits, and avoid confrontation.

🤰 5. Prenatal care in the community

  • Early and adequate prenatal care improves outcomes.
  • Telemedicine.
  • In-home care: infusion therapy, fetal monitoring or surveillance, monitoring diabetic or cardiac status, monitoring mothers at risk for preterm labor.

Care settings: physicians' offices, client homes, churches and shelters, clinics, hospital outpatient departments, health departments, urgent care centers.

🔍 Go deeper: Home visits and telemedicine
  • Home visit assessment: vital signs, fetal heart rate, weight, glucose, home safety, supplies, emotional status, and understanding of teaching.
  • Telemedicine benefits: reaches rural clients, saves travel, and supports remote blood pressure and glucose monitoring.
  • Limits: needs a device and internet, cannot replace hands-on exams, and privacy at home must be checked (especially with IPV risk).
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: community services, regionalized care, and home services
Service (Box 2.3)Key points
State public health prenatal clinicsSliding-scale fees or Medicaid
Federally funded community clinicsPrenatal, pediatric, adult, and dental care. Sliding scale or Medicaid
Hospital outpatient clinicsOften at teaching hospitals with students and residents rotating
Private OB/GYN officesFor people with insurance. Some accept Medicaid
Free community clinicsFor people with limited resources
Freestanding birth centersPrenatal care for low-risk patients and childbirth classes. Most accept insurance and Medicaid
Midwifery servicesMany payment plans
WICFederal program run by each state. Food, nutrition counseling, and access to health services. People on Medicaid, food stamps, or AFDC are automatically eligible
Childbirth classesUsually in the third trimester
La Leche LeagueParent-to-parent breastfeeding and infant care support, often in a member's home
  • Early, adequate prenatal care improves outcomes: early and continuing risk assessment, health promotion, medical and psychosocial interventions, and follow-up. Nurses link people to resources regardless of income.
  • Regionalized perinatal care: recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics. Level III regional centers and community prenatal surveillance programs give better risk-adjusted mortality.
  • Telehealth: a provider uses real-time audio and video to assess, diagnose, and treat a patient at a distance.
  • Services that can be given at home: infusion therapy for infection or dehydration, hypertension monitoring for gestational hypertension, uterine monitoring for preterm labor risk, fetal monitoring, diabetic or cardiac monitoring, and portable ultrasound for a biophysical profile. Home care can cut costs while keeping women safe.

🏥 6. Birth settings

SettingBest forNotes
HospitalHigh-risk pregnancies and deliveriesFull emergency capability
Birthing centerLow-risk womenHome-like. Close to a hospital in case of complications. Midwives are the providers. Preserves the "normalcy" of birth.
HomeLow-risk womenFamily-centered. Least expensive. Limited availability of pain medication.
🔍 Go deeper: Providers and when to transfer
SettingTypical providersPain reliefIf something goes wrong
HospitalObstetricians, CNMs, nursesEpidural, IV medication, nitrous oxide, nonpharmacologicOn-site surgery, blood bank, NICU
Birthing centerCNMs and midwivesMostly nonpharmacologic, some IV or nitrousTransfer by ambulance to the nearby hospital

Choose a lower-risk setting only for low-risk pregnancies. Reasons to transfer or avoid out-of-hospital birth include hypertension, diabetes, preterm labor, bleeding, nonreassuring fetal heart rate, breech presentation, and multiples.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: birth center and home birth pros and cons
SettingAdvantagesDisadvantages
Birth centerHome-like, noninterventional, freedom to eat and move, any birth position, any number of family present. Lower rates of cesarean, preterm birth, low birth weight, and induction, and lower cost than hospitalRigid screening criteria, strict rules for transfer (prolonged labor, ruptured membranes), usually no epidural, short stay (4 to 8 hours), may not be covered by insurance, often no pediatrician on staff
Home birthLeast expensive, privacy and comfort, control over positions and support people, fewer interventions, immediate bonding and breastfeedingLimited pain medication and danger if an emergency arises (abruption, uterine rupture, cord prolapse, fetal distress). Delay to the hospital can cost lives
HospitalMedical technology, skilled staff, and neonatal services for high-risk pregnanciesMore interventions and cost
  • Choose by risk: high-risk (medical or social factors) belongs in a hospital. Low-risk people may use a birth center or home. The choice also depends on preference, finances, and distance to a hospital.
  • Safe planned home birth needs low risk, a qualified midwife certified by the American Midwifery Certification Board, equipment and supplies, timely hospital transfer, and good communication between home and hospital providers.
  • Nurse role: present the facts, protect safety, and respect autonomy and family-centered care in every setting. Midwives are often the sole providers in freestanding birth centers, with obstetricians as backup.

🍼 7. Postpartum and newborn community care

  • Telephone consults, outpatient clinic, postpartum home visits, support groups, online forums, high-risk newborn home care.
  • Home visit checklist: physical and emotional well-being of the family, postpartum depression screen, tobacco and substance abuse screen, contraception teaching.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: telephone care, home visits, support, and high-risk newborns at home
  • Why it matters: hospital stays average 24 to 48 hours or less after vaginal birth and 72 to 96 hours after cesarean. At discharge many still have perineal pain, cramping, fatigue, and constipation, and may feel unsure about feeding. Early postpartum depression is common.
  • Telephone consultation: the unit gives a number at discharge. Nurses know the birth history, so they can help with adjustment to the new role.
  • Outpatient clinics: exam of mother and newborn, cord care, postpartum and infant care, and nutrition.
  • Home visit: review the prenatal and birth history, physical and emotional well-being, complications for either, signs of postpartum depression, tobacco and substance screening, infant feeding, confidence with newborn care, links to social and housing programs, role adjustment, contraception teaching, and a bridge to follow-up care. Technology (calls, texts, video) can extend care.
  • Support groups: usually 6 to 12 parents, weekly, led by an experienced facilitator. Online forums give anonymous, nonjudgmental support.
High-risk newborn at homeDetails
CandidatesPreterm infants needing oxygen, low birth weight infants needing special formulas or tube feeding, infants with hydrocephalus or cerebral palsy
EquipmentVentilators, apnea monitors, oxygen, IV equipment, nebulizers, phototherapy, suction
Preparedness assessmentParenting education (handling, nutrition, hygiene, elimination, growth, immunizations, recognizing illness), postpartum care (body image, sleep, fatigue, role adjustment), and support systems (family help, community programs)
TeachingDemonstrate and let the family practice. Anticipate problems: keep extra supplies, enough medication or formula for the weekend, and backup batteries or portable oxygen. Safety of the infant is the outcome

🏘️ 8. Roles of the community-based nurse

RoleIncludes
CommunicatorVerbal and nonverbal skills, working with an interpreter, communicating with deaf clients and families
Direct care providerContraception and abortion counseling, STI screening, infertility care, preconception risk assessment
EducatorTeaches individuals and groups
Discharge planner and case managerCoordinates the transition and services
Advocate and resource managerSpeaks up and connects clients to resources
🔍 Go deeper: Roles in action and care of the family
  • Communicator: interpreters, sign language, and written materials at her reading level.
  • Educator: uses teach-back and demonstrations.
  • Advocate: speaks up when services are denied or delayed.
  • Case manager: follows referrals until they are completed.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: communication, interpreters, Deaf patients, and educator tasks
  • Overall: community nurses spend more time as educator, communicator, and manager than acute care nurses. Home care includes a lot of supervision and management.
  • Communicator: trust, respect, and empathy create therapeutic communication. Sit at eye level to show openness. Active listening uncovers fears questions may miss and makes people feel taken seriously. Check that verbal and nonverbal messages match. With families, be honest, treat them as equal partners, and explain equipment and procedures.
  • Interpreter use: identify language needs at first contact. Work as a team: the nurse questions or informs and the interpreter conveys it completely and accurately. Many facilities use Language Line (phone interpreting in about 170 languages). Apps can help when no interpreter is present. Interpreters must maintain confidentiality.
Deaf or hard of hearing patientsKey points
ScopeAbout 60.7 million US adults have hearing loss, the third most common chronic condition. It is an invisible condition and pregnant women with hearing loss are often neglected
Find the preferred methodLip reading, American Sign Language, CART (real-time captioning on a tablet or phone), or a mix
If you are not fluent in ASLProvide an ASL interpreter. The Americans with Disabilities Act requires effective communication for Deaf patients and family members
TipsFace the person and get their attention first. Normal lip movement and eye contact. Plain English at normal speed and volume. Use gestures, diagrams, and expressions. Keep confirming understanding. Show patience
  • Direct care provider: assessment extends to the home and community. The nurse often decides whether to start, continue, change, or end care. Areas include contraception, abortion, infertility, STI screening, and preconception risk assessment.
  • Educator: begin teaching early because stays are short. The aim is independence. Education overcomes feelings of powerlessness, supports informed decisions, and can cut readmissions.
  • Discharge checklist (9 items): reason for admission, primary care at home, case management, follow-up plans, home care referrals, communication with community providers, medication management, telehealth access, and patient education.
  • Education steps follow the nursing process: assess, plan, implement, evaluate, and document. Reassess after each step. Use competency-based teaching and teach-back.
  • Documentation has four purposes: communication among the team about what was learned, legal evidence of education, proof of meeting accrediting standards (The Joint Commission and CMS), and information for payers.
  • Discharge planner and case manager: plans safe discharge and coordinates services while balancing quality and cost. Advocate and resource manager: ensures access to resources such as help with other children for a woman on bed rest, transportation, equipment, and Medicaid or Medicaid waivers (state-run programs for people with certain conditions).

🎯 9. Techniques to help clients learn

  • Slow down and repeat information often
  • Speak in a conversational style using plain language
  • Chunk information and teach in small bits
  • Prioritize: survival skills first
  • Use visuals: pictures, videos, and models
  • Teach hands-on: show me and return demonstration
⭐ High yieldRead the teaching techniques as a unit: plain language, small chunks, repeat, survival skills first, show and do.
🔍 Go deeper: Learning domains and readiness
DomainExampleHow to teach
Cognitive (knowing)Name the danger signsExplain, quiz, teach-back
Affective (feeling)Accept a new role as a parentListen, validate, share stories
Psychomotor (doing)Diaper, bathe, or position for latchDemonstrate, then return demonstration
  • Readiness: teach when she is comfortable and not in pain or exhausted. Immediate needs first (Maslow).
  • Adult learners want practical, relevant, and respectful teaching.
  • Evaluate: teach-back and return demonstration, not "Do you understand?"
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: teaching tips and health literacy aids
  • Ask without blame: "Many people have trouble reading and remembering the information on this paper. Is this ever a problem for you?" Then adjust your teaching and tell the team.
  • Techniques: slow down and repeat, know language and education limits, conversational plain language, involve family, small logical steps, prioritize survival skills, use visuals, and teach hands-on.
  • Low health literacy aids: pictures or illustrations, video or audio, color coding (medication bottles or procedure steps), and a backup family member.
Case: Maria (Spanish-speaking, first baby, home visit)On visit 1 there was no interpreter, only gestures, and the nurse moved the baby from his tummy to his back without explaining. That conveyed disrespect and decreased trust. Back sleeping is correct to lower the risk of sudden unexplained infant death, but it needed to be explained. Preparing: arrange an interpreter, learn about her culture, and plan the teaching. On visit 2 the nurse brought an interpreter, explained back to sleep, and demonstrated feeding and holding positions. Maria smiled and asked when the nurse would return. Interpreter use, explanation, and demonstration are culturally congruent care.

🔍 Textbook: cultural issues, diversity, and barriers to culturally congruent care

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: cultural issues, diversity, and barriers to culturally congruent care
  • Diversity is growing. About one in seven US residents is foreign-born. By about 2030, immigration will account for more than half of population growth. Nurses must show humility, not only competence.
  • Cultural concepts to learn: time orientation, personal space, family orientation (patriarchal, matriarchal, egalitarian), and language.
  • Cultural humility goes beyond cultural competency. It is a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation, willingness to learn, and not holding set ideas based on stereotypes. Look through your own eyes and the patient's. Ask: "Do you have treatment preferences you would like me to include?" Consider fasting seasons and food preferences.
  • Barriers: provider-related (lack of knowledge, different beliefs) and system-related (agencies designed for one way of doing things that expect everyone to conform).
Evidence (Box 2.1)A systematic review of strategies to reduce stigma and discrimination in sexual and reproductive health care found that educating providers about their own behaviors to improve empathy, and policy reform, helped. Stigmatized people may get substandard care and avoid future care. Nurses should reexamine whether their practice is respectful, safe, family centered, and high quality.
Lesson from the Guatemala caseA fracture left untreated for a year meant a girl could not marry in her community. The nurse reminded herself not to impose her own values and to accept local customs without judgment so the family would feel accepted and the nurse could help.
Case: Fatime (23, Muslim, newly arrived from Mali, first pregnancy)What to assess
Modesty and genderPreference for a female provider, privacy, who may be present
Religious practicePrayer times, fasting, halal diet
LanguageNeed for a qualified interpreter
Family rolesWho makes decisions, role of husband and extended family
Beliefs about pregnancy and birthPostpartum customs, pain expectations, feeding plans

🔍 Textbook: community-based female health services

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: community-based female health services
Center typeOffers
