Women use more health care than men, make as many as 80% of health care decisions, and tend to live longer. Care is increasingly given by nurse midwives, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants as well as obstetricians and family providers.

🚨 Ch 9: Violence and Abuse

How to spot abuse, how it cycles, and exactly what the nurse does first.

🧠 The big idea

Abuse is about control, and pregnancy raises the danger.
Control → Cycle repeats and escalates → Higher risk in pregnancy → Nurse: alone, ask, safety

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Cycle: tension-building, physically abusive, reconciliation (honeymoon).
  2. Abused women are at HIGHER risk during pregnancy.
  3. Interview her alone, then ask directly, then assess immediate safety.
  4. Document and report findings, give emotional support, offer a safety plan.
  5. Sexual violence care: support, evidence, STI check, pregnancy prevention, PTSD screen.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Never use the partner as the interpreterHe blocks disclosure and can raise her danger.
⚠️ Never blameDo not ask why she stayed or doubt her story. Believe, validate, and say it is unacceptable.
🩺 Think like a nurseSafety before everything. Separate her privately, ask, assess immediate danger, then document, support, and plan.

🚨 1. Intimate partner violence (IPV)

Actual or threatened physical or sexual violence, or psychological or emotional abuse. Threats count when used to control a person's actions.

Other names: domestic abuse, domestic violence, gender-based violence, spouse abuse, battering, rape.

Risk characteristics

  • Use and abuse of substances
  • Negative affect
  • History of childhood abuse
  • Characteristics of the perpetrator's partner
  • Traditional gender role expectations
🔍 Go deeper: Power and control, reproductive coercion, and why women stay
TacticLooks like
IsolationControls who she sees, phone, and transportation
Economic controlTakes her paycheck, forbids work
Intimidation and threatsThreats to hurt her, the children, pets, or herself
Emotional abuseInsults, blaming, humiliation
Using childrenThreatens custody or uses them to control her
Reproductive coercionHides or destroys birth control, pressures her to get pregnant, or forces pregnancy outcomes
Stalking and digital abuseTracks her phone or location

Why women stay: fear for life or her children, financial dependence, lack of housing, love and hope he will change, isolation, cultural or religious pressure, and immigration concerns. Never ask "why don't you just leave?"

Effects on pregnancy: miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight, placental abruption, delayed prenatal care, STIs, injury to the abdomen, depression, and substance use.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: RADAR screening

RADAR: Routinely screen every patient, Ask direct questions, Document your findings, Assess safety before she leaves, Review options and make referrals. Pregnancy is often when abuse starts or escalates. Nurses are often the first contact for an injured victim and should empower her, not rescue her.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: scope, incidence, and who is affected
  • Global: about 1 in 3 women has experienced physical or sexual intimate partner violence or nonpartner sexual violence. The UN definition covers acts likely to cause physical, sexual, or mental harm, including threats, coercion, and deprivation of liberty, in public or private life.
  • US: about 5.7 million women experience IPV each year. 41% of women will have some form of physical violence in a lifetime. About 1 in 5 homicide victims is killed by an intimate partner, and nearly half of women who are murdered are killed by a current or past partner. Nearly 1 in 4 women and 1 in 26 men have been raped.
  • Pregnancy: homicide was found to be a leading cause of death during pregnancy and the postpartum period, higher than other leading causes of maternal death, with a firearm often involved. Risk is very high for Black women and women under 24. Screen every pregnant woman at each visit.
  • IPV often starts as emotional abuse and progresses to physical. Physical violence is usually accompanied by sexual abuse. Intimate partners include current and past dating, living-together, and married partners.
  • Men and LGBTQIA+ people: about 1 in 9 men experience rape, physical violence, aggression, or stalking by a partner. IPV in the LGBTQIA+ community occurs at rates equal to or higher than in heterosexual relationships. Transgender people are especially vulnerable, so screen everyone at every encounter.
  • Laws: the Violence Against Women Act was reauthorized in 2022 and covers same-sex partners and LGBTQIA+ survivors. Healthy People 2030 aims to reduce IPV, homicides, and nonfatal assault injuries and to improve screening.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: risk factors, generational effects, and myths
Individual (victim)RelationshipCommunitySocietal
Young age (under 24), prior IPV, depression, low income, witnessing violence as a child, refugee statusMarital conflict, dominance or control, reproductive coercionHigh crime and violence, poverty, low social supportNorms that support violence, traditional gender expectations, war
  • Risk factors for perpetration: exposure to violence in childhood, unresolved PTSD, recent job loss, and substance use disorder.
  • Generational cycle: children who witness abuse can develop aggression, conduct problems, anxiety, sleep problems, depression, low self-esteem, school problems, risky sexual behavior, and substance use. About 1 in 7 children is abused each year.
MythFact
Only poor people are abusedViolence occurs in all socioeconomic classes
Substance use causes violenceViolence is learned. Drugs and alcohol can make it worse but do not cause it
It happens to few women1 in 3 women in a lifetime
It is a one-time physical eventIt is a pattern of coercion and control using intimidation, threats, money, isolation, sexual abuse, and injury
Women can easily leaveLeaving is often the most dangerous time
Only men with mental illness abuseAbuse is a choice. Abusers often seem normal
Pregnant women are protectedIPV often begins or increases in pregnancy
Women provoke abuse and the abuser lost controlAbuse is a deliberate choice to gain power and control
It is rare in same-sex relationshipsRates are similar or higher

🔄 2. Cycle of violence

PhaseWhat happens
1. Tension-buildingMinor incidents, victim walks on eggshells, abuser grows angry
2. Physically abusive (acute battering)The explosion: hitting, choking, assault
3. Reconciliation (honeymoon)Apologies, gifts, promises to change

The cycle increases in intensity over time.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: the three phases in detail
PhaseWhat happens
1. Tension building (usually the longest)Name-calling, jealousy, friction. The victim walks on eggshells, feels she must keep the peace, and may blame herself
2. Physically abusive incidentThe explosion of violence, rarely triggered by the victim. Many victims call themselves lucky it was not worse and may refuse treatment
3. Reconciliation (honeymoon)Remorse, apologies, gifts, and promises it will never happen again. The victim wants to believe he can change. Excuses and minimizing follow, he may blame outside stress or alcohol, and both feel things are back to normal. He may gaslight her to regain control

The cycle gets more frequent and severe. The calm after reconciliation shortens and disappears, and the abuser stops apologizing. The cycle is also called the power and control wheel.

📋 3. Types of abuse

TypeExamples
EmotionalInsults, humiliation, threats, isolation
PhysicalHitting, kicking, choking, burns
FinancialControlling money, forbidding work
SexualForced or coerced sex
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: examples of each type
TypeExamples
EmotionalThreats to harm her, children, pets, or friends. Degrading acts. Name-calling and ridicule. Isolation. Silent treatment. Destroying valued items. Controlling every move
PhysicalHitting or grabbing leaving marks, throwing things, slapping, biting, burning, choking, kicking, slamming against things, weapons, and controlling access to health care for injuries
FinancialPreventing her from working, refusing money for expenses, controlling all spending, not contributing
SexualForced vaginal, oral, or anal sex, biting breasts or genitals, nonconsensual photos or videos, inserting objects, forcing degrading acts

🪞 4. Profiles

VictimAbuser
Rarely describes herself as abused (battered woman syndrome)Feels insecure, powerless, and helpless
Reacts with withdrawn behaviorUses violence to control the victim
May feel inadequateHas few close relationships
Often has poor self-esteemHistory of substance abuse or trouble with the justice system
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: victim and abuser profiles
  • Victims often do not call themselves abused. They feel terrified, trapped, and helpless, react to anger with avoidance and withdrawal, and may believe the abuse is their fault. Many were abused as children and may have PTSD, depression, limited education, or substance use disorder.
  • Abusers come from all walks of life. They often feel insecure, powerless, and helpless and use violence to feel in control. Features include blaming others, trouble accepting responsibility, history of substance use or childhood abuse, trouble with the law, few close relationships, sensitivity to criticism, extreme jealousy, controlling behavior, and unstable employment.

🤰 5. Violence against pregnant women

⚠️ TrapAbused women are at HIGHER risk of violence during pregnancy. Abuse threatens both mother and fetus. Higher risk of postpartum depression.

Signs of abuse in pregnancy

  • Missing prenatal appointments
  • Weight fluctuations
  • Unrealistic fears
  • Difficulty with pelvic exams
  • Nonadherence to treatment

Nursing care: safety assessment, emotional support, counseling.

🔍 Go deeper: Screening: when, how, and with what tools
  • When: at every visit, including the first prenatal visit and postpartum.
  • How: alone, in private, with a professional interpreter if needed. Say that you ask every woman. Use plain, direct words.
  • Tools: Abuse Assessment Screen, HITS, HARK, and the Danger Assessment for lethality risk.
  • Sample questions: "Has anyone hurt you since you became pregnant?" "Do you feel safe at home?" "Has anyone forced you to do something sexual?"
⚠️ Red flags for lethal riskStrangulation or choking, threats to kill, access to a gun, escalating violence, extreme jealousy, forced sex, violence during pregnancy, and separation. Ask directly: "Has he ever choked you?"
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: pregnancy specifics
  • The strongest predictor of abuse during pregnancy is prior abuse. Violence in pregnancy is more common than conditions routinely screened for, such as gestational diabetes. Having children does not protect a woman, and IPV may last longer if she has children.
  • Risk factors in pregnancy: low self-esteem, prior IPV, less than a high school education, low income, unemployment, lack of social support, economic stress, a partner with substance use disorder, and lack of community resources.
  • Injuries can involve the head, face, neck, chest, breasts, and abdomen. Mental health effects include depression, PTSD, and fearfulness, often appearing postpartum.
  • Adverse outcomes: stillbirth, preterm labor, low birth weight, smoking and substance misuse.
  • Signs: poor attendance, unrealistic fears, weight fluctuation, difficulty with pelvic exams, nonadherence, vague somatic complaints (for example repeated headaches, as in Dorothy's case). A fear of harm to the baby often motivates a woman to try to leave.
  • Interventions: safety planning, emotional support and counseling, referral to community services, continued prenatal care, and follow-up.

👵 6. Elder abuse

  • Physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, financial exploitation, neglect, abandonment, or self-neglect of a vulnerable elder by a caregiver.
  • Bruises, grip marks, and lacerations are among the most common signs.
  • State laws require healthcare workers to report.
🔍 Go deeper: Types, signs, and reporting
TypeSigns
PhysicalBruises, grip marks, burns, fractures, restraint marks
NeglectDehydration, malnutrition, pressure injuries, poor hygiene, unmet medical needs
EmotionalWithdrawal, fearfulness, passivity
FinancialMissing money, sudden changes to a will, unpaid bills
SexualGenital injury, STIs
Abandonment and self-neglectLeft without care, or unable to care for self

Report to Adult Protective Services. Healthcare workers are mandated reporters in most states.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: elder abuse details
  • About 3% to 10% of older people experience abuse, and many cases go unreported. In about 90% of cases the abuser is known to the victim, usually family. Older women are abused more than older men, and risk rises with age.
  • Risk factors: illness, disability, isolation, widowhood, dependency, dementia, low income, depression, and caregiver burnout.
  • Signs: bruises, grip marks, lacerations, depression, insomnia, chronic pain, difficulty trusting, thoughts of suicide, substance abuse, atypical chest pain, and other vague symptoms.
  • All 50 states require health care providers to report elder or vulnerable person abuse. Ask what the patient has already tried, listen without judgment, and know referral resources (housing, transportation, medical services, support groups).

🩺 7. Nursing management of IPV

Early recognition and intervention reduce the illness and death tied to IPV.

Signs of IPV to notice

  • Injuries
  • Mental health problems
  • Delay in seeking medical care
  • STIs or pelvic inflammatory disease
  • The partner's behavior at the visit (hovering, answering for her)

Interventions

  1. Separate the patient from her partner and family so she can speak privately. (Your slide says "isolate patient from family immediately.")
  2. Ask direct or indirect questions about abuse.
  3. Assess immediate safety.
  4. Document and report findings.
  5. Provide emotional support.
  6. Offer a safety plan.
⚠️ TrapSafety assessment comes before teaching, counseling, or paperwork. Always interview alone. Never use the partner or a family member as the interpreter.

Therapeutic statements

GoalExample from your slide
Listening"I hear and understand what you are saying."
Communicating belief"That must have been frightening for you."
Validating the decision to disclose"It must have been difficult for you to talk about this today."
Emphasizing it is unacceptable"You don't deserve to be treated this way."

Use a domestic violence screening and documentation form.

🔍 Go deeper: Documentation, reporting, and the safety plan
  • Document: her words in quotes ("states"), injuries with location, size, shape, and color, a body map, and photographs with consent. No guessing about cause. Records may be used in court.
  • Protect confidentiality: do not give discharge papers or pamphlets she cannot hide safely. Do not discuss IPV in front of anyone else.
  • Reporting: laws differ by state. Child and elder abuse are mandatory reports. Some states require reporting weapon injuries. Tell the client the limits of confidentiality first.
Safety plan itemExamples
Safe place and exitKnow a safe room with an exit, and a safe place to go
Emergency bagID, insurance cards, medications, cash, keys, copies of documents, phone charger
Code wordA word that tells a trusted person to call for help
Hotlines and protective ordersNational Domestic Violence Hotline 1-800-799-7233, local shelter, legal advocate
Children and petsPlan for their safety
Backup phoneA phone the abuser cannot track

The time of leaving is the most dangerous. Her decision and timing belong to her. The nurse supports and plans, and never forces.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: screening clues, how to ask, SAVE, and the Danger Assessment
ClueExamples
InjuriesBruises on upper arm, chest, or abdomen, blunt trauma scars, lacerations on face, head, or neck
Injury effectsHeadaches, hearing loss from ruptured eardrum, joint pain, sinus infection, bite marks, missing hair, dental trauma, pelvic pain, breast or genital injury
History does not match injuryExplanation is inconsistent with what you see
Mental healthDepression, anxiety, panic, substance use, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts, PTSD
Care patternsFrequent urgent care or ER visits, nonadherence, delay in care, repeated injuries, missed visits, late prenatal care
Partner behaviorOverly solicitous or controlling, will not leave her alone, answers for her
  • Screen at every visit. No single sign proves abuse, and no single tool is best. A single routine question like "Do you feel safe in your relationship?" can raise detection.
  • Isolate her immediately and privately. Use any private area, such as imaging, an elevator, a restroom, or the lab. Never ask in front of the abuser.
  • Direct questions: "Does your partner hit you?" Indirect: "We see many women with injuries or complaints like yours and often they are being abused, so I ask every patient." Both work equally well.
  • Assess immediate safety: Does she feel safe going home? Does she need a safe place for herself and her children tonight? Does she have an escape plan or another exit? Who can she call?
  • Educate her that the violence and her symptoms are connected, help her name what happened, and offer referrals.
SAVE model (sexual violence screening)Meaning
S: ScreenScreen all patients. Ask about touching against will, control over sexual relationships, and forced sexual activity
A: AskDirect questions, nonjudgmentally. Normalize, eye contact, stay calm, never blame, do not minimize, be patient, avoid medical jargon and leading questions
V: ValidateSay you believe her, it is not her fault, she is not alone, it is brave to tell, and help is available
E: Evaluate, Educate, ReferWhat type of violence, is she in danger now, how does she feel, does she know the consequences and community resources
Danger Assessment (Campbell)A 20-item questionnaire plus a calendar of incidents scored 1 to 5 in severity. It assesses risk of homicide in an ongoing abusive relationship. It is recommended for every patient who screens positive. Items include: violence increasing in severity or frequency, a gun in the house, leaving after living together, threats to kill, a weapon used or threatened, forced sex, choking or strangulation (and whether it happened more than once or caused blackouts), controlling daily life, violent jealousy, beaten while pregnant, threats to hurt children, stalking, suicide threats by either person, drug use, and problem drinking. It is free and has versions for specific groups.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: documentation, reporting, nursing analyses, interventions, and EMPOWER
  • Document: frequency and severity of abuse, location and extent of injuries, treatment given, and her exact words in quotes ("He choked me."). Use a body map and photographs with informed consent (or document that she refused).
  • Reporting: many states require reporting injuries from knives, firearms, or other deadly weapons and life-threatening emergencies. If reporting is required, tell the patient.
Possible nursing analyses
Knowledge deficiency about the cycle of violence and resources
Anxiety related to threat to self-concept and situational crisis
Low self-esteem related to negative family interactions
Powerlessness related to a lifestyle of helplessness
Altered individual and family coping related to abusive patterns
  • Helpful statements: Listening ("I hear and understand what you are saying"). Belief ("That must have been frightening"). Validating disclosure ("It must have been difficult to talk about this today"). Unacceptability ("You don't deserve to be treated this way").
  • Goal: help her regain control of her life. Give sensitive, predictable care, explain each step, let her take part and make decisions, pace care, and stay nonjudgmental. Control matters as much as safety, because lack of control keeps people from leaving.
EMPOWERMeaning
EEmpathetic listening
MMake time to document accurately (her words, injuries, first, worst, and most recent incident, photos with consent)
PProvide information about the cycle of violence and that it escalates
OOffer choices and options
WWork with domestic abuse specialists
EEncourage planning for safety (the most important part)
RRefer to local services and support groups
Prevention levelViolence example
PrimaryCommunity education to break the cycle
SecondaryScreening high-risk people and acting at early stages
TertiaryLong-term help for severe abuse survivors and rehabilitation of abusers
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: emotional support and safety plan
  • National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 or thehotline.org. Give her the number and shelter information even if she says no at first.
  • Emotional support: strengthen control (coping skills, daily living help, let her make decisions, teach about PTSD), set realistic goals (problem solving, social activity), and allow grieving (shock, disbelief, anger, depression, acceptance).
  • Tell her: abuse is never okay, she did not ask for it, she is not alone, it is a crime and she is a victim, alcohol, drugs, money, depression, and jealousy do not cause violence, it is not her fault, and you believe her.
  • The choice to leave belongs to her. Leaving is a process. Victims may try 7 or 8 times, and the final attempt is often when victims are killed. The nurse is a guide, not a savior. Just letting her talk can be the most valuable intervention.
Emergency kit for leaving (Teaching Guidelines 9.1)
Driver's license or photo ID, Social Security number or green card or work permit, birth certificates for her and the children
Phone numbers for social services and shelters, the deed or lease, court papers or orders
Prescription medications, a change of clothes for her and the children
Pay stubs, checkbook, credit cards, cash, health insurance cards, car keys, money
Back the car into the driveway and keep the tank full. Memorize important phone numbers. Rehearse the plan and share it with a trusted person. Any 24-hour health facility can be a safety net

🆘 8. Sexual violence

Short and long term effects: chronic pelvic pain, STIs, headaches, backaches, pregnancy, fear, withdrawal, sleep disturbances, guilt, phobias, PTSD.

Nursing management

  • Early intervention and immediate counseling
  • Supportive care
  • Evidence collection and documentation
  • STI assessment
  • Pregnancy prevention
  • PTSD assessment
🧠 Memory anchor: S.E.P.P.
Support, Evidence, Pregnancy prevention, PTSD screen (plus STI check).
🔍 Go deeper: After an assault: evidence, prophylaxis, and trauma response
  • Slide list for sexual violence: early intervention and immediate counseling, supportive care, evidence collection and documentation, STI assessment, pregnancy prevention, and PTSD assessment. Her lecture notes mention four phases of psychological trauma recovery, but neither the slides nor the textbook name them, so no set of phases is listed here. Learn the slide list above.
  • Evidence: a trained examiner (SANE) collects it with her consent, ideally within 72 to 120 hours. Ask her not to bathe, change, or eat if possible. Bag clothing in paper. Keep a chain of custody.
  • Treatment she is offered: emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, hepatitis B and tetanus as needed, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (best within 72 hours), injury care, and follow-up.
  • Support: advocate, counseling, and a safe place to go. Screen for PTSD, depression, and suicide risk. The Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is 988.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: scope, abuse, incest, rape, and myths
  • Scope: over 50% of women experience sexual violence involving contact in a lifetime. About 1 in 4 women and 1 in 26 men experience attempted or completed rape. Nine out of 10 rape victims are women. Women 12 to 24 are at highest risk. Sexual violence includes IPV, trafficking, incest, FGM/C, forced prostitution, exploitation, and sexual assault.
  • Effects: pelvic pain, genital injury, headaches, STIs, pregnancy, anxiety, fear, sleep problems, substance misuse, depression, sexual health problems, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts.
  • Sexual abuse: forced sexual contact of any kind without consent. Females are more often abused by someone they know than a stranger. Marriage does not mean consent. About 1 in 4 girls and 1 in 13 boys experience childhood sexual abuse, and fewer than half of assaults are reported. Childhood abuse raises the risk of repeat victimization.
  • Incest: sexual activity between people so closely related that marriage is prohibited. It is a crime and a symptom of family dysfunction. Every nurse is a mandated reporter of child sexual abuse.
  • Rape: an act of violence, not a sexual act. The FBI definition covers penetration, no matter how slight, without consent. Statutory rape is sexual activity between an adult and a person under 18, even if the minor was willing. Acquaintance rape and date rape account for 80% to 90% of campus rapes, and 8 out of 10 assaults are by someone known.
Rape mythFact
Victims get over it quicklyRecovery can take years
Most victims tell someoneMost never tell. Almost two-thirds never report to police
Women lie about it or deserve it if they drankFew lie. No one is to blame except the perpetrator
It is not rape if it is a girlfriend or wifeRape is always rape, whatever the relationship
Men reach a point of no returnMen can stop at any point. It is premeditated violence, not uncontrolled passion
Only attractive women or women in certain clothing are rapedAnyone can be raped. Clothing and lifestyle never invite assault
It is only rape if there are visible injuriesVictims may freeze. Coercion and threats are also used
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: rape drugs, PTSD, SANE, and nursing care
Rape drugDetails
Rohypnol ("roofies")Dissolves in drinks with no taste, odor, or color. About 10 times stronger than diazepam. Effects within 30 minutes and memory loss up to 8 hours
GHB ("liquid ecstasy")Depressant. Euphoria, sleepiness, memory loss. Acts in about 15 minutes and lasts 3 to 4 hours. Can cause unconsciousness, coma
Ketamine ("special K")Acts quickly on the central nervous system and separates perception from sensation

Alcohol with these drugs makes effects stronger and can be fatal. Protection teaching: pour your own drinks, never leave a drink unattended, do not accept drinks from others, avoid punch bowls, stay with friends, leave your phone on, and call 911 if you think you were drugged.

PTSD symptom groupExamples
IntrusionNightmares, flashbacks, recurrent thoughts
AvoidanceAvoiding reminders, social withdrawal, emotional numbing
HyperarousalExaggerated startle, irritability, trouble sleeping or concentrating
Cognitive and moodNegative thoughts, depression, excessive guilt and self-blame

Symptoms usually begin within 3 months (sometimes years later) and must last more than a month to count as PTSD. Early intervention and immediate counseling can speed recovery. Rape is a situational crisis.

  • SANE: a registered nurse trained to do sexual assault evidence exams, give crisis intervention, STI testing, and emergency contraception.
  • Nursing care: supportive care, collect and document evidence, assess for STIs, prevent pregnancy, and assess PTSD. Take her to a private, secure area. Offer a change of clothes, shower after evidence collection, and a private waiting area for support persons.
  • Evidence: she should bring all clothing worn at the time, especially undergarments, and should not shower or bathe before care. A SANE usually collects the evidence. The pelvic exam is done gently with every step explained.
  • Emergency contraception: one dose within 72 to 120 hours. Most effective within 12 hours and less effective with every 12 hours of delay. It works by preventing ovulation, fertilization, or implantation.
  • Case: Lucy (20, assaulted at a party): nursing analysis acute psychological trauma. Stay with her, explain procedures, assist with evidence, give ordered pregnancy and STI prophylaxis, wound care, hygiene help, active listening, identify her strengths, rape counselor contact, follow-up, a support person to accompany her home, and written instructions.

🔒 9. Human trafficking

  • Build trust.
  • Know the at-risk groups in your community.
  • Observe the relationship of the person who came with the patient.
  • Screen in a private room.
  • Document your suspicion in the notes.
  • Assess hydration, nutrition, and hygiene.
  • Assess safety.
🔍 Go deeper: Indicators and response
  • Indicators: someone else controls her ID, money, or speaks for her, scripted or inconsistent story, signs of abuse or branding tattoos, does not know her address, works long hours, fearful or submissive, and reluctant to be seen alone.
  • Response: see her alone, use a professional interpreter, build trust, document objectively, and follow your facility protocol. The National Human Trafficking Hotline is 1-888-373-7888.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: definition, risk factors, health effects, indicators, and response
  • UN definition: recruitment, transportation, transfer, harboring, or receipt of people by threat, force, coercion, abduction, fraud, or deception for exploitation. One in three victims worldwide is a child. In the US, forced labor sectors are private industry (63%), commercial sexual exploitation (23%), and state-imposed labor (14%). Profits are estimated at about $150 billion per year.
  • US law: the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act (2000) set the three Ps: protection, prevention, and prosecution.
  • Risk factors: poverty, marginalized community, rural location, low education, disability, little family support, running away, LGBTQIA+ identity, recent migration, a history of child abuse, sexual abuse, or IPV, and community or gang violence. Girls 12 to 16 are at particular risk.
  • Health risks: violence, rape, burns, fractures, PTSD, pregnancy, HIV and STIs, cervical cancer, dehydration, malnutrition, and substance use.
Clues from Box 9.6Examples
Appearance and healthPoor health, malnourished, ill-fitting clothes, few belongings, neglect or abuse, jaw or neck problems, debris in the vagina or rectum
BehaviorClosed body language, avoids eye contact, nervous, fearful, withdrawn, submissive, depressed, appears coached, vague about address, inconsistent story about injury
ControlSomeone else controls ID, passport, money, or immigration papers, a "sponsor" will not leave her alone, lives with the employer, branding tattoos
In careRefuses a gown or exam, refuses follow-up, reluctant to give any information

Sample questions: Can you leave your job or situation if you want? Can you come and go as you please? Have you been threatened if you try to leave? Who has your immigration papers? Are you paid? Do you have to ask permission to eat, sleep, or use the bathroom? Is there a lock on your door? Are you afraid?

  • Interventions: build trust (top priority), know at-risk groups, observe the relationship with the accompanying person, listen, screen privately, reassure, one-on-one time, examine all injuries, assess hydration, nutrition, and hygiene, do not use the patient's companion as interpreter, ask about safety, paraphrase to clarify, stay calm, understand the risk she takes by disclosing, and document your suspicion.
  • Report: notify local law enforcement and a regional social service organization experienced with trafficking. The National Human Trafficking Hotline is 1-888-373-7888.

🔍 Textbook: female genital mutilation or cutting (FGM/C)

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: female genital mutilation or cutting (FGM/C)
  • What it is: any injury to the external female genitalia for cultural or nontherapeutic reasons. It is a human rights violation and a form of violence. About 230 million women and girls have undergone it, and it is practiced in over 25 countries. It is cultural, not required by any religion. It has no health benefit.
  • US law: it is illegal to perform it on a child under 18.
WHO typeDescription
Type IRemoval of the prepuce, with removal of part or all of the clitoris
Type IIRemoval of the clitoris and part or all of the labia minora, with or without the labia majora
Type III (infibulation)Removal of part or all of the external genitalia and stitching or narrowing of the vaginal opening
Type IVAll other harmful procedures: pricking, piercing, cutting, stretching, burning, scraping, corrosive substances, or herbs placed to narrow the vagina
  • Complications: infertility, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, sexual dysfunction, infection, hemorrhage, vaginal stenosis, chronic vaginitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, urinary retention and chronic UTI, difficult childbirth, clitoral dermoid cysts and labial fusion, and anxiety, flashbacks, depression, and PTSD.
  • Nursing care: stay nonjudgmental, because many women do not see it as mutilation. Use the term the patient uses. Use plain language, pictures, and a professional interpreter (speak to the patient, not the interpreter). Include male family members in education because they influence the practice. Protect privacy and confidentiality, use trauma-sensitive language, and repeat back your understanding. Check your own feelings first.

🔍 Textbook: trauma-informed care

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: trauma-informed care
  • Every patient is a potential trauma survivor. Trauma includes IPV, sexual assault, childhood abuse, discrimination, an adverse childbirth experience, disasters, war, and separation from family.
  • Trauma survivors may have depression, mood swings, fear, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, poor concentration, anger, flashbacks, poor trust, and trouble following treatment or feeling safe in care.
  • Key components: avoid reinjury by creating physical and emotional safety, empower the patient and focus on strengths and resilience, support healing and recovery, and build survivorship skills.
  • Practical steps: ask permission before touching, let her stay clothed until the exam, and cover her during the exam.
Case: DorothyCues: repeated visits for headaches, tearful, took a phone call and said she was at the store, admitted she is afraid at home "at times," partner does not want her to work. Later she returned with anemia, poor weight gain, bruises on her face and neck, and second-trimester bleeding, with her partner staying close. The nurse should separate her privately, ask directly, assess immediate safety, document in her words with a body map and consented photos, and report as required by law.

🧬 Ch 10: Fetal Development and Genetics

From fertilization to birth: stages, placenta, fluid, circulation, and the genetics behind it.

🧠 The big idea

The placenta does the breathing, so the fetus skips the lungs.
Placenta supplies oxygen → Lungs not needed → Three shunts bypass lungs and liver → Shunts close after birth

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Stages: preembryonic (to week 2), embryonic (15 days to week 8), fetal (week 8 to birth).
  2. Cord has 2 arteries and 1 vein. The vein carries oxygen-rich blood.
  3. Oligohydramnios is under 500 mL. Hydramnios is over 2000 mL.
  4. Shunts: ductus venosus, ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale.
  5. Teratogens include alcohol, ACE inhibitors, warfarin, and the TORCH infections.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Lungs mature at 30 weeks?False. Not fully mature at 30 weeks.
⚠️ Embryo vs fetusEmbryonic stage ends at week 8. After that it is called a fetus.
⚠️ Carrier x carrier25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected for an autosomal recessive disease.
🩺 Think like a nurseTrace the blood: placenta, vein, around the liver, to the heart, then skip the lungs through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, back to the placenta by two arteries.

🧬 1. Genetics review

  • Humans have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male).
  • Chromosomes are strands of DNA. Genes are segments of DNA.
  • Anomalies can occur before fertilization, prenatally, or postnatally.
  • Most anomalies are fatal and end in spontaneous abortion (miscarriage).
  • The most common survivable anomaly is a trisomy.
TrisomyName
Trisomy 21Down syndrome (most prevalent)
Trisomy 18Edwards syndrome
Trisomy 13Patau syndrome
🧠 Memory anchor
Alphabet runs backward with the numbers: Down 21, Edwards 18, Patau 13. D then E then P, and 21 then 18 then 13.

Dominant and recessive

  • Two dominant genes: dominant trait.
  • One dominant plus one recessive: dominant trait.
  • Two recessive genes: recessive trait.
  • Many disorders come from a defective recessive gene. Autosomal dominant: one defective gene is enough. Autosomal recessive: the person carries and passes it on, and shows disease only with two. X-linked or Y-linked: gene sits on a sex chromosome.

Common genetic diseases

DiseaseInheritanceKey points
Turner syndromeMissing or incomplete X (45,X)Female. Short stature, webbed neck, ovarian failure
Cystic fibrosisAutosomal recessiveThick mucus in lungs and pancreas, salty sweat
Sickle cell anemiaAutosomal recessiveAbnormal hemoglobin, pain crises
PKU (phenylketonuria)Autosomal recessiveCannot break down phenylalanine. Newborn screen. Special diet
Tay-Sachs diseaseAutosomal recessiveProgressive nervous system destruction
Huntington diseaseAutosomal dominantAdult-onset movement and mental decline
HemophiliaX-linkedClotting factor deficiency, bleeding
Duchenne muscular dystrophyX-linkedProgressive muscle weakness in boys
Fragile X syndromeX-linkedIntellectual disability

Your slide also lists cancer among genetic abnormalities. Birth defects and genetic disorders occur in 1 in 33 infants and cause 1 in 5 infant deaths. Accurate diagnosis has improved treatment and outcomes.

Genomic medicine

  • Human Genome Project completed in 2003.
  • Newborn screening, circulating DNA as a cancer biomarker.
  • Pharmacogenomics: gene-specific drug development.
  • Genetic testing: carrier testing, prenatal testing.

🔍 Go deeper: Prenatal screening and diagnostic tests
TestWhenWhat it doesNursing point
First-trimester screen11 to 14 weeksNuchal translucency ultrasound plus blood markersScreening only, not diagnostic
Cell-free DNAFrom about 10 weeksScreens for common trisomies from maternal bloodPositive results need diagnostic confirmation
Chorionic villus sampling10 to 13 weeksPlacental tissue for chromosomes. DiagnosticSmall miscarriage risk. Consent and counseling

Reasons for genetic counseling: maternal age 35 or older at delivery, family history of a genetic condition, a previous child with an anomaly, abnormal screening, recurrent miscarriage, teratogen exposure, and known carrier status.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: race, ethnicity, and genetic conditions

Sickle cell anemia is more common in Black and Mediterranean groups. Tay-Sachs is more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish or French-Canadian descent. Both can occur in any ethnic group. Offer preconception genetic counseling and carrier screening to everyone at risk. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis can test embryos made by IVF.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: genetics vocabulary, mutations, and technology
TermMeaning
GeneticsStudy of heredity and variation
GenomicsStudy of all of a person's genes and how they interact with each other and the environment
PharmacogenomicsHow genes influence drug effects and side effects
GeneUnit of heredity on a segment of DNA at a specific place (locus) on a chromosome
AlleleOne of two or more versions of a gene. One comes from each parent
HomozygousTwo matching alleles. WW is homozygous dominant and ww is homozygous recessive
HeterozygousTwo different alleles (Ww). The dominant one is usually expressed
GenotypeThe specific genetic makeup
PhenotypeThe observed characteristics, set by genotype plus environment
KaryotypePicture of the number, form, and size of chromosomes, made from white blood cells or fetal cells in amniotic fluid. 46,XX is a typical female and 46,XY is a typical male
  • Numbers: 1 in 33 US infants has a birth defect or genetic disorder, and they cause 1 in 5 infant deaths. About 8 million newborns worldwide have a birth defect each year.
  • Mutations: inherited (passed in egg or sperm), spontaneous (new in an egg or sperm at conception), or acquired (in body cells after conception, passed to daughter cells). Cystic fibrosis is an inherited mutation. Marfan syndrome is inherited as autosomal dominant.
  • Human Genome Project: 1990 to 2003. Maps, sequences, and finds the function of the human genome.
  • Gene therapy adds, replaces, or repairs genes. It has been used for conditions including cystic fibrosis, blindness, hemophilia, sickle cell disease, and leukemia.
  • Newborn screening is the most widely used application of genetics. Preconception carrier screening is offered for conditions such as Tay-Sachs in groups at higher risk (Ashkenazi Jewish, French-Canadian, or Cajun descent).
  • Nuchal translucency: increased thickness on ultrasound between 11 and 14 weeks may suggest trisomy 21. Amniocentesis is diagnostic but invasive.
  • Law (GINA 2008): protects against genetic discrimination by health insurers and employers. It does not cover life, disability, or long-term care insurance.
  • Ethical issues: privacy, who can access genetic information, stigma, reproductive decisions, and whether to test when there is no cure.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: inheritance patterns in detail
PatternKey featuresExamples
Autosomal dominantOne altered gene (heterozygous) is enough. 50% chance each child. Males and females equal. Male-to-male transmission possible. Variable expression and reduced penetrance can hide a family history. New mutations occurAchondroplasia, neurofibromatosis, Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta type 1
Autosomal recessiveTwo altered genes needed. Both parents are carriers. 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected. Usually one generation. Higher chance with consanguinityCystic fibrosis, galactosemia, PKU, Tay-Sachs, sickle cell disease
X-linked recessiveMore males affected because they have one X. No male-to-male transmission. An affected father has carrier daughters. A carrier mother: 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriersHemophilia, color blindness, Duchenne muscular dystrophy
X-linked dominant (rare)Affected father: all daughters and no sons affected. Affected mother: 50% of children. Males more severe and often lethalHypophosphatemic (vitamin D-resistant) rickets
MultifactorialMany genes plus environment. Risk rises with closer relatives. Identical twins are not 100% alikeCleft lip and palate, spina bifida, pyloric stenosis (more in males), clubfoot, hip dysplasia (more in females), heart defects
MitochondrialPassed from the mother to all children. Affects high-energy tissues like brain, eye, and muscle. ProgressiveKearns-Sayre syndrome, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Genomic imprintingOnly the maternal or paternal allele is expressed, so the effect depends on which parent it came fromPrader-Willi, Angelman, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: chromosomal abnormalities
  • Chromosomal abnormalities occur in about 1% to 2% of live births and much more often in miscarriages and stillbirths. They often come with congenital anomalies and intellectual disability. Most happen by random events, not inheritance.
  • Number errors: usually from nondisjunction, failure of a pair to separate in cell division. Monosomy (one copy) almost always ends in early miscarriage. Trisomy (three copies) can survive when the chromosome has few genes: 21, 18, 13, and X. Mosaicism means only some cells carry the error, and symptoms are usually milder.
  • Structure errors: deletion (missing piece), duplication (extra piece), inversion (flipped piece), ring chromosome, and translocation (a piece moves to another chromosome, the most clinically significant). Balanced changes have no gain or loss, so the person is usually normal but has a higher risk of miscarriage and abnormal children. Unbalanced changes gain or lose material and cause severe effects.
  • Sex chromosome abnormalities are usually milder: Turner syndrome (females) and Klinefelter syndrome (males). They may cause infertility, growth problems, and learning problems.

☠️ 2. Teratogens

⭐ High yieldTeratogens mess with fetal development. A teratogen is any substance, organism, physical agent, or deficiency that can cause abnormal structure or function during gestation.
GroupExamples
EnvironmentPesticides, air quality, lead
DrugsAlcohol, ACE inhibitors, anticonvulsants, cocaine, warfarin
InfectionsCMV, varicella, rubella, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, Zika
🧠 Memory anchor: TORCH
Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, Zika), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes.
🔍 Go deeper: Critical periods and what each teratogen does

Timing matters. In the first 2 weeks the effect is usually all or nothing (loss or no harm). Weeks 3 to 8 is the period of greatest structural risk. After week 8 teratogens more often affect growth and the brain.

TeratogenEffect
AlcoholFetal alcohol spectrum disorders: growth restriction, facial changes, learning and behavior problems
ACE inhibitors and ARBsFetal kidney injury and low amniotic fluid
WarfarinNasal and bone abnormalities, central nervous system defects, bleeding
Phenytoin and valproateFacial changes and growth problems. Valproate raises neural tube defect risk
IsotretinoinCraniofacial, heart, and brain defects. Contraception required
TetracyclineTooth staining
LithiumHeart defects
CocaineAbruption, preterm birth, growth restriction
ThalidomideLimb defects
CytomegalovirusSmall head, hearing loss, eye damage, brain calcifications
RubellaCataracts, deafness, heart defects
ToxoplasmosisHydrocephalus, eye damage. Avoid cat litter and undercooked meat
SyphilisRash, bone changes, nasal discharge, stillbirth
VaricellaLimb scarring and underdevelopment
ZikaMicrocephaly
Lead, mercury, radiationBrain and growth effects
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: classification, timing, and teratogen effects
  • Four types: physical agents, metabolic conditions, infection, and drugs or chemical agents.
  • Effects: physical deformities, behavior and emotional problems, lower IQ, preterm labor, and spontaneous abortion. The embryo is most susceptible during the critical period of differentiation (embryonic stage). Effects depend on timing and the stage of development.
  • FDA 2015: the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule replaced the old letter categories to help providers counsel pregnant patients.

HormoneSourceJob

Oogenesis and the menstrual cycle

Oogenesis is the development of the ovum in the ovary. Final events take place over about 12 days.

CyclePhaseWhat happens
Ovarian (the ova matures)FollicularStarts day 1 of menses. Lasts 12 to 14 days
OvulatoryEstrogen peaks and the oocyte is released. Some women feel mid-cycle pain called mittelschmerz

Endometrial (the uterus responds)MenstrualEndometrium sheds

Order of the endometrial phases in time: menstrual, proliferative, secretory. The ovarian phases (follicular, ovulation, luteal) run alongside these.

🥚 4. Conception and stages

  • Conception happens in the fertile time of the cycle. Fertilization occurs in the fallopian tube.
  • Division: zygote, then morula, then blastocyst.
  • The blastocyst starts to implant in the endometrium about day 5 to 6. Implantation (attachment and placental formation) is complete 7 to 10 days after conception.
  • Sex is set at fertilization by the sperm: XX is a female zygote, XY is a male zygote.
StageWhenKey events
PreembryonicFertilization through week 2Conception, cell division, implantation
Embryonic15 days after conception through week 8Basic structures of all organs complete. Heart beats at a regular rhythm. CNS forms. Cord and amniotic sac form. Placenta begins working
FetalEnd of week 8 until birthThe embryo is mature enough to be called a fetus. Growth and organ maturation
⭐ High yieldSlide question answers: heartbeat at regular rhythm in the embryonic stage = TRUE. Lungs fully mature at 30 weeks = FALSE.
🔍 Go deeper: Fertilization, implantation, and twins
  • Sperm capacitate, release enzymes (acrosomal reaction), and penetrate the zona pellucida of the egg. The zygote has 46 chromosomes.
  • Cleavage divides the zygote. By day 3 to 4 it is a morula. The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (becomes the embryo) and trophoblast (becomes the placenta and membranes).
  • The lining where it implants is called the decidua.
  • hCG appears in blood about 8 to 11 days after conception. It doubles about every 48 to 72 hours in early pregnancy and peaks around weeks 8 to 11.
TwinsHow they formPlacenta and sacs
Dizygotic (fraternal)Two eggs, two spermSeparate placentas, chorions, and amnions. Can be different sexes
Monozygotic (identical), split days 0 to 3One egg splits earlyTwo chorions, two amnions
Monozygotic, split days 4 to 8One egg splits laterOne chorion, two amnions
Monozygotic, split days 8 to 12Late splitOne chorion, one amnion (high risk)
Monozygotic, split after day 13Very late splitConjoined twins
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: fertilization step by step, germ layers, and implantation
  • Dating: an average pregnancy is about 280 days (40 weeks) from the LMP. Fertilization usually happens about 14 days after the LMP, so true gestation is about 266 days.
  • Fertilization takes about 24 hours and happens in the outer third of the ampulla of the fallopian tube. Sperm swim about 7 inches. More than 200 million sperm per mL are in semen, but only one enters the ovum. The zona pellucida blocks the rest and disappears in about 5 days.
  • Meiosis and chromosomes: gametes are haploid (23 chromosomes). Fertilization restores the diploid number (46). The zygote has about 25,000 genes. The sperm (X or Y) determines the baby's sex.
  • Cleavage: the zygote divides as it moves through the tube. After four divisions the 16-cell solid ball is the morula ("little mulberry"), which reaches the uterus about 72 hours after fertilization. A fluid-filled space forms and it becomes the hollow blastocyst.
  • Blastocyst: the inner cell mass becomes the embryo and amnion. The outer trophoblast becomes the chorion and helps form the placenta.
  • Implantation: the trophoblast attaches to the endometrium about 7 to 10 days after conception, usually in the upper uterus (fundus). The fundus has a rich blood supply, strong muscle fibers that clamp blood vessels after the placenta separates, and the thickest lining, so the placenta does not attach too deeply.
Germ layerBecomes
EctodermCentral nervous system, special senses, skin, and glands
MesodermSkeletal, urinary, circulatory, and reproductive organs
EndodermRespiratory system, liver, pancreas, and digestive system
  • Membranes: the chorion has fingerlike chorionic villi. The amnion comes from the ectoderm. The yolk sac forms on day 8 or 9 and feeds the embryo in weeks 2 and 3 before the placenta works, then becomes part of the cord. The amnion expands until it touches the chorion to form the amniotic sac (bag of waters).
  • Twins: identical (monozygotic) twins come from one egg that splits, usually share one placenta, and have the same genes and sex. Fraternal (dizygotic) twins come from two eggs and two sperm, usually have separate placentas, share about 50% of genes, and can be different sexes. Fraternal twins are more common.

StructureJob
PlacentaNutrient, metabolic, and gas exchange by diffusion. Hormone production
Embryonic membranesSterile environment and protection. Amnion and chorion (the bag of water)
Amniotic fluidCushions, protects, warms
Umbilical cordConnects the fetus to the placenta. 2 arteries and 1 vein. Cushioned by Wharton jelly

Hormones made by the placenta

HormoneJob
hCGKeeps the corpus luteum alive so it keeps making estrogen and progesterone. Detected by pregnancy tests
hPL (hCS)Raises maternal blood glucose for the fetus. Breast growth
EstrogenUterine growth, breast development, more blood flow
ProgesteroneMaintains the endometrium and quiets the uterus

🧠 Memory anchor: Cord = 2 A, 1 V
Two Arteries, One Vein. "AVA": Arteries Vein Arteries. Unlike the adult body, the vein carries the oxygen-rich blood.

Amniotic fluid

  • Volume changes with gestational age.
  • Made from fluid moved from maternal blood and from fetal urine.
  • Needed for growth, especially lung development.
  • Functions: keeps temperature steady, allows growth, cushions trauma, keeps the cord free from compression, allows fetal movement.
AlterationAmount at term
Oligohydramnios (too little)Less than 500 mL
Hydramnios (too much)More than 2000 mL
🔍 Go deeper: Placenta, transport, and amniotic fluid
  • Placenta: forms from the trophoblast and the maternal decidua. Works well by weeks 10 to 12. At term it weighs about 500 g. The fetal side is shiny (Schultze) and the maternal side is rough and lobed (Duncan).
  • Functions: respiratory, nutritive, excretory, endocrine, and a limited barrier. Many viruses, alcohol, and drugs cross.
  • Cord: about 50 to 60 cm long with 2 arteries and 1 vein. A single umbilical artery can signal anomalies.
How things crossExamples
Simple diffusionOxygen, carbon dioxide, water
Facilitated diffusionGlucose
Active transportAmino acids, vitamins, minerals
PinocytosisLarge molecules such as IgG antibodies

IgG crosses the placenta and gives the newborn temporary immunity. IgM does not cross, so a high IgM in a newborn points to infection before birth.

Amniotic fluidDetails
Amount at termAbout 800 to 1200 mL. Clear to pale straw
CycleFetus swallows it and urinates it back, so it keeps recycling
Testing for ruptured membranesNitrazine paper turns blue (alkaline). Ferning pattern under a microscope
Oligohydramnios causesFetal kidney problems (renal agenesis), growth restriction, postterm pregnancy, ruptured membranes
Hydramnios causesMaternal diabetes, multiples, fetal gastrointestinal atresia (cannot swallow), neural tube defects
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: placenta, hormones, cord size, amniotic fluid, and complications
  • Placenta: trophoblast cells first appear about 4 days after fertilization. The placenta usually forms at the fundus and its structure is complete by about week 12. It is a transient fetal organ and a complex endocrine organ. It exchanges gas, nutrients, and waste, protects the fetus from the mother's immune system, and near birth makes hormones that mature fetal organs.
  • No blood mixing: fetal and maternal blood never mix. Layers of fetal tissue (the placental barrier) separate them, and exchange is by diffusion. Uterine arteries deliver nutrients and uterine veins carry waste away.
  • Hormones: hCG, human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS or hPL), progesterone, estrogen, and glucocorticoids.
  • The placenta is a pass-through, not a barrier. Almost everything the mother takes in (food, alcohol, drugs) reaches the fetus. Nine in ten pregnant women take medicine, and many drugs have not been studied in pregnancy, so every medication must be checked with the provider.
  • Cord: forms from the amnion about the end of week 2. One large vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus. Two small arteries carry deoxygenated blood and waste to the placenta. Wharton jelly prevents compression. At term it is about 50 to 60 cm (20 to 24 inches) long and about 2 cm wide.
  • Amniotic fluid is about 98% water and 2% organic matter, slightly alkaline, and contains albumin, urea, uric acid, creatinine, bilirubin, lecithin, sphingomyelin, epithelial cells, vernix, and lanugo. It comes from fluid moved from maternal blood and fetal urine, and the fetus swallows and voids it. Volume is about a liter at term. It peaks around 34 weeks and then gradually decreases.
AlterationComplications (textbook)
Oligohydramnios (too little)Uteroplacental insufficiency, umbilical cord compression, meconium aspiration, fetal deformation, pulmonary hypoplasia
Polyhydramnios (too much)Premature rupture of membranes, preterm labor and birth, macrosomia, cord prolapse, maternal respiratory compromise, prolonged second stage of labor, postpartum uterine atony

❤️ 7. Fetal circulation

Blood flows from the placenta to and through the fetus and back to the placenta. Three shunts let blood skip the fluid-filled lungs and the immature liver.

ShuntConnectsClosure after birth
Ductus venosusUmbilical vein to the inferior vena cavaCloses when the cord is clamped
Ductus arteriosusMain pulmonary artery to the aortaInitial closure within 72 hours in a term infant. Permanent closure at 3 to 4 weeks
Foramen ovaleRight atrium to left atriumInitial closure within 1 to 2 hours. Permanent closure by the 6th month
  1. Oxygenated blood leaves the placenta in the umbilical vein.
  2. Ductus venosus carries most of it past the liver to the inferior vena cava and the right atrium.
  3. Foramen ovale sends it to the left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta to the brain and body.
  4. Blood returning from the head and arms enters the right side, and most skips the lungs through the ductus arteriosus.
  5. Two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.
🔍 Go deeper: Why the shunts close at birth
  • Fetal lungs have high resistance, so little blood goes there. Fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen tightly, which helps in a low-oxygen environment.
  • First breath: lung resistance drops and blood flows to the lungs. Left atrial pressure rises and pushes the foramen ovale flap shut.
  • Ductus arteriosus: higher oxygen and lower prostaglandins cause it to close. Indomethacin can help close a patent ductus. Prostaglandin E1 keeps it open in certain heart defects.
  • Clamping the cord removes the low-resistance placenta and closes the ductus venosus.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: purpose of fetal circulation
  • The fetal heart starts developing about 22 days after conception. Gas exchange happens at the placenta, with oxygen saturation of about 70% to 80%.
  • The shunts send oxygen-rich blood to vital areas (heart and brain) first and keep oxygen-poor blood away from the underdeveloped lungs and liver. Prostaglandins from the placenta keep the shunts open during fetal life.
  • Because the placenta does the work of the lungs and liver, large volumes of oxygenated blood are not needed there.
🔍 Go deeper: When the fetal lungs are mature and when the shunts close
QuestionAnswer
When does the fetus start making surfactant?About 24 weeks (edge of viability)
When are the lungs considered mature?36 to 38 weeks. They are not mature at 30 weeks
How is maturity confirmed?Amniotic fluid L/S ratio of 2:1 or greater and phosphatidylglycerol present. Under 2:1 or no phosphatidylglycerol means immature lungs and risk of respiratory distress syndrome
What helps if birth is expected early?Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) speed surfactant production
Do the lungs finish growing at birth?No. New alveoli keep forming after birth through early childhood
ShuntFirst (functional) closurePermanent closureBecomes
Ductus venosusWhen the cord is clampedAfter birth as flow stopsLigamentum venosum
Foramen ovaleWithin 1 to 2 hoursBy the 6th monthFossa ovalis
Ductus arteriosusWithin 72 hours in a term infant3 to 4 weeksLigamentum arteriosum
🧠 Why they close
The first breath drops lung resistance and raises left atrial pressure, which pushes the foramen ovale shut. Higher oxygen and falling prostaglandins close the ductus arteriosus. Cord clamping ends flow through the ductus venosus.

🔍 9. Infertility

ItemContent
Risk factorsAutoimmune and endocrine disorders, eating disorders and malnutrition, excess alcohol or exercise, older age, obesity (female), STIs, pollutants, smoking, impotence (male)
CausesOvulatory dysfunction, tubal and pelvic pathology, cervical mucus factors
DiagnosisSTI screening, laboratory tests, semen analysis, ovulatory, endometrial, and radiological exams
TreatmentHormones, lifestyle change, steroids, antibiotics, surgery
ARTIVF, donor sperm or eggs. Ethical dilemmas. Nurse's role: support and reinforce education
🔍 Go deeper: Definition, workup, and treatment
  • Definition: no pregnancy after 12 months of unprotected sex (under 35), or 6 months (35 and older).
  • Workup: semen analysis (count of about 15 million per mL or more, plus motility and shape), ovulation tracking and progesterone level, hysterosalpingogram for tubal patency, and sometimes laparoscopy.
  • Treatment: ovulation drugs such as clomiphene (hot flashes, multiple births), intrauterine insemination, IVF (stimulate ovaries, retrieve eggs, fertilize, transfer embryos), and ICSI (inject one sperm into an egg).
  • Risks: multiple gestation and ovarian hyperstimulation. Offer emotional support. Infertility is stressful for both partners.

👩‍⚕️ 10. Nurse's role in genetics and genetic counseling

  • Preconception counseling for women at risk of passing on a genetic disorder.
  • Prenatal care for women with genetically linked disorders.
  • Screen infants for birth defects and genetic disorders.
  • Participate in risk assessments for genetic conditions.
  • Give current, accurate information as technology changes.
  • Give emotional support and refer to support groups.

Genetic counseling advises patients or relatives at risk of an inherited disorder about its nature, the chance of developing it, and the options for management and family planning. The ideal time is before conception.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: genetic counseling, pedigree, and nurse roles
  • Genetic counseling is a communication and education process that explains genetics, the disorder, how it is inherited, and the options for testing, management, and family planning. It is more than giving information: the patient alone decides, and information is given in a nondirective, nonjudgmental way. Ideal time is before conception.
  • Consultation purposes: confirm, diagnose, or rule out conditions, find management issues, calculate and explain risk, discuss ethics and law, and arrange psychosocial support.
  • Pedigree: a family tree diagram, ideally three generations, built from a detailed family history. It may reveal private facts (adoption, IVF, nonbiologic parent), so confidentiality is essential. Records may be requested for relatives.
  • Urgency: information is needed fast when a defect is found prenatally or a baby is born with one. In other situations the family needs time over several meetings.
Who may benefit from counseling (Box 10.2)
Maternal age 35 or older at birth, or paternal age 40 or older
A previous child, parent, or close relative with an inherited disease, anomaly, metabolic, developmental, or chromosomal disorder
Consanguinity or incest, or an X-linked family history, or known carrier status
Abnormal pregnancy screening (alpha-fetoprotein, triple or quad screen, amniocentesis, ultrasound), a stillborn with anomalies, or two or more pregnancy losses
Teratogen exposure or risk, or concerns about a disorder common in their ethnic group
Abnormal newborn screening, a child with a major malformation, growth abnormality, developmental delay, intellectual disability, blindness, or deafness
Focused genetic history questions (Box 10.3)
Cause and age of death for relatives who died young. Any consanguinity
Serious or chronic illness and age of onset. Cancers in close relatives
Female relatives with miscarriages, stillbirths, diabetes, or alcohol or drug use in pregnancy. Ages at childbearing, especially over 35
Intellectual disability, developmental delay, metabolic disorders such as PKU, chromosomal disorders, progressive neurologic disorders, affective disorders
Current ages of both parents. Racial and ethnic background
  • Nurse roles: take the family history, explain tests, schedule testing, answer questions, give emotional support, refer to genetic specialists, social workers, clergy, or an ethicist, and follow up after counseling. Help families weigh facts, values, and context.
  • Robert and Kate (Kate is 41, 3 years trying): first step is a thorough family health history and referral for genetic counseling. Age 35 or older is a reason for counseling. Prenatal tests could include a nuchal translucency scan, cell-free DNA or screening, and possibly chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.
  • Martin case (cystic fibrosis): Mr. Martin is a carrier and wants his wife tested. Mrs. Martin does not. The nurse gives clear information about carrier probability (if both carry, 25% affected), testing options, and counseling, supports their communication, and respects that the decision is the couple's. If the nurse disagrees, she must stay nonjudgmental and not push her own view.
  • Ethics: prenatal results can lead to a decision to end a pregnancy, even when results are not conclusive. The choice is the patient's, and support must be nondirective and nonjudgmental.

🤰 Ch 11: Maternal Adaptation During Pregnancy

Signs of pregnancy, what every body system does, nutrition, and the emotional road.

🧠 The big idea

Hormones and blood volume change every system, which causes the symptoms.
More hormones and blood volume → Every system adapts → Symptoms and lab changes → Normal vs complicated

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Presumptive = she feels it. Probable = examiner finds it. Positive = only a pregnancy can cause it.
  2. A positive pregnancy test is PROBABLE, not positive.
  3. Positive signs: ultrasound, Doppler heart tones, fetal movement felt by a clinician.
  4. Blood volume rises 1200 to 1600 mL, so hemoglobin falls from dilution.
  5. First trimester ambivalence is normal.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ OxytocinReleased by the POSTERIOR pituitary. Prolactin is anterior.
⚠️ Expected findingNausea is expected in pregnancy. Hypertension, dry mouth, and diarrhea are not.
🩺 Think like a nurseAlways ask: is this a normal adaptation or a warning sign? Normal: nausea, frequency, fatigue, constipation. Warning: severe headache, visual changes, sudden swelling, bleeding.

🔎 1. Signs of pregnancy

⭐ High yieldSort by who finds it. Presumptive = the woman feels it (subjective). Probable = the examiner finds it, but something else could cause it (objective). Positive = only a pregnancy can cause it (definite).
Presumptive (subjective)When
Amenorrhea4 weeks

❌ Watch outA positive pregnancy test is a PROBABLE sign, not a positive sign. hCG can be raised by other conditions. This was class slide question #1: the answer is false.
🧠 Memory anchor
Positive signs are the baby itself: the baby is SEEN (ultrasound), HEARD (Doppler), or FELT by a clinician (movement). Anything else is probable or presumptive.
🔍 Go deeper: hCG and fundal landmarks
  • hCG: blood tests detect it about 8 to 11 days after conception and urine tests slightly later. It doubles about every 48 to 72 hours early on and peaks around 8 to 11 weeks. A rise that is too slow raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage.
  • Quickening: 16 to 25 weeks. It is often felt earlier in later pregnancies.
GestationTop of the uterus (fundus)
12 weeksAt the symphysis pubis
16 weeksHalfway between symphysis and umbilicus
20 weeksAt the umbilicus
36 weeksAt the xiphoid process
38 to 40 weeksDrops as the baby settles into the pelvis (lightening), often earlier in a first pregnancy
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook Box 11.1: the three sign groups
GroupWho noticesSigns (time of occurrence)
Presumptive (subjective)The pregnant personAmenorrhea, breast enlargement and tenderness, nausea and vomiting, urinary frequency without dysuria, excessive fatigue, quickening (18 to 20 weeks), skin hyperpigmentation
Probable (objective)The provider on examBraxton Hicks contractions (16 to 28 weeks), positive pregnancy test (4 to 12 weeks), enlarged abdomen, ballottement (16 to 18 weeks), Goodell sign (8 weeks), Chadwick sign (6 to 8 weeks), Hegar sign (softening of the lower uterine segment, about 6 weeks), palpable fetal outline
Positive (diagnostic)Directly from the fetusFetal heart rate seen on ultrasound (5 to 6 weeks), ultrasound outline of embryo or fetus, fetal movement felt by an experienced clinician (about 20 weeks), auscultation of fetal heart tones
  • Only positive signs are 100% certain. A pregnancy test is a PROBABLE sign.
  • Other causes of presumptive signs: amenorrhea (early menopause, endocrine problems, malnutrition, anemia, diabetes, long-distance running, cancer, stress), nausea (GI disorders, infection, eating disorders), fatigue (anemia, stress, viral illness), breast tenderness (cystic mastitis, premenstrual changes, oral contraceptives), urinary frequency (infection, cystocele, pelvic tumors).
  • Other causes of probable signs: uterine tumors, polyps, infection, and pelvic congestion can change uterine shape and size.
  • Ballottement: the examiner pushes against the cervix on pelvic exam and feels the floating fetus rebound.
  • Case: Marva, 17, thought she had a stomach virus. Nausea, exhaustion, two missed periods, and unprotected sex led to a positive test. Next: confirm, estimate gestational age, give early pregnancy information, start prenatal care, and give nonjudgmental support.

🧫 2. Pregnancy tests (Table 11.1)

TypeSpecimenExamplesRemarks
Agglutination inhibition (qualitative)UrinePregnosticon, GravindexIf hCG is present, agglutination does NOT occur, which is positive. Reliable 14 to 21 days after conception. 95% accurate
Immunoradiometric assayBlood serumNeocept, PregnosisMeasures ability of blood to inhibit binding of radiolabeled hCG. Reliable 6 to 8 days after conception. 99% accurate
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)Blood serum or urineOver-the-counter home and office tests. PreciseEnzyme bonds with hCG in urine. Reliable 4 days after implantation. 99% accurate if hCG-specific
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: hCG details and home test limits
  • hCG is a glycoprotein and the earliest biochemical marker. Many tests detect the beta subunit. Below 5 mIU/mL is negative. Above 25 mIU/mL is positive.
  • Doubling time: hCG usually doubles about every 48 to 72 hours in early pregnancy and peaks around 8 to 10 weeks. This peak matches the morning sickness period of about 6 to 12 weeks. Appears in the maternal blood as early as day 8 after conception.
  • Interpretation: low levels are linked to ectopic pregnancy and higher than expected levels to multiples. Doubling time helps separate normal from abnormal pregnancies.
  • False positives: ovarian cancer, choriocarcinoma, and hydatidiform mole can raise hCG.
  • Home tests: available in the US since 1977. Highly accurate, convenient, and private. Some detect 97% of pregnancies one day after a missed period but others only 50% to 60% on that day. The main concern is a false negative from testing too early. If menses stay absent, retest in 1 week. Confirm a positive with a Doppler, ultrasound, exam, or serum test.
  • After a positive test: estimate gestational age and give counseling and early pregnancy teaching. Prenatal care schedule is set.

🫀 3. Physiologic adaptations by system

Your slide shows normal findings and the complicated pregnancy version for each system. Learn both columns.

SystemNormal pregnancyIf complicated
CardiovascularCardiac output and heart rate rise. Heart enlarges. Peripheral arteries dilate, so varicose veins and lower blood pressure in mid-pregnancyGestational hypertension, preeclampsia. Cardiomyopathy. High maternal death with structural heart disease, including pulmonary arterial hypertension
HematologicBlood volume up 1200 to 1600 mL. Hemoglobin and platelets fall from dilution. More iron, folic acid, and B12 needed. More white blood cells and fibrinogen. Hypercoagulable stateVenous thrombosis (clots)
RespiratoryMore oxygen use and more minute ventilation. Vital capacity falls as the uterus shrinks the chest cavity late. DyspneaPulmonary edema in severe preeclampsia, pulmonary emboli, pneumonia
RenalKidneys enlarge and GFR rises. Less reabsorption by tubules. Ureters relax and compress, mostly on the rightHydronephrosis, UTI, pyelonephritis, kidney stones. Anuria and high creatinine in severe preeclampsia
DigestiveSlower gut motility causes constipation. Cardiac sphincter relaxes causing refluxSevere hyperemesis with dehydration. Esophagitis and gastritis
LiverLower transaminases and bilirubin from dilution. Slower gallbladder emptying. More cholesterol and triglyceridesHELLP syndrome (high liver enzymes). Cholelithiasis. Fatty liver. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
PancreasMore insulin production. Stable enzyme secretionPancreatitis. Gestational diabetes. Worse control in type 1 diabetes
NervousSedation and fatigue from allopregnanoloneLower seizure threshold in preeclampsia. Cerebral edema and stroke in severe preeclampsia. Hyperreflexia
ImmuneSuppressed immune responseSevere systemic infections
Bone and muscleMore calcium turnover. Insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. Posture changesOsteoporotic fractures late. Severe back and pelvic girdle pain
BreastsMore alveoli, larger glands, more supportive tissueNot known
SpleenEnlarges, probably from more blood flowNot known
AdiposeMore fat in early pregnancy, used laterObesity. Excessive gain with gestational diabetes
⚠️ TrapClass slide question #2: which would a nurse expect in a pregnant woman? Complaints of nausea. Not hypertension, dry mouth, or diarrhea. Pregnancy brings constipation, more saliva (ptyalism), and mid-pregnancy BP drops.
