🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: reproductive system in detail (Table 11.1)
OrganTextbook adaptations
UterusWeight 70 g to about 1,100 g. Capacity 10 mL to 5,000 mL. Size about 20 times and capacity about 500 times nonpregnant. Walls thin to 1.5 cm or less. Pear shaped and solid becomes a soft hollow globe. Exits the pelvis by 12 weeks. Growth early is hyperplasia, later mostly hypertrophy from stretch. 80% to 90% of uterine blood flow goes to the placenta. The uterine artery diameter about doubles. Braxton Hicks contractions begin in the first trimester
Lower uterine segment (isthmus)Thins and softens (Hegar sign) at about 6 weeks. Causes exaggerated anteflexion early
Fundus landmarksUmbilicus and 20 cm at 20 weeks. Xiphoid process at about 36 weeks. Drops at 38 to 40 weeks with lightening. Fundal height best matches weeks between 18 and 32 weeks. Obesity, hydramnios, and fibroids reduce accuracy
LighteningThe head descends and engages. First pregnancy: about 2 weeks before labor. Later pregnancies: at the onset of labor. Breathing eases but bladder pressure and frequency return
CervixSoftens (Goodell) at about 8 weeks from vasocongestion and estrogen. More glands and mucus. Progesterone forms the mucus plug. Bluish color (Chadwick). Cervical ripening starts about 4 weeks before birth
VaginaThicker mucosa, loosened connective tissue, longer vault. Leukorrhea in the second trimester. Vaginal pH rises, which increases risk of candidiasis. Thrush in the newborn if infected at birth
OvariesEnlarge until about weeks 12 to 14. Ovulation stops because estrogen and progesterone block FSH and LH. The corpus luteum regresses and the placenta takes over progesterone at about weeks 6 to 7
BreastsFuller, tender, visible veins, larger and more erect nipples, darker areolae, prominent Montgomery tubercles, striae. Blood flow doubles. Colostrum can be expressed by the third trimester
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: gastrointestinal and cardiovascular system numbers
SystemTextbook details
Gums and mouthGums hyperemic, swollen, and friable from estrogen and more blood vessels. Saliva more acidic. Ptyalism (up to 2 L a day) often resolves in the second trimester. More plaque and periodontal disease (gingivitis and periodontitis). Evidence for harm to the pregnancy is inconclusive
MotilityProgesterone relaxes smooth muscle. Gastric emptying slows. Peristalsis decreases, so more water is absorbed. Constipation (also from low fiber, low fluids, iron, inactivity, and a displaced bowel). Hemorrhoids follow. Reflux and heartburn come from a relaxed cardiac sphincter
GallbladderSlow emptying. Gallstones about 12% in the perinatal and postpartum period. Risks: BMI over 30 and multiparity. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is safe in any trimester
Nausea and vomitingUp to 90%. Starts about 6 weeks, peaks 6 to 12 weeks, usually gone by 20 weeks. Linked to hCG, estrogen, progesterone, reflux, genetics, and low tone and motility
Blood volumeUp 1,100 to 1,600 mL, about 30% to 50%. Begins at weeks 10 to 12, peaks at weeks 30 to 34, slightly lower by week 40. Plasma volume rises about 40% to 60%, which is about 75% of the increase. Supports hydration, uterine perfusion, and a reserve for blood loss at birth
Physiologic anemiaPlasma rises more than red cell mass, so hemoglobin and hematocrit fall (hemodilution). Normal adaptation
Cardiac outputUp 30% to 50%, typically peaks at 20 to 24 weeks, then eases slightly. Left lateral position increases venous return. Supine position lowers output and can cause dizziness and tachycardia.
Heart rateUp 10 to 15 bpm, up to about 30 near term. Persists to term
Blood pressureSlightly lower, especially diastolic, from progesterone vasodilation. Falls 5 to 10 mm Hg in the second trimester (starts about 7 weeks, lowest mid-pregnancy) and returns to baseline by term
Red cells and ironRed cell number up 20% to 30%. Erythropoietin rises 50%. Iron is needed. Many start pregnancy with low stores
ClottingFibrinogen and clotting factors rise. Hypercoagulable. Venous stasis raises DVT risk. Preexisting heart disease may decompensate as volume peaks. Monitor closely at 28 to 35 weeks
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: respiratory, renal, musculoskeletal, skin
SystemTextbook details
RespiratoryDiaphragm rises up to 4 cm. Chest circumference up 2 to 3 inches. Breathing becomes thoracic. Tidal volume up 30% to 40%. Oxygen use up 20% to 40%. Hyperventilation and hypocapnia. Airway resistance and lung compliance unchanged. Dyspnea in 60% to 75%. Nasal congestion and nosebleeds. Women with asthma or pneumonia can decompensate sooner
RenalKidneys enlarge 1 to 1.5 cm. Pelvis and ureters dilate, especially on the right, so urinary stasis and infection risk rise. Renal blood flow up 50% to 80%. GFR up to 50% from the second trimester. Drugs cleared by the kidney may need higher or more frequent doses. Bladder capacity doubles by term. Kidneys work more when she lies on her side. Changes take 4 to 6 weeks to settle after birth
MusculoskeletalRelaxin and progesterone loosen the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis (peaks at the start of the third trimester). Forward tilt of the pelvis, lordosis, compensatory curve in the neck and upper back, waddling gait, low back pain. Joint laxity raises injury risk
SkinHyperpigmentation from estrogen, progesterone, and MSH (nipples, areolae, umbilicus, perineum, axilla). Melasma in up to 75%. Linea nigra from umbilicus to pubis. Striae are most prominent at 6 to 7 months, more common in younger people, with a family history, larger infants, or higher BMI. Cocoa butter and olive oil are not proven. Vascular spiders and palmar erythema from estrogen. Varicosities. Hair: fewer follicles rest, then shedding follows birth. Nails grow faster and may be brittle
Varicosity preventionElevate both legs, change positions often, rest on the left side, walk daily, avoid tight clothing and knee-high hose, support hose if already present
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: endocrine, placental hormones, and immune system (Table 11.2)
Hormone or glandRole in pregnancy
hCGMaintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over. Basis of pregnancy tests. Appears as early as day 8. Peaks at 8 to 10 weeks and then declines
hCS or hPLPrepares breasts for lactation. Insulin antagonist. Raises free fatty acids and lowers maternal glucose use so glucose reaches the fetus
RelaxinFrom the placenta and corpus luteum. Loosens the pubic symphysis, dilates the cervix, may delay labor by suppressing oxytocin
ProgesteroneThe hormone of pregnancy. Maintains the endometrium, inhibits contractions, suppresses the maternal immune response, and develops breasts. Relaxes smooth muscle
EstrogenEnlarges uterus, genitals, and breasts. Increases vascularity. Relaxes ligaments. Linked to skin changes, salivation, gum and nasal hyperemia
ThyroidEnlarges slightly and makes more hormone. Maternal T4 is critical for fetal brain development before 20 weeks. Basal metabolic rate rises 20% to 25%
PituitaryFSH and LH suppressed. Prolactin up 10 times, but progesterone blocks its effect on the breast until the placenta is delivered. Oxytocin (posterior) triggers contractions, milk let-down, and afterpains. ADH unchanged
Pancreas and glucoseEarly pregnancy: glucose falls because the fetus takes it. Second half: hPL, cortisol, and other hormones cause insulin resistance, so she makes more insulin. Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta. Too few beta cells leads to gestational diabetes
AdrenalCortisol clearance falls so levels rise. 80% to 90% is inactivated by the placenta to protect the fetus. Aldosterone rises. Progesterone causes salt wasting. Volume expands
ProstaglandinsLocal chemical mediators from membranes and fluid. Soften the cervix and increase uterine contractions and sensitivity to oxytocin
Immune systemInnate immunity is enhanced and adaptive immunity is suppressed so the fetus is not rejected. More risk of infection such as UTI. Diabetes may worsen and asthma may stabilize, but this varies

CervixSoftens (Goodell) and turns blue (Chadwick). Mucus plug (operculum) forms

🔍 Go deeper: Term labels, anemia, and when to worry
  • Physiologic anemia vs true anemia: hemoglobin under 11 g/dL (first and third trimesters) or under 10.5 g/dL (second trimester) is anemia. Iron deficiency is the most common cause.
  • Supine hypotension: lying flat compresses the vena cava after about 20 weeks. Use left side lying.
  • Warning signs vs normal: mild ankle swelling at the end of the day is common. Sudden swelling of the face and hands, severe headache, or visual changes need a BP check right away.

First trimester gain is about 1 to 4 lb. After that, about 1 lb per week for a normal BMI.

Food concerns

  • No alcohol. Limit caffeine to 200 mg per day.
  • Avoid raw or undercooked fish, meat, and eggs, unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses, and deli meats unless heated until steaming (listeria risk).
  • Avoid high-mercury fish: shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish.
  • Pica (eating clay, starch, ice) can signal iron deficiency.

  • Lactose intolerance: lactase products or fortified alternatives for calcium.

  • Pica: eating non-food items such as clay or ice. Check for iron deficiency and discourage harmful items.

  • Supplements: 27 mg ferrous iron and 400 to 800 mcg folic acid daily for most. A history of a neural tube defect needs a higher dose. Protein goes to 71 g a day in the second and third trimesters. Folic acid sources: dark green vegetables, baked beans, black-eyed peas, citrus, peanuts, liver.

Dieting is never recommended.
  • Artificial sweeteners: FDA considers acesulfame K, advantame, aspartame, neotame, saccharin, luo han guo extract, steviol glycosides under 95% purity, sucralose, and stevioside safe. Use minimally.
  • Mercury: avoid shark, swordfish, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, bigeye tuna, and tilefish for 6 to 12 months before conception and through pregnancy. Choose shrimp, white albacore tuna (limit 6 oz a week), salmon, lobster, sole, tilapia, cod, haddock, pollock, and catfish. Check local fish advisories.
  • Vitamin D (evidence): adequate levels are linked to less preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and low birth weight. Deficiency can cause newborn hypocalcemia and rickets.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: listeriosis prevention
  • Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus in soil, water, animals, and processed foods. Pregnant women are about 10 times more likely to get listeriosis. It can look like flu in the mother but cause miscarriage, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death. It crosses the placenta even when she has no symptoms. Treat with IV ampicillin or oral amoxicillin for 7 days.

Store-made salads (ham, chicken, egg, tuna, seafood)
Hot dogs and deli meats unless heated until steaming hot
Raw or lightly cooked sprouts

Other steps: wash hands, refrigerate perishables within 2 hours, keep the fridge at 40 F or below and the freezer at 0 F, thaw and marinate in the fridge, check dates, wash all produce, clean the refrigerator, and keep hot dog package fluid off other foods.

  • BMI: kg divided by height in meters squared, or pounds divided by inches squared times 704.5. Under 18.5 underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 to 39.9 obese.
  • Low gain or low BMI: risk of preterm birth and low birth weight (under 2,500 g or 5.5 lb). Suggest high-calorie snacks such as nuts, peanut butter, shakes, cheese, fruit, yogurt, and ice cream. Refer to a nutritionist and consider an eating disorder.
  • High gain or obesity: larger baby, cephalopelvic disproportion, cesarean, miscarriage, gestational diabetes and hypertension, preeclampsia, and congenital anomalies. Never restrict calories severely. Steady gain means she is getting enough calories.
  • Lactose intolerance: missing lactase, so gas, discomfort, and diarrhea. More common in people of African, Asian, and South American descent. Use lactose-free dairy, fortified orange juice, or soy milk.
  • Vegetarian types: lacto-ovo (eggs and dairy), lacto (dairy only), vegan (no animal foods). Watch protein, iron, calcium, vitamin D, and B12. Soy, beans, lentils, nuts, vitamin C with iron foods, fortified products, and a B12 supplement help.
  • Pica: craving nonfood items for at least 1 month. Main types: geophagia (soil or clay), pagophagia (ice), amylophagia (laundry starch). Risks: iron deficiency anemia, poor weight gain, constipation, toxins, parasites, hypokalemia, tooth fractures. Suspect pica when anemia occurs despite a good diet. Ask without judgment.

💭 6. Psychosocial adaptations

TrimesterTypical response
FirstAmbivalence is normal (class slide question #4: TRUE). Focus on self and physical changes
SecondAcceptance. Quickening makes the baby real. Fantasies and bonding grow. Often called the "glow" period
ThirdAnxiety about labor and birth, awareness of the body, nesting, preparing for baby

Rubin's maternal role tasks

  1. Ensuring safe passage for herself and the baby
  2. Securing acceptance of the baby by others
  3. Binding-in to the unborn child
  4. Learning to give of oneself

Also on the slide: pregnancy and sexuality (desire shifts across trimesters, intercourse is safe in a normal pregnancy), pregnancy and the partner (couvade, role change, anxiety), pregnancy and siblings (prepare them with age-appropriate teaching and include them).

  • Sexuality: desire changes by trimester. Intercourse is safe in a normal pregnancy. Avoid with bleeding, ruptured membranes, or placenta previa.
  • Mood: mild mood swings are common. Persistent sadness, anxiety, or thoughts of self-harm need follow-up.
  • Rubin's tasks: ensuring safe passage, securing acceptance, binding-in, and learning to give of oneself.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: emotions, Rubin tasks, sexuality, partner, siblings
  • Mood disorders: significant depression or anxiety in about 15% to 20% of pregnant and postpartum people. Risk is higher with adverse childhood experiences, poverty, violence, language barriers, unsafe housing, and food insecurity. Ask about emotional well-being at every visit.
  • Common responses: ambivalence (first trimester, normal, usually becomes acceptance by quickening), introversion (first and third trimesters), acceptance (second trimester, with movement, ultrasound, and heartbeat), mood swings, and body image changes.
Rubin taskFirst trimesterSecond trimesterThird trimester
Ensuring safe passageFocus on herselfAttachment of great value to the fetusConcern for herself and baby as a unit
Seeking acceptance of infant by othersAcceptance of the pregnancyFamily relates to the fetus as a memberUnconditional acceptance
Seeking acceptance of self as parent (binding in)Accepts the idea of pregnancy, not the infantQuickening makes the fetus separateLongs to hold the infant, tired of being pregnant

  • Sexuality: desire is lower in the first trimester (fatigue, nausea), often higher in the second, and limited by size in the third. Intercourse in a healthy pregnancy has not been shown to be harmful. Abstain with vaginal bleeding, preterm cervical dilation, risk of preterm labor, or placenta previa. Offer comfortable positions and noncoital intimacy. Normalize the topic.
  • Partner: may enjoy nurturing, feel alienated, or feel proud. Couvade syndrome is weight gain and nausea in the partner. Ambivalence early, caregiver role in the second trimester, and worry about labor support in the third. Struggling partnerships may see withdrawal. Stable partnerships find tasks (nursery, car seat, classes).
  • Siblings: reactions depend on age. Toddlers may regress. Older children may avoid. Prepare by age, include them in choices, give one-on-one time after birth, and reassure love.

🩺 Ch 12: Nursing Management During Pregnancy

The prenatal visit schedule, labs, discomforts by trimester, self-care teaching, and danger signs.

🧠 The big idea

Regular prenatal care catches problems early and teaches the mother.
Visits on schedule → Labs and assessments → Teaching → Danger signs reported fast

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Nagele's rule: first day of LMP, minus 3 months, plus 7 days.
  2. Visits: every 4 weeks to 28, every 2 weeks 28 to 36, weekly after 36.
  3. Glucose test 24 to 28 weeks. Group B strep swab 35 to 37 weeks. Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks if Rh negative.
  4. Avoid saunas, hot tubs, live vaccines, and lying flat on the back.
  5. Danger signs: bleeding, severe headache, visual changes, gush of fluid, decreased fetal movement.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Urinary frequency at 18 weeksExpected in the 1st and 3rd trimesters. Mid-pregnancy frequency is the one to report (UTI).
⚠️ MultiparaA multipara is NOT pregnant for the first time. That is a primigravida.
🩺 Think like a nurseMatch the complaint to the trimester. If it does not fit, or it is a danger sign, report it. Teach the rest as comfort measures.

🥚 1. Preconception care

  • Goals: promote the health of the woman and partner before pregnancy. Find and change biomedical, behavioral, and social risks to her health or the outcome through prevention and management.
  • Nursing management: screen for risk factors (chronic illness, medications, smoking, alcohol, drugs, diet, weight, genetics, immunizations, violence), teach, and refer.
  • Folic acid 400 mcg daily starting before conception. Update immunizations. Review medications for teratogens.

MedicationsTeratogens such as isotretinoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors, some anticonvulsants. Herbs and supplements too
ImmunityRubella and varicella immunity. Give MMR or varicella at least 1 month before conception. Tdap and flu as due
Folic acid400 mcg daily. Higher dose with a prior neural tube defect

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: preconception and interconception care
  • Preconception care: promotes the health of the person and partner before pregnancy by finding and changing biomedical, behavioral, and social risks. Interconception care is care between pregnancies, especially after a poor outcome. Every visit with a person who can become pregnant should include it. Ask: "Would you like to become pregnant in the next year?"
  • Reproductive life plan: a personal plan for whether and when to have children, shared with providers.
  • Folic acid 400 to 800 mcg a day. Vaccines: influenza, rubella and varicella if not immune, Tdap if due. MMR at least 1 month before pregnancy and varicella at least 3 months before.
  • Healthy BMI: 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2.
  • Statistics: 10.38% of infants are born preterm (14.5% Black, 9.5% White) and 8.6% have low birth weight. 5.4% smoke in pregnancy, 13.5% drink alcohol, and over 50% are overweight or obese. The highest sensitivity of the embryo is days 17 to 56 after conception, often before the first visit.
CDC preconception recommendation (Box 12.1)
1 Individual responsibility: a reproductive life plan. 2 Consumer awareness. 3 Preventive visits with risk assessment
4 Interventions for identified risks. 5 Interconception care after an adverse outcome. 6 A prepregnancy checkup
7 Insurance coverage for low incomes. 8 Public health programs. 9 Research. 10 Monitoring improvements

  • Nursing history areas: immunizations, medical conditions, reproductive and sexual history, nutrition and BMI, lifestyle and work, genetic carrier status, stress and abuse, medications and substances, and support systems. Offer the same genetic screening as in pregnancy and screen for IPV. Decision to have a baby belongs to the patient or couple.

📝 2. The first prenatal visit

  • Establish a trusting relationship.
  • Focus on wellness teaching.
  • Detect and prevent problems.
  • Comprehensive health history, obstetric history, physical exam, laboratory tests.

Obstetric history

Use GTPAL (see the Basics tab). A multipara is NOT a first-time mother. First-time pregnant = primigravida. Class slide question #1 was FALSE.

Pelvic exam

Your slide shows a bimanual exam and measuring the pelvis (pelvimetry). The exam checks the vagina, cervix, and uterus, collects the Pap smear and cultures, and assesses the bony pelvis.

  • Rh negative: Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth of an Rh positive baby, and after bleeding, trauma, or amniocentesis.
  • High-risk flags: under 15 or 35 and older, hypertension, diabetes, prior preterm birth, multiples, obesity, substance use, and IPV.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: history, due date, gravida and para, and physical exam
  • Goals of the first visit: baseline data, estimate gestational age, screen for teratogenic drugs, and find risk factors. Delayed prenatal care is linked to more NICU admissions.
  • Prenatal care models: individual, or CenteringPregnancy group care (up to about 12 people at similar gestation, 10 sessions of 1.5 to 2 hours) with more education and support.
  • Gestational diabetes: about 8.3 per 100 births. Early A1C screening for high-risk women (prior GDM, BMI over 25 plus another risk factor, relative with diabetes, PCOS, age over 35, and so on).
  • Smoking causes vasoconstriction, less placental perfusion, small babies, and newborn nicotine withdrawal.
Nagele's ruleStep
1Use the first day of the LMP
2Subtract 3 months
3Add 7 days
4Add 1 year. Result plus or minus 2 weeks

Example: LMP August 10 gives May 10, then May 17, so the EDD is May 17. Shortcut: add 7 days and 9 months. Birth 2 weeks before or after is normal. Less accurate with irregular cycles, conception while breastfeeding, or before periods return. First-trimester ultrasound is the most accurate dating tool.

TermMeaning
GravidaTotal number of pregnancies, including the current one and multiples as one
Nulligravida / primigravida / secundigravida / multigravidaNever pregnant / first / second / at least third
ParaBirths at 20 weeks or more, counting multiples as one
Nullipara / primipara / multiparaNo births at 20 weeks / one / two or more
GTPAL exampleMary, pregnant 4th time: an abortion at 8 weeks, a daughter at 40 weeks, a son at 34 weeks. Gravida 4, para 2. TPAL 1112 (1 term, 1 preterm, 1 abortion, 2 living). Term is 37 to 42 weeks and preterm is 20 weeks to before 37 weeks.
  • Exam: vitals, height, and weight (report under 100 lb, over 200 lb, or sudden gain). Thyroid slightly enlarged is normal. Soft systolic murmur is common. Heart rate up 10 to 15 bpm starting between 14 and 20 weeks. Breasts fuller and nodular. Fundus at symphysis 12 weeks, midway 16 weeks, umbilicus 20 weeks (20 cm), just below xiphoid 36 weeks (36 cm). Calf pain with walking suggests DVT. Dependent edema is normal in the third trimester, but early edema may signal hypertension.
  • Pelvic exam: external genitalia, speculum (cervix: Goodell, Hegar, Chadwick), Pap and cultures, bimanual (uterine size, ovaries), rectal last. Stay in the room, explain every step, label specimens.
  • Pelvic measurements: diagonal conjugate (12.5 cm or more, the most useful), true or obstetric conjugate (diagonal minus 1 to 2 cm, average 11 cm, smallest front-to-back inlet diameter), and ischial tuberosity diameter (10.5 cm or more is adequate). Not needed after a prior vaginal birth.

📆 3. Follow-up visits

GestationVisit frequency
Up to 28 weeksEvery 4 weeks
28 to 36 weeksEvery 2 weeks
36 weeks to birthWeekly
❌ Watch outClass slide question #2: a woman at 24 weeks follows up every 2 weeks. FALSE. At 24 weeks it is every 4 weeks.

What happens at each visit

  • Assessments: weight, blood pressure, urine for protein and glucose, fundal height, fetal heart rate, fetal movement, edema, and danger signs.
  • Teaching: nutrition, discomforts, danger signs, preparation for birth.
  • Diagnostics: the lab schedule above.
🧠 Fundal height
Measured in cm from the symphysis pubis. From 20 to 36 weeks it matches the number of weeks, give or take 2 cm. At about 20 weeks the top of the uterus is at the umbilicus.
🔍 Go deeper: Fetal checks at every visit
  • Fetal heart rate: normal is about 110 to 160 beats per minute, heard with a Doppler from about 10 to 12 weeks.
  • Fundal height: measure in cm from the symphysis. From 20 to 36 weeks it matches the weeks of gestation within about 2 cm. A big difference needs an ultrasound (multiples, too much fluid, big baby, dating error, or poor growth).
  • Fetal movement counts: start about 28 weeks. Same time daily, lying on the left side after a meal. At least 5 kicks in 1 hour (or 10 in 2 hours) is reassuring. If not reached, drink something cold and recount, then call the provider.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: visit schedule, glucose screening, Rh, preterm labor, and fetal assessment
GestationVisit interval
Up to 28 weeksEvery 4 weeks
29 to 36 weeksEvery 2 weeks
37 weeks to birthEvery week
  • Every visit: weight and BP compared with baseline, urine protein, glucose, ketones, and nitrites, fundal height, fetal movement, fetal heart rate (110 to 160), questions, anticipatory guidance, nutrition, and prenatal vitamin adherence.
  • Gestational diabetes screening 24 to 28 weeks (earlier for high risk). One-step: fasting 75 g glucose, 2-hour plasma glucose. Two-step: nonfasting 50 g, blood at 1 hour. If elevated, fasting 100 g, with levels at 1, 2, and 3 hours. Diagnosis if at least two values are elevated.
  • 29 to 36 weeks: add edema assessment (face, hands, pretibial, and rings that are tight are abnormal). Rh-negative antibody titer. Anti-D immune globulin also after spontaneous abortion or amniocentesis. Reevaluate hemoglobin and hematocrit. Ask about preterm labor signs. Discuss feeding choice and a pediatric provider. Teach fetal movement counting.
  • 37 to 40 weeks: screen for group B strep, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. Leopold maneuvers for presentation and position. Review labor signs. Send the prenatal record to the hospital. Review family planning and feeding. A car seat is required to bring the baby home.
  • Fundal height (McDonald method): centimeters from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the fundus, lying on the back with knees slightly flexed. Should match weeks until 36 weeks. After 36 it drops. Flat or stalled growth suggests growth restriction. Larger than expected suggests multiples or hydramnios.
  • Fetal movement: quickening 16 to 25 weeks, earlier in multiparas. Decreased movement can mean hypoxemia. Kick count: sit quietly and feel for at least 5 kicks in 1 hour (10 in 2 hours is also reassuring). If not reached, try a cold drink and recount, then call. Count at the same time daily in a relaxed semi-Fowler or side-lying position.
  • Fetal heart rate with a Doppler (Nursing Procedure 12.1): find the fetal back by palpation, gel, move the Doppler until it is loudest, compare with her pulse so you do not count hers, count a full minute, record (110 to 160 bpm).
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: danger signs by trimester and preterm labor
TrimesterReport right away
FirstSpotting or bleeding (miscarriage), painful urination (infection), severe persistent vomiting with weight loss (hyperemesis), fever over 100 F, dizziness or fainting, worsening headache, lower abdominal pain with dizziness, shoulder pain, and bleeding (ruptured ectopic)
SecondRegular contractions, back pain, more discharge (preterm labor), calf pain worse with foot flexion (DVT), gush or leak of fluid (prelabor rupture), no fetal movement for more than 12 hours
ThirdSudden weight gain, face or periorbital swelling, severe upper abdominal pain, headache with vision changes, extreme swelling of face or hands (preeclampsia), decreased movement for more than 24 hours (hypoxia), late-pregnancy bleeding (previa, abruption, accreta)
  • Preterm labor signs: contractions every 10 minutes or more often, discharge change, pelvic pressure and cramps, low dull backache, menstrual-like cramps, diarrhea. About 10% of US births are preterm and almost 3% are under 34 weeks (14% in non-Hispanic Black people, 9.1% White, 9.7% Hispanic). Cervical dilation over 3 cm supports the diagnosis. Complications for the baby include cerebral palsy, chronic lung disease, intellectual disability, seizures, vision and hearing loss.
  • Self-care: stop activity, lie on the left side for 1 hour, drink 2 to 3 glasses of water. If symptoms worsen or do not stop, call.
  • Braxton Hicks versus labor: Braxton Hicks go away with walking or rest and are felt in the abdomen. True preterm contractions often come with low back pain.
  • Preterm evaluation: record review, contractions, vitals, FHR, pelvic exam for dilation and effacement, membranes, and urine culture for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Medications to stop contractions may be ordered.

😮‍💨 4. Discomforts of pregnancy

TrimesterCommon discomfortsTeaching
FirstNausea and vomiting, urinary frequency, breast tenderness, fatigue, nasal stuffiness, ptyalism, leukorrheaSmall frequent meals, dry crackers before rising, rest, empty the bladder often, supportive bra
SecondHeartburn, flatulence with bloating, constipation, hemorrhoids, varicose veins, backache, leg cramps, leukorrheaSmall meals, fiber and fluids, avoid long standing, pelvic rocking, elevate legs, flex the foot for cramps
ThirdUrinary frequency returns, dyspnea, backache, ankle edema, insomnia, Braxton Hicks, heartburnSide lying, rest with legs up, comfort positioning, report sudden or severe swelling
⚠️ Trap"Report as unusual" at 18 weeks (class slide Q3): urinary frequency. It is expected in the 1st and 3rd trimesters but not typical in the middle of the 2nd, so assess for a urinary tract infection. Backache, leukorrhea, and flatulence with bloating are all common in the 2nd trimester.

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: trimester-by-trimester management details
ProblemTextbook details
Urinary frequencyFirst and third trimester. Rule out infection and diabetes. Reduce fluids 2 to 3 hours before bed, limit caffeine, pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, report burning
FatigueFirst and third trimesters. Rule out anemia and infection. Rest, nap, left side with pillows, relaxation, exercise
Nausea and vomitingStarts about week 5, peaks 8 to 12, resolves by 16 to 18 weeks. 80% have it all day. Small bland low-fat meals 5 or 6 times, crackers before rising, vitamin B6 foods, ginger (up to 1 g a day), acupressure wristbands (FDA approved), fluids between meals, avoid greasy foods and strong odors. Vitamin B6 10 to 25 mg every 6 to 8 hours. Doxylamine 10 mg with pyridoxine 10 mg (Diclegis): 2 tablets at bedtime, then add 1 in the morning and 1 mid-afternoon if needed. Others: diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, meclizine, prochlorperazine, promethazine, ondansetron. Treat the distress too
Breast tendernessOften the first symptom. Supportive bra with wide straps, even for sleep
ConstipationUp to 40%. Fiber, 6 to 8 glasses of water, exercise, warm fluids on rising, prunes, foot stool. Bulk-forming laxative (Metamucil) if needed. Iron and calcium add to it
Nasal stuffiness, bleeding gums, nosebleedsHumidifier, fluids, blow gently one side at a time, avoid decongestant sprays. Nosebleed: sit with head forward, pinch nostrils 10 to 15 minutes, ice to the bridge. Gums: soft brush, floss, saline rinse, dentist if persistent
Cravings and picaCravings are common. Pica (clay, starch, ice, soap, paint chips) can signal deficiency. Ask without judgment
Leukorrhea1 to 4 mL a day is normal, clear to whitish yellow. Cotton underwear, no douching or tampons, no tight nylon
BackacheUp to 60%. Posture, low heels, pelvic tilt on all fours, one foot on a stool when standing, pillow between legs, firm mattress, swimming, heat, acetaminophen. Rule out contractions and UTI
Leg crampsUp to 50%, second and third trimester, often at night. Dorsiflex the foot and straighten the leg, avoid pointing toes, calf stretches against a wall before bed, elevate legs, hydrate, walk, calcium or magnesium foods, change position every 2 hours
VaricositiesAbout 50%. Gradient support hose on after elevating legs 10 minutes in the morning, elevate legs 5 to 10 minutes twice a day, avoid knee-high hose and crossing legs, ice for vulvar varicosities
HemorrhoidsAbout 40%. Fiber, 2 L of fluid, foot stool, avoid prolonged sitting on the toilet, witch hazel, topical agents if allowed, sitz bath
FlatulenceAvoid gas-forming foods and carbonated drinks, eat slowly, walk after meals, knee-chest position
Dyspnea60% to 75%. Posture, pillows or raised head of bed, left side, avoid large meals, stretch arms overhead. Improves with lightening. Report if severe or with heart or lung disease
Heartburn40% to 85%. Small meals, upright 1 to 3 hours after eating, avoid trigger foods (caffeine, fat, citrus, spice, chocolate, mint, alcohol), raise head of bed 10 to 30 degrees, sips of water, antacids sparingly
Dependent edemaTotal body fluid up 6 to 8 L. Elevate legs, compression stockings, change positions, walk, left side, limit sodium, 6 to 8 glasses of water, stop every 2 hours on car trips. Face edema with sudden gain over 5 lb a week suggests preeclampsia
Braxton HicksIrregular, painless, no dilation. Change position, hydrate, rest on left, breathing

🔍 Go deeper: Exercise, immunizations, medications, and warning signs
  • Exercise: about 150 minutes of moderate activity per week. Use the talk test. Avoid contact sports, scuba, heights, overheating, and flat on the back. Stop and call for bleeding, dizziness, chest pain, leaking fluid, or contractions.
  • Medications: take only what the provider approves. Acetaminophen is the usual pain reliever. Avoid NSAIDs from about 20 weeks onward unless the provider says otherwise because they can affect fetal kidneys and the ductus arteriosus.
VaccineIn pregnancy
Inactivated influenzaRecommended in any trimester
TdapRecommended every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks
MMR and varicellaLive vaccines. Not given in pregnancy. Give after birth
Live nasal influenzaNot given in pregnancy
Rho(D) immune globulinNot a vaccine. Given to Rh negative women
⚠️ Preterm labor warning signs (before 37 weeks)Regular contractions every 10 minutes or less, low dull backache, pelvic pressure, menstrual-like cramps, leaking fluid, or a change in vaginal discharge. Teach: empty the bladder, drink 2 to 3 glasses of water, lie on the left side, and count contractions for an hour. If they continue or any sign persists, call.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: hygiene, dental, clothing, exercise, sleep, sexuality, work, and travel
  • Hygiene: more sweat and vaginal secretions. Shower more often, cotton underwear. Shower rather than tub bath near term (balance). Avoid hot tubs, saunas, whirlpools, and tanning beds (heat can cause fetal tachycardia). No douching, no panty liners, no perfumed products.
  • Dental: brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, floss, see the dentist before conception or in the first trimester and every 6 months. Dental x-rays and usual dental medications are safe. Treat pain and infection promptly. After vomiting rinse with 1 teaspoon baking soda in 1 cup warm water. Periodontal disease is linked to preterm and low birth weight infants.
  • Breasts: firm supportive bra with wide straps, bigger size halfway through. Plain water only on nipples (Montgomery glands lubricate). Nipple preparation only if nipples are inverted. Breast pads for colostrum leakage.
  • Clothing: loose, layered, low heels, no constricting girdles, no knee-high hose.
  • Exercise: at least 30 minutes of moderate activity daily, ideally 150 minutes a week. Benefits: less constipation, less GDM and hypertension, better sleep and mood, easier recovery. Contraindications: preterm labor, placenta previa, incompetent cervix, second or third trimester bleeding, PPROM, significant heart or lung disease, preeclampsia, severe anemia. Stop and call for: bleeding, dizziness, fainting, chest pain, headache, weak muscles affecting balance, calf pain or swelling, contractions, decreased movement, leaking fluid. Walking, swimming, biking, and low-impact aerobics are ideal. Avoid contact sports, skiing, surfing, scuba, ice hockey, overheating, jerky or high-impact moves, and lying flat after the fourth month. Drink fluids. Never exercise to exhaustion.
  • Sleep: regular schedule, wind down, no screens for 1 hour, cool dark room, no caffeine after noon, limit fluids after dinner, modified Sims position with pillows, avoid lying on the back after the fourth month.
  • Sexual activity contraindications: unexplained vaginal bleeding, placenta previa, ruptured membranes, preterm cervical dilation or effacement, and preterm contractions. Otherwise intercourse will not injure the fetus.
  • Work: most people can work to term if no complications. Rest breaks, change position every 2 to 3 hours, avoid heavy lifting and toxic exposures, smoke-free area. Hazardous jobs include health care, child care, construction, manufacturing, flight attendants, firefighters, farm and greenhouse work. Ask about teratogens, temperature extremes, and standing.
  • Travel: safest in mid-pregnancy (14 to 28 weeks). Defer international travel in the third trimester. Some airlines allow travel to 36 weeks. Carry the prenatal record, find obstetric care at the destination, aisle seat, walk every 2 hours, calf exercises, support hose, hydrate. Avoid unpasteurized milk, raw produce, and local water if unsafe. Cook meat well (toxoplasmosis). Mosquito-borne infections (Zika, malaria) are a risk.
  • Car safety: always a three-point belt. The shoulder strap goes between the breasts and over the upper abdomen above the uterus. The lap belt sits on the hip bones below the belly. Keep airbags on and sit as far from the dashboard as possible. Motor vehicle crashes cause more than 50% of trauma in pregnancy and can cause placental separation.
  • Report while traveling: bleeding, abdominal pain, contractions, preeclampsia signs, ruptured membranes, leg swelling or pain.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: vaccines and medications in pregnancy
Give if indicated (Box 12.5)Avoid in pregnancy
Hepatitis B, inactivated influenza injection, Tdap, RSV, COVID-19Live attenuated nasal influenza, HPV, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, BCG, recombinant zoster vaccine, typhoid
  • No evidence of risk from inactivated vaccines or toxoids. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are avoided. Avoid pregnancy for 28 days after MMR and 3 months after varicella vaccine.
  • Medications: about 80% take at least one OTC or prescription drug. Less than 10% of drugs approved since 1980 have enough data on birth defect risk. Always ask a provider first, including herbs and vitamins. For seizures, hypertension, or asthma the benefits of continuing medication usually outweigh the risks. Avoid fetal drug exposure in the first 12 weeks when possible. The FDA now uses the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule: Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females and Males of Reproductive Potential subsections replace the old letter categories. Herbal products vary in potency and can cross the placenta.

🎒 6. Preparation for labor, birth, and parenthood

  • Perinatal and childbirth education: Lamaze, Bradley, and hospital classes. Teach labor signs and coping.
  • Birth setting options: hospital, birthing center, home.
  • Care providers: obstetrician, certified nurse-midwife, family physician. A doula gives support but is not a clinician.
  • Feeding choices: discuss breastfeeding and formula without judgment.
  • Final preparation: hospital bag, car seat, when to leave for the hospital, who to call.
⚠️ TrapDanger signs. Call the provider now: vaginal bleeding, severe headache, visual changes, severe abdominal pain, a gush or leak of fluid, decreased fetal movement, persistent vomiting, fever, burning with urination, sudden facial or hand swelling, calf pain.
🧠 Kick counts
After 28 weeks she counts movements daily. Reassuring: at least 5 kicks in 1 hour (10 in 2 hours is also reassuring). Fewer than that: try a cold drink and recount, then call the provider.

  • Go to the hospital or call: regular strong contractions (often every 5 minutes for an hour for a first baby, per the provider), ruptured membranes (note the time, color, and odor), bleeding, or decreased fetal movement.
  • Birth plan: setting, support persons, pain options, positions, newborn care, and feeding. Plans can change for safety.
  • Feeding choice: teach benefits of breastfeeding and respect an informed decision. Breastfeeding is not advised with untreated HIV in the US or in galactosemia.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: childbirth education methods and breathing
MethodWho and key idea
Lamaze (psychoprophylactic)Fernand Lamaze, French obstetrician, popularized in the 1960s. Conquer fear with knowledge and conditioning. Breathing and relaxation, focal point, effleurage, massage, imagery. Breathing is one of many comfort strategies
Bradley (partner-coached)Robert Bradley, 1965, Husband-Coached Childbirth. Unmedicated birth. Slow deep abdominal breathing. The partner is trained as coach
Dick-Read (natural childbirth)Grantly Dick-Read, British obstetrician, Childbirth Without Fear (1933). Fear creates tension and pain. Education and abdominal breathing break the fear-tension-pain cycle
HypnoBirthingMarie Mongan, 1989. Dick-Read plus self-hypnosis, suggestion, relaxation, meditation
Lamaze breathingDetails
Cleansing breathAt the start and end of every contraction
Slow-pacedHalf the normal rate (6 to 9 breaths per minute). Most relaxed. Used throughout labor
Modified-pacedQuiet upper chest breaths. Increases with intensity but never more than twice the normal rate
Patterned-pacedModified with a rhythm, such as 4/1 (four breaths, then a blow out like a candle)
  • Nurse role: encouragement and presence. Remain quiet during imagery and focal points. Use eye contact if she appears overwhelmed in transition. Involve and praise the partner and offer breaks. Do not stereotype. The aim of any method is mastery and an internal locus of control.
  • Perinatal education covers anatomy and physiology of birth, fetal growth, exercise, emotional changes, sex, nutrition, teratogens, labor signs, rights, comfort measures, pain options, complications, positions, infant feeding and care, CPR, and family planning.
🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: birth settings, providers, feeding, and the final checklist
  • Hospital: most common site and necessary for high risk. Best for complications. Clinical atmosphere and restrictions. A birthing suite lets her stay in one room for labor, birth, and recovery.
  • Freestanding birth center: home-like, for low risk. Often midwives. No routine IV or continuous monitoring. Must transfer quickly in an emergency. Low-risk outcomes are as good or better. Lower racial disparity and discrimination in one study.
  • Home birth: about 1.5% of US births. ACOG says hospitals and accredited birth centers are safest but respects choice. Planned home birth is considered safe with a low-risk, singleton, cephalic, term pregnancy with no prior cesarean, a qualified attendant, and an emergency transfer plan.
  • Providers: obstetricians (4-year residency), certified nurse midwives (registered nurses with a graduate degree, ACME accredited program, national exam, write prescriptions, attend about 10.3% of US births), and family physicians. A doula ("woman's servant") is a layperson who gives continuous emotional and physical support and does no clinical procedures.
  • Breastfeeding: exclusive for 6 months and continuing for a year or longer. Benefits for the baby: fewer infections (otitis media, respiratory, GI, UTI, sepsis), lower SUID, allergy, celiac, IBD, obesity, diabetes, and leukemia. For the mother: faster uterine involution and less bleeding, suppressed ovulation (not reliable birth control), and lower breast, ovarian, endometrial cancer, heart disease, and type 2 diabetes. Contraindications: untreated HIV or not virally suppressed, HTLV I or II, illicit drug use, and suspected or confirmed Ebola. Offer a pacifier once breastfeeding is established (2 to 4 weeks). The most common cause of nipple pain is a poor latch. Inverted nipples need lactation help.
  • Bottle-feeding: cow's milk-based formula usually. Follow the label, measure water first then powder, never microwave, boil questionable water for 5 minutes, prepared formula keeps 24 hours in the refrigerator or 2 hours out. Semi-upright cradle hold, keep the nipple full, burp every ounce, feed every 3 to 4 hours, never prop a bottle or put the baby to bed with one (nursing caries).
  • Final checklist: classes, setting, support people, birth plan, tour, packed bag, care for siblings and pets, labor signs and what to do if membranes rupture, how to reach the provider, pain preferences, discussion of cesarean, feeding choice, circumcision decision, car seat, pediatrician, crib slats 2 inches apart or less, and a family planning method.

🔍 Textbook: antepartum fetal tests (ultrasound, Doppler, AFP, screens, NT, amniocentesis, CVS, NST, BPP)

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: antepartum fetal tests (ultrasound, Doppler, AFP, screens, NT, amniocentesis, CVS, NST, BPP)
TestWhen and howKey pointsNursing care
UltrasoundSound waves. First trimester transvaginal to confirm pregnancy and exclude ectopic or molar. 18 to 20 weeks for anomalies and dates. 32 to 36 weeks for size, fluid, placentaNoninvasive. Most accurate dating. 3D and 4D existFull bladder early. Gel feels cold. No sensation
Doppler flow studiesBlood flow in umbilical and fetal vesselsUsed with growth restriction, hypertension, preeclampsia. Absent or reversed diastolic flow is seriousSame as ultrasound
MSAFP16 to 18 weeks (offered 15 to 20)High: neural tube defect, multiples, abdominal wall defects, renal abnormalities, threatened miscarriage. Low: dating overestimated, fetal death, mole, higher maternal weight, trisomy 21 or 18Accurate LMP, weight, race, number of fetuses, diabetes. Venipuncture
Triple, quad, penta screens15 to 22 weeks (16 to 18 best)Triple: AFP, hCG, unconjugated estriol. Quad adds inhibin A. Penta adds hyperglycosylated hCG. Screening onlyExplain that a diagnosis needs more tests
First-trimester screen (PAPP-A)11 to 14 weeksLow PAPP-A: poor placenta function, stillbirth, preterm birth, preeclampsia, chromosome problemsCounsel

Nuchal translucency11 to 14 weeks (ultrasound)Increased fluid at the neck suggests trisomies 21, 18, 13, heart defects, and fetal lossCounsel

A 22-gauge needle. Fluid goes in an amber or foil-covered tube. Results up to 3 weeks. Risks: cramping, leakage, chorioamniotic separation, infection, fetal injury, lossEmpty bladder first. 20 minute fetal monitoring before. Vitals and FHR every 15 minutes for an hour after. Anti-D immune globulin if Rh negative. Report fever, leaking fluid, bleeding, contractions, or movement change

Report fever, cramping, bleeding
Amniotic fluid finding (Table 12.2)Meaning
Port wine colorMay indicate abruption
Bilirubin present at termHemolytic disease of the newborn
MeconiumFetal hypoxia or distress (normal in breech)

Phosphatidylglycerol absentLung immaturity

BacteriaChorioamnionitis

🔍 Textbook: nonstress test and biophysical profile

🔍 Go deeper: Textbook: nonstress test and biophysical profile
  • Nonstress test (NST): from 32 weeks until birth for high-risk pregnancies. Noninvasive and no contractions are started. Pregnant person eats first and lies in left lateral or semi-Fowler position. External monitor with a uterine sensor and an FHR sensor. She presses an event marker each time she feels movement. Lasts 20 to 30 minutes.
  • Reactive: at least two accelerations of 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Nonreactive: not met after 40 minutes. Causes include fetal sleep, immaturity, smoking, drugs, sepsis, and cardiac or neurologic anomalies. More than half of nonreactive tests are false positives, so repeat the test, use vibroacoustic stimulation, or do a BPP or contraction stress test.
BPP componentTo score 2 points
Body movements3 or more discrete limb or trunk movements
Fetal tone1 or more episodes of full extension and flexion
Fetal breathing1 or more breathing movements lasting over 30 seconds
Amniotic fluid1 or more pockets over 2 cm
NSTNormal (reactive)
  • Score: 10 possible with the NST (8 without). 8 to 10 is normal (low risk of chronic fetal asphyxia) if fluid is adequate. 4 to 6 is abnormal (chronic fetal asphyxia suspected) and needs more evaluation. Under 4 is abnormal (chronic fetal asphyxia strongly suspected). Allow 30 minutes. A score of zero for absent movement, tone, or breathing needs at least 30 minutes of observation.
  • Order of loss with hypoxia is the reverse of development: tone (8 weeks), movement (9 weeks), breathing (20 weeks), reactivity of FHR (24 weeks). Amniotic fluid is a chronic marker because it reflects urine output.
  • Modified BPP: NST plus amniotic fluid volume.
  • Nursing: support and explain. Do the NST before the BPP. The BPP is done in imaging.

🖼️ From her Ch 11 and 12 slides

Slide topicWhat the slide says
Breast changesEstrogen and progesterone prepare the breasts for lactation. Enlargement of breasts, nipples and areola, with tingling and tenderness
Blood and circulationBlood volume up 30 to 50%. Cardiac output up 30 to 50%. Plasma volume up 40 to 60%. Physiologic anemia from hemodilution. Hypercoagulability (clot formation). Higher venous pressure causes edema, varicosities and hemorrhoids
RespiratoryTidal volume up 30 to 40%. Oxygen consumption up 20 to 40%. Vascular engorgement causes dyspnea, nasal and sinus congestion and epistaxis (nosebleeds). The diaphragm is displaced upward
Couvade syndromePartner has pregnancy symptoms such as weight gain and nausea or indigestion
Diagnostic testsDiagnostic tests give a definitive answer but are often invasive and risky. They include chorionic villus sampling (CVS), amniocentesis and percutaneous umbilical cord blood sampling (PUBS)
Cell-free DNA screeningScreens for common fetal aneuploidies by analyzing cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood. Starts around 9 to 10 weeks. Can identify fetal sex. It is a screen, not a diagnosis
Foods to avoid: germsRaw or undercooked meat, poultry, fish, eggs and sprouts (food poisoning, E. coli, Salmonella). Raw eggs (Salmonella). Deli meat and pate (Listeria). Soft cheeses: brie, camembert, roquefort, feta, gorgonzola, queso blanco, queso fresco (Listeria)
Foods to avoid: otherFish high in mercury: shark, swordfish, mackerel, tilefish. Smoked seafood (safe if cooked thoroughly). Raw shellfish (algae-related infection). Fresh-squeezed juice. Unwashed vegetables (toxoplasmosis)

💓 FHR Monitoring

How to monitor the fetal heart rate properly, read the tracing, and act. Your instructor stressed this, and it is also where nurses face the most legal risk.

⚖️ Why this matters

The fetal heart rate is how you see fetal oxygenation.
Misreading or not acting on a tracing delays care
→ injury to the baby and claims against nurses and providers. Nurses are legally responsible for fetal monitoring and assessment.

  • Use standard NICHD terms so everyone describes the tracing the same way.
  • Clinical judgment: recognize the cue, analyze it, prioritize, act, and evaluate. Then report with SBAR and use the chain of command if no one responds.
  • Evidence-based practice sets how often you assess and what you do for each pattern.

🩺 Methods of monitoring

MethodHowNotes
Intermittent auscultationFetoscope or handheld Doppler over the fetal back. Listen for 30 to 60 seconds after a contractionUsed for low-risk labor. Count the rate, note rhythm, and the response to a contraction
External electronic monitoringUltrasound (Doppler) transducer for FHR and a tocodynamometer ("toco") over the fundus for contractions, held by beltsNoninvasive. The toco shows frequency and duration of contractions, not intensity
Internal electronic monitoringFetal scalp electrode for FHR and an intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC) for contractionsNeeds ruptured membranes, enough cervical dilation (about 2 to 3 cm), and an accessible presenting part. More accurate. Invasive
🔍 Go deeper: Contraction assessment
  • Frequency: from the start of one contraction to the start of the next.
  • Duration: from the start to the end of the same contraction.
  • Intensity by palpation: mild feels like the tip of the nose, moderate like the chin, strong like the forehead. An IUPC measures pressure in mm Hg.
  • Resting tone: the uterus should relax and be soft between contractions.
  • Tachysystole: more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes.

✅ Step by step: monitoring properly

  1. Explain the procedure, wash hands, and get consent. Place her in a comfortable position, not flat on her back (left side, semi-Fowler, or sitting)
  2. Do Leopold maneuvers to find the fetal back. Heart tones are loudest over the fetal back (for a vertex baby, the lower quadrant of the abdomen)
  3. Place the Doppler over the fetal back and the toco at the fundus. Secure the belts and recheck often
  4. Check the maternal pulse to be sure you are recording the baby and not the mother (a rate of 70 to 90 may be maternal)
  5. Assess contractions: frequency, duration, resting tone, and intensity
  6. Look at a 10 minute window. Identify baseline, variability, accelerations, and decelerations and how they relate to contractions
  7. Label it as Category I, II, or III
  8. Act on the category. Start intrauterine resuscitation for a nonreassuring pattern and call with SBAR
  9. Document on time, in standard terms, with what you did and who you told

⏱️ How often to assess

RiskActive first stageSecond stage (pushing)
Low riskEvery 30 minutesEvery 15 minutes
High risk or oxytocinEvery 15 minutesEvery 5 minutes

These are the commonly taught intervals (ACOG and AWHONN). Always follow your facility protocol and your instructor's version for exams. Reassess after any change: rupture of membranes, medication, epidural, change in contractions, or a change in her condition.

📏 Terms and normal values (NICHD)

TermDefinition
BaselineAverage rate over 10 minutes, rounded to 5 bpm, excluding accelerations and decelerations. Normal 110 to 160 bpm
TachycardiaBaseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more
BradycardiaBaseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more
VariabilityFluctuation in baseline. Absent: undetectable. Minimal: 5 bpm or less. Moderate (normal): 6 to 25 bpm. Marked: more than 25 bpm
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more (under 32 weeks: 10 bpm for 10 seconds). Reassuring
Prolonged acceleration2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Sinusoidal patternSmooth wave-like pattern. Ominous

📉 Decelerations: cause and nursing action

🧠 Memory hook
VEAL CHOP
Variable = Cord compression. Early = Head compression. Acceleration = OK. Late = Placental insufficiency.
PatternWhat it looks likeCauseNursing action
EarlyGradual drop and return. A mirror image of the contraction. Lowest point matches the peak of the contractionFetal head compressionBenign. Continue to monitor. No intervention needed
VariableAbrupt drop (under 30 seconds to the low point) of 15 bpm or more, lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes. Shape and timing vary (V, U, or W)Umbilical cord compressionChange maternal position (side to side), stop oxytocin, check for cord prolapse by vaginal exam, give oxygen and IV fluid, notify provider. Amnioinfusion may be ordered
LateGradual drop that begins after the contraction starts, and the lowest point comes after the peak. Returns after the contraction endsUteroplacental insufficiency (poor oxygen to the fetus)Turn her to the left side, give IV fluid and oxygen, stop oxytocin, check her BP, notify provider now, prepare for possible urgent birth. Recurrent late decelerations are ominous
ProlongedDrop lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutesCord prolapse, uterine hyperstimulation, maternal hypotension (supine or after an epidural), rapid descent, maternal seizureFind and fix the cause. Reposition, fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin, check for prolapse, notify provider
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more for 15 seconds or moreFetal movement or stimulation. A sign of a well-oxygenated fetusReassuring. Document it
Minimal or absent variabilityFlat line patternFetal sleep (usually under 40 minutes), opioids, magnesium sulfate, acidemiaLook for the cause. Stimulate the fetus. Absent variability with decelerations is serious

🚦 NICHD three-tier system

CategoryFindingsMeaning and action
I (normal)Baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations. Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absentNormal acid-base status. Routine care and routine monitoring
II (indeterminate)Everything that is not Category I or III. Examples: tachycardia, bradycardia without absent variability, minimal or marked variability, recurrent variable decelerations, prolonged decelerationsNeeds evaluation, continued surveillance, and often resuscitation measures. Notify provider
III (abnormal)Absent variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal patternAbnormal acid-base status. Immediate action: resuscitation measures, notify provider, prepare for prompt birth

🩹 Intrauterine resuscitation (for a nonreassuring pattern)

Do these together, quickly, and tell the provider. Follow your facility protocol.

  1. Reposition her to the left side (or right, hands and knees) to improve blood flow
  2. Stop or reduce oxytocin if infusing, especially with tachysystole
  3. Give an IV fluid bolus (isotonic)
  4. Give oxygen by nonrebreather mask at about 10 L/min as protocol directs
  5. Do a vaginal exam to rule out cord prolapse and check dilation
  6. Check her vital signs and treat hypotension
  7. Notify the provider with SBAR. The provider may order a tocolytic (such as terbutaline) for tachysystole or amnioinfusion for variable decelerations
  8. Prepare for operative or assisted birth if the tracing does not improve

📞 SBAR for an abnormal tracing

PartExample
Situation"This is the nurse for Ms. J in room 4, 39 weeks, in active labor. She has recurrent late decelerations for the last 20 minutes."
Background"G2 P1, oxytocin at 12 milliunits per minute, epidural placed an hour ago, no allergies."
Assessment"Baseline 150 with minimal variability. Late decelerations with every contraction. BP 92/50, contractions every 2 minutes. I turned her left, started a fluid bolus, gave oxygen, and stopped the oxytocin."
Recommendation"I need you to come to the bedside now and evaluate for birth. Do you want me to prepare for a cesarean?"

📝 Documentation and legal protection

  • Chart the baseline, variability, accelerations, type of decelerations, contraction pattern, category, interventions, her and the baby's response, who you notified, the time, and the provider's response.
  • Use standard terms. Do not write "reassuring" or "nonreassuring" alone. Describe what you see.
  • Label and keep the strip. Never alter or erase an entry. Late entries are labeled as late.
  • If the provider does not respond to a concerning tracing, use the chain of command (charge nurse, then supervisor, then chair) and document that you did.
  • Patient safety comes before convenience.

🧪 Before labor: NST and biophysical profile

  • Nonstress test (NST): from 32 weeks for high-risk pregnancies. She eats first and lies on her left side. External monitor, event marker for movements, 20 to 30 minutes. Reactive: at least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Nonreactive: not met after 40 minutes. More than half are false positives, so repeat, use vibroacoustic stimulation, or do a BPP.
BPP component2 points if
Body movements3 or more
Fetal tone1 or more flexion and extension
Fetal breathing1 or more lasting over 30 seconds
Amniotic fluid1 pocket over 2 cm
NSTReactive

Score 8 to 10 normal, 4 to 6 abnormal, under 4 strongly abnormal. See Ch 12 for amniocentesis, CVS, and the other antepartum tests.

🗓️ Trimesters, weight gain, and due date

TopicWhat she taught
TrimestersFirst: weeks 1 to 12. Second: weeks 13 to 27. Third: week 28 to birth (40 weeks or beyond). The "fourth trimester" is the immediate postpartum period.
Weight gainFirst trimester: about 1 to 4 lb. Second trimester, normal BMI: about 1 lb per week. Underweight: a little more than 1 lb per week. Overweight: about half a pound a week or a little more.
Food choicesMyPlate (myplate.gov)
Naegele's ruleLMP minus 3 months, plus 7 days (and plus 1 year). Class example: LMP Nov 1, 2025 gives an EDB of Aug 8, 2026.
When not to use itUnreliable historian (a young teen unsure of her LMP), irregular cycles, or cycles longer than 28 days. Use ultrasound to find the EDB instead
Gestational wheelLine up the first day of the LMP on the wheel and it shows the due date. You may see one in offices

PartWhat to get or do

ExamHead to toe assessment. Pelvic exam (shows the shape of the pelvis and whether the baby's head can fit). Ultrasound
LabsUrinalysis, CBC, blood type and Rh, rubella immunity, hepatitis B, HIV, RPR (syphilis), and a Pap smear
