1️⃣ First trimester: what to expect and teach

TopicWhat she taught
Common discomfortsInsomnia, fatigue, mood swings, breast tenderness, more vaginal discharge, dyspareunia (painful intercourse), orthostatic hypotension (dizzy when sitting up), congestion, urinary frequency, nausea and vomiting, leg cramps, acne, headaches
Warning signs (call or go in)Bleeding, cramping, no fetal heart rate, fever or chills, and dysuria (painful urination)
ReassureDiscomforts are normal, self-limiting, and will pass. Help with them
Nausea and vomitingAvoid triggers (strong odors, spicy, greasy foods). Small frequent meals eaten slowly. Dry crackers before getting up. Ginger. Brush teeth after eating. Severe cases may need medication, but many are not ideal in pregnancy
HeartburnStay upright after eating. Small frequent meals. Avoid spicy, fatty, fried foods
Mental healthPregnancy can worsen depression, anxiety, and stress. Refer to counseling and help her find support
ActivityRegular exercise is good. Do not start a new extreme routine. No hot yoga or hot Pilates (overheating). No contact sports, skydiving, or horseback riding (fall risk)
SleepNot flat on her back
PetsMost are fine. Do not clean the cat litter box (toxoplasmosis, one of the TORCH infections that cross the placenta)
SexContinue as normal. Fatigue, nausea, and breast tenderness may lower interest. The "you will hurt the baby" idea is a myth
TravelSafe if low risk. Stop to stretch and walk often (clot risk), wear compression socks, carry a copy of the prenatal record, and avoid Zika areas (risk of microcephaly)
VaccinesNo live vaccines (no chickenpox, no MMR). Flu shot is recommended in season

2️⃣ Second trimester: what to expect and teach

TopicWhat she taught
AssessmentVitals and weight each visit. Urinalysis for glucose, protein, leukocytes, ketones. Fetal heart rate 110 to 160. Leopold maneuvers feel fetal parts and position
QuickeningFirst time she feels the baby move, at 16 to 25 weeks. Once felt, movement should not stop. Feeling it today but not tomorrow is still concerning
ScreensOptional genetic and neural tube defect screens
Warning signsBleeding, cramping, no fetal movement, fever or chills, dysuria
DiscomfortsSimilar to the first trimester. Nausea and vomiting usually ease
Plan aheadChoose the delivery hospital (tours, register), choose a pediatrician (register), plan baby care after birth
SexUsually no issues. Desire often returns once nausea eases
Vaccines and labsRhoGAM if Rh negative. Gestational diabetes screen at 24 to 28 weeks
Preterm laborTeach the signs: rhythmic cramping and low back pain. Go to labor and delivery
Fetal movementFeel the baby move daily. A sudden drop in movement can mean distress. See kick counts below

3️⃣ Third trimester: what to expect and teach

TopicWhat she taught
GBS swabVaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks on all pregnant women. It is not an STI, just bacteria some women carry. If positive, penicillin in labor prevents neonatal sepsis
Other testingRepeat H&H if not done. Repeat gonorrhea, chlamydia, RPR, and HIV if there is a reason or they were not done earlier
Glucose tolerance test24 to 28 weeks. If the screen is high, a 3 hour test follows. Failing the 3 hour test means gestational diabetes
Kick countsKeep doing them daily
TeachTrue versus false labor. Select a pediatrician. Prepare siblings (no surprise baby). Continue or start childbirth classes
DiscomfortsHeartburn, low back pain, ankle edema, varicose veins, hemorrhoids
Warning signsRhythmic cramping and low back pain (labor), leaking amniotic fluid (go to labor and delivery), severe headache and visual changes (preeclampsia)
TravelMost airlines do not allow flying past 36 weeks. International flights stop much sooner. Cruises do not allow pregnant clients past 24 weeks
VaccinesTdap again (passes pertussis protection to the baby). RSV vaccine in season (fall and winter)
SexCan continue. Pelvic precautions (nothing in the vagina, including sex) if she is at risk for preterm labor. Sex can help bring on labor
Signs labor is nearRhythmic lower abdominal cramping or pain, backache, pelvic pressure, leaking fluid (better safe than sorry), more vaginal discharge, and bloody show (pink-tinged spotting)

🔄 True versus false labor

FeatureTrue laborFalse labor (Braxton Hicks)
PatternRegular and consistentIrregular and unpredictable
Over timeLonger and stronger, and they do not go awayTaper off and do not get more painful
Position change or walkingDoes not ease themOften better
Where it is feltStarts in the back and moves forwardFront of the abdomen only
CervixDilation and effacement. Water may break or mucus plug may be lostNo cervical change

Braxton Hicks are not a sign she is going into labor, but they can be mistaken for it.

🧪 Antenatal testing: the big picture

TopicWhat she taught
Why high risk mattersHigh risk can mean many things (pre-existing conditions, problems in pregnancy). It affects self-esteem and life in general
Risk factor groupsBiophysical (mother, baby, genetic, nutritional, OB). Psychosocial (smoking, drug use, alcohol). Socioeconomic (access to care, age, parity, income). Environmental (workplace hazards, chemicals, radiation)
Who may need testingHypertension, cardiac disease, fetal anomalies, multiple gestation, preeclampsia, and many more
Nurse roleEducate. Support mom and family. Assist with procedures. Conduct tests such as the nonstress test. Monitor mom and baby response
ConsentThe provider has the first discussion about risks and benefits and explains the procedure. The nurse can sign as a witness
Screening testIdentifies those not affected by a disease. Offered to all pregnant women (some only to high risk). Example: ultrasound
Diagnostic testIdentifies a disease or problem. Often invasive, so most are kept for high risk pregnancies. Examples: amniocentesis, MRI
Genetic testsDetect health problems and let parents make fully informed decisions
Goal of testingReduce preventable stillbirths and avoid unneeded interventions such as a C-section. Use the information responsibly and support informed choices

🩻 Biophysical tests versus biochemical tests

TestKey points
Ultrasound (screening)Noninvasive with little risk. First trimester: confirms the pregnancy and dates it, usually transvaginal, and finds an ectopic pregnancy. Anatomy scan in the second trimester. More in the third if there are concerns. An abdominal scan early on needs a full bladder, which can be uncomfortable
MRIUsed to see structures such as the placenta, brain anomalies, and complicated defects. No known harm. No metal. Do not lay her flat for long, so use a left lateral tilt with a rolled blanket
Doppler flow studiesMeasure how fast red blood cells travel to the uterus. Good for growth restriction and placental perfusion. Not the best test for fetal compromise (oxygen)
Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)Diagnostic. Placental tissue is aspirated to check chromosomes and DNA. Done early, at 10 to 13 weeks, so it can guide choices sooner than amniocentesis. Risks: fetal loss, infection, rupture of membranes. RhoGAM if Rh negative. Teach her to report cramping, bleeding, pain, or fever
AmniocentesisDiagnostic. A needle through the abdomen (usually ultrasound guided) removes amniotic fluid. Genetic testing at 15 to 20 weeks. Later it checks fetal lung maturity. Can also be therapeutic for polyhydramnios. Risks: trauma to the baby or placenta, bleeding, preterm labor, infection, and a risk of passing HIV, hepatitis B or C to the fetus. RhoGAM if Rh negative
PUBS (cordocentesis)Diagnostic. Blood is removed from the umbilical cord at about 18 weeks or later to look for metabolic and blood disorders. Highest fetal loss rate of the three procedures
After CVS, amnio, or PUBSGet informed consent. Monitor fetal well-being (FHR) for at least 2 hours after the procedure
Maternal assaysMom's blood is tested for baby's DNA. Can show fetal sex as early as 9 to 10 weeks and screen for some congenital anomalies

Test question: which test best answers whether the baby has a congenital defect? A diagnostic test.

🧬 AFP and the multiple marker screen

  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a glycoprotein made in the liver. It is a simple blood test.
  • Low AFP: concern for Down syndrome. High AFP: concern for a neural tube defect.
  • The problem: many false positives. Causes include increased maternal weight (obesity).
  • Quad screen (multiple marker screen): checks hormone levels at 15 to 22 weeks for several congenital anomalies. She asked you to focus on what high and low AFP mean.

👶 Antenatal fetal surveillance (mom is still pregnant)

TestKey points
Kick countsSit quietly and feel for 5 kicks in 1 hour (10 in 2 hours is also reassuring). Then she can go on her way. Cheap, easy to teach, reassuring. If baby is quiet, drink something cold (orange juice) and recount. Still no movement: go to the OB or labor and delivery
Nonstress test (NST)Mom is hooked to a monitor. Looks for accelerations and a good FHR. One of the best measures of fetal well-being. Some false positives. Example: a mom in a car accident. Nurses do these
Contraction stress test (CST)Done in labor and delivery, in a place that can deliver a baby, because contractions are induced. About 20 minutes. If there are no spontaneous contractions, start them with oxytocin or the nipple stimulation test (releases oxytocin, not always successful). It cannot work without contractions
Amniotic fluid index (AFI)Ultrasound measure of amniotic fluid volume
Biophysical profile (BPP)Uses 5 variables (see below)
Vibroacoustic stimulationVibration and sound to wake the baby

📊 Biophysical profile (BPP)

PartLooking for
MovementAt least 3 movements
ToneGood flexion and extension (not lying still)
Breathing movementsChest rising and falling (practice breathing in the womb)
Amniotic fluidMeasures adequate
Nonstress testReactive (nonreactive is bad)
ScoreMeaning
8 to 10Normal. Reassuring. Low risk of chronic fetal asphyxia
4 to 6Abnormal. Chronic fetal asphyxia suspected
Under 4Abnormal. Chronic fetal asphyxia strongly suspected

She will not ask you to score one. Know the 5 parts and what a good versus bad score is. A 10 is perfect and a 2 is terrible.

🧍‍♀️ Body systems (Oct 7)

SystemWhat changes
ReproductiveUterus grows about 20 times its normal size. Higher estrogen and progesterone enlarge the breasts, nipples, and areola (can be uncomfortable) and soften the vagina (more discharge). No periods, because ovulation stops
CardiovascularMore blood volume, cardiac output, and plasma volume. Physiologic anemia from hemodilution. Hypercoagulable (more fibrinogen and clotting factors): protective against bleeding at birth, but a clot risk, so watch for DVT. More venous pressure: edema, varicosities, hemorrhoids
Supine hypotensionFlat on her back, the large uterus presses on the inferior vena cava. Less blood returns to the heart and BP drops. Use left side lying
RespiratoryMore tidal volume and a slight rise in inspiratory capacity, with slight hyperventilation. Estrogen causes engorged, congested nose and sinuses and nosebleeds. The uterus pushes the diaphragm up: fundus at the umbilicus by 20 weeks and at the xiphoid process by 36 weeks
RenalHigher GFR, BP, and urine output, with more UTI risk. Urgency early is hormonal, eases in the second trimester, and returns in the third because the baby presses on the bladder (mechanical)
GIMorning sickness in the first trimester. Heartburn in the second and third. Bloating, gas, and constipation from more progesterone
PicaCraving nonfood items (laundry starch, dirt, clay). Often linked to iron deficiency anemia, so check iron. Physiologic anemia is one reason it happens
MusculoskeletalCenter of gravity shifts forward, so lordosis (anterior curve of the lumbar spine) and a fall risk. Hormones loosen ligaments: round ligament spasms and a waddle. Diastasis recti (rectus muscles separate): usually benign and heals in 3 to 6 months, then physical therapy and rarely surgery
SkinLinea nigra (dark midline). Melasma (mask of pregnancy over cheeks and forehead, more common in darker skin and with sun). More pigment in the nipples, areola, and vulva. More perspiration. Striae gravidarum (stretch marks, tears in the subcutaneous tissue on the abdomen, breasts, hips, which stay as scars). Varicosities, spider nevi, palmar erythema
EndocrinehCG is high early and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, then the placenta takes over. Progesterone maintains the pregnancy. Estrogen causes breast changes. Prolactin starts lactation. Oxytocin causes contractions and helps breastfeeding. hPL is an insulin antagonist, so more glucose is available to the baby and mom needs more glucose

💞 Psychosocial adaptation and preconception care

TopicWhat she taught
Rubin's maternal tasks1. Ensure safe passage for herself and the child. 2. Ensure social acceptance of the child by significant others. 3. Binding in (attachment to the baby). 4. Giving of herself (accepting the demands and sacrifices of motherhood)
Relationship issuesSeeing herself as a mother can be hard. Relationships with grandparents and partners can be strained
Preparing for laborChildbirth classes (Lamaze is common). Fantasies turn into realistic expectations. Nesting comes from an adrenaline rush. Some have fears, such as past trauma
Paternal adaptationThe father takes part and his role changes. He wants a safe, financially stable home. His relationship with his partner changes
Couvade syndromeAlso called sympathetic pregnancy. The father has symptoms such as weight gain, nausea, and indigestion
Preconception careIdeally everyone gets it, including genetic counseling (the best time). Find social, behavioral, and environmental risks and give anticipatory guidance
Preconception teachingHealthy weight and activity. At least a folic acid supplement. Cut risky behaviors (alcohol, drugs, tobacco, over-the-counter drugs). Safe sex, seat belts, carbon monoxide detectors, sunscreen. After stopping contraception, ideally 2 to 3 normal periods before conceiving. Obesity raises risks for mom and baby
Why folic acid earlyIt is needed for neural tube development. The neural tube forms early, often before she knows she is pregnant, so a lack of it can cause neural tube defects

🥗 Foods to avoid in pregnancy (Oct 7)

AvoidWhy
Raw or undercooked meat (including steak), poultry, fish, eggs, and sproutsFood poisoning: E. coli and salmonella
Deli meat and cold cutsListeria. Most OBs say heated until steaming hot (microwave or oven) is okay, because heat kills listeria
Fish high in mercuryShark, swordfish, mackerel, tilefish
Smoked seafoodListeria, unless cooked thoroughly
Raw shellfishAlgae-related infections
Raw eggsSalmonella
Soft cheeses (brie, camembert, roquefort, feta, gorgonzola, queso blanco, queso fresco) and pateListeria
Fresh-squeezed juice and unwashed vegetablesToxoplasmosis
CaffeineLimit to 200 mg a day (American Pregnancy Association). It is a diuretic, so drink enough water
Herbal supplementsNot regulated by the FDA. The exception is ginger, which helps nausea

Anti-nausea medicine: some OBs use a few, but it is not ideal. It is a risk and benefit talk with the OB, so try everything else first.

🩺 Class case study: first prenatal visit

25-year-old, G1 P0, thinks she is 10 weeks. Multiple past partners, now in a committed 5-month relationship. Poor eater, nausea, heartburn, vomiting, recent weight loss. Excited and nervous. Poor sleep. Executive with a master's degree. Family lives across the country. Drinks 3 to 5 drinks a week (more on weekends), occasional marijuana, no tobacco.

ProblemInterventionsOutcome (SMART goal)
Risk for fetal harm from alcohol and THCEducation. Community resources and referral for help with alcohol and THCShe restates the education and cuts back or stops
Imbalanced nutrition (weight loss)24 hour diet recall. Dietitian. Prenatal vitamins (with crackers or at night if needed). Find and avoid triggers. Antiemetics only after a risk and benefit talk with the OBGains 1 to 4 lb in the first trimester (closer to 4 since she lost weight). Takes her prenatal vitamin. Avoids trigger foods
Lack of support (and anxiety)Support groups and community resources. Give clear information, since the unknown raises anxietyJoins a support group for expecting parents
STI risk (multiple partners)STI testing, retested laterResults are negative

At 20 weeks she met her goals: adequate weight gain, less nausea and heartburn, sleeping, in a support group with her partner, no marijuana, and one drink a week (the ideal is none). She is still at high risk for relapse postpartum, so support groups stay important. Orders: glucose tolerance test and ultrasound.

Oct 5: Chapters 1, 2, 9, and 10

✅ Action items from class

  • Notify your employer in writing of any personal beliefs that may interfere with essential job duties.
  • Review ATI Chapter 1 and Chapter 2.

🧩 Barriers and communication

TopicKey points
Barriers to prenatal careInsurance and finances, transportation, and no child care. Case management coordinates resources
FixesOnsite child care, flexible clinic hours, cultural assessment, translation services, and more community resources
Culturally competent end-of-life careRespect different post-mortem practices, use translation services, and identify financial and insurance obstacles
Health literacyAccessible language and no medical jargon. Stay nonjudgmental and advocate
Digital interpretationUse interpretation tools and professional interpreters for diverse patients

⚖️ Ethics and law

PrincipleMeaning in OB nursing
BeneficenceObligation to do good and promote the well-being of mother and infant
NonmaleficenceObligation to do no harm, including prevention through patient education
FidelityLoyalty and continuity of care, such as a complete shift handoff
VeracityHonest disclosure of risks and benefits
AutonomySelf-determination. The foundation of informed consent
JusticeFair allocation of resources
Health care frameworkFocus
UtilitarianMaximize collective welfare
LibertarianIndividual autonomy and free markets
EgalitarianEqual access, with lifestyle taxation
  • Dual patient: mother and fetus are both patients. The duty is primarily to the mother's health, and her autonomy is preserved.
  • Moral distress: manage with education and communication, and tell leadership about belief conflicts ahead of time, in writing.
  • Never abandon a patient because of personal bias. Always give high-quality emergency care. Know your nurse practice act and conscientious objection rights.
  • AWHONN values and nursing tenets: professional and social responsibility, accountability, and advancing nursing science.

📝 Informed consent and minors

  • Provider educates about risks and benefits. Nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding. The nurse does not give the first explanation.
  • Minors: parental consent is required unless the minor is emancipated or legally an adult. Laws vary by jurisdiction.
  • Virginia: minors can legally get birth control without parental consent. Parental involvement is encouraged but not required. Protect confidentiality.
  • Keep personal morality separate from professional ethics.

⚠️ Malpractice and legal risk

TopicKey points
OB nursingA highly litigated area. Fetal heart rate monitoring carries high risk and needs specialized training
ElementsDuty, breach, causation, and damages
Court rulesState-specific statute of limitations and burden of proof. Past actions can create legal vulnerability
Leading causeFailure to communicate
How to lower riskEvidence-based practice, facility policies, clear communication, clinical judgment, and complete documentation

🏛️ Virginia reproductive law (as taught)

  • States set their own laws after the court decisions.
  • Gestational limit: 26 weeks and 6 days.
  • Third trimester: strict medical certification is required.
  • Parental consent for minors and telehealth access are part of the slide.

🏠 Community-based nursing

TopicKey points
DefinitionCommunity is a social structure with shared interests
SettingsHome, school, hospice, ambulatory, long-term care. Hospitals still employ most nurses
FocusHealth promotion, disease prevention, primary care, discharge planning, Healthy People 2030
InterventionsScreening, education, referral, counseling, and teleconsultation for triage
Primary preventionPrevents disease: promotion and risk reduction
Secondary preventionEarly detection: mammograms
Tertiary preventionLimits progression: rehabilitation and strengthening exercises
CAMWidely used: prayer, aromatherapy, massage. Check herbal safety. Ask without judgment
Prenatal accessEarly, adequate care. Telemedicine plus in-person visits (hybrid)
Birth settingsHospital for high risk. Birth centers are low-risk and near hospitals. Home birth has no epidural and limited pain relief
PostpartumHome and clinical assessment, mental health and substance screening, contraception teaching
TeachingPlain language, small chunks, survival skills first, visuals, demonstration, hands-on practice

🚨 Violence and abuse

  • IPV includes physical, sexual, emotional harm and coercive control. Also called domestic abuse or gender-based violence.
  • Cycle: tension building, physical abuse, reconciliation. It repeats and escalates.
  • Sexual assault recovery: the lecture notes mention four phases of psychological trauma recovery. They are not on the slides and were not named, so the guide follows the slide list of nursing management in the Chapter 9 assault deep dive.
  • Abuse types: emotional (isolation), physical (and restricting health care), financial, and sexual.
  • Pregnancy: higher risk. Clues are missed visits and nonadherence. Use the long relationship with the prenatal client to detect early.
  • Elder abuse: physical, sexual, emotional, financial, neglect, abandonment. Health care workers are mandated reporters under state law.
  • Management: separate the patient from an overbearing partner, assess safety directly, document and report, give emotional support, and offer a voluntary safety plan. Preserve forensic evidence.
  • Also watch for trafficking red flags and private screening.

🧬 Genetics and development

TopicKey points
InheritanceTwo alleles, one from each parent. Homozygous or heterozygous. Dominant traits show in the phenotype. Autosomal versus sex-linked
TrisomiesDown (21, most common), Edwards (18, severe, high infant mortality), Patau (13, not inherited)
Sex chromosome conditionsTurner (monosomy X), Klinefelter (47,XXY, low testosterone), Triple X (47,XXX, often found incidentally), Jacob syndrome (47,XYY in males)
DisordersSickle cell, cystic fibrosis (lungs and pancreas), Tay-Sachs, PKU (restrict phenylalanine), Huntington, hemophilia (factor VIII), muscular dystrophy
ScreeningNewborn screening now goes beyond PKU after the Human Genome Project
TeratogensSeverity depends on dose, duration, and substance. Greatest organ risk in the first 8 weeks (embryonic weeks 3 to 8). After 13 weeks, exposure causes growth restriction and smaller organs. Many do not know they are pregnant
CycleOvarian: follicular, ovulatory (LH surge), luteal. Endometrial: menstrual (first 5 days), proliferative, secretory. Mid-cycle pain with ovulation. Fertile cervical mucus. Progesterone dominates the luteal phase
Early developmentFertilization in the fallopian tube. Zygote to blastocyst. Sex set at fertilization. Implantation in the endometrium. Regular heartbeat by week 5. Fetal stage from week 9
Placenta and cordGas, nutrient exchange and hormones (hCG, estrogen, progesterone, placental lactogen). Cord has 2 arteries and 1 vein (AVA) and Wharton jelly. Fluid comes from maternal blood and fetal urine
ShuntsDuctus venosus closes at cord clamping. Ductus arteriosus constricts with higher arterial oxygen. Foramen ovale closes after the first breaths. Persistent shunts may need surgery

💊 Contraception and infertility

MethodTeaching points from class
Natural family planningStandard Days Method (CycleBeads) needs regular cycles. Basal body temperature, cervical mucus. Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation (LAM). Postpartum ovulation is unpredictable
CondomsPerfect versus typical use differ. Use water-based lubricant with latex because oil weakens latex. Male condoms do not cover all skin contact. The female condom covers more skin but is harder to use
SpermicideChemical barrier. Alone it is weak. Can disrupt vaginal flora, cause yeast infection, and raise HIV and STI risk. Timing of insertion and removal matters
Diaphragm, cap, spongeProfessional fitting. Refit after weight change or pelvic surgery. Risk of toxic shock syndrome and urinary tract infection. Follow time limits
Combined oral contraceptiveEstrogen plus progestin stops ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. Contraindicated with smoking over 35, clots, cardiovascular disease, and migraine with aura. Drug interactions need backup
Progestin-only pillSame time every day. Safe with breastfeeding. Drug interactions
Emergency contraceptionStops ovulation and fertilization. Less effective at higher BMI. Nausea is common. Heard in lecture, not on the slides: bariatric surgery and certain cancer histories were named as contraindications. Oral pills may not absorb well after bariatric surgery, and the copper IUD does not depend on absorption
PatchWorks with water activities. Less effective at higher weight. Skin reactions
InjectionEvery 12 to 13 weeks. Bone loss, so calcium and vitamin D. Delayed return of fertility
RingSilicone, in 3 weeks and out 1. May be removed briefly for sex
ImplantRod under the skin. 3 years. Irregular bleeding. Bone density concerns were mentioned in lecture, not on the slides. The method with the established bone loss warning is the Depo-Provera shot
IUDT-shaped, hormonal or copper. Check the string. Risks: ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, perforation
SterilizationPermanent. Tubal ligation carries surgical and anesthesia risk. Vasectomy needs a test to confirm sterility. No STI protection
InfertilityFailure to conceive after 6 to 12 months. Causes include ovulatory, endocrine, autoimmune, lifestyle, and pelvic factors. Workup, hormone treatment, surgery, and assisted reproduction with ethics and education

See the Ch 10 contraception card for generic names and brands.

❓ Advanced questions she posed

QuestionModel answer
How does the dual-patient dilemma complicate autonomy when a mother refuses life-saving treatment for the fetus?Both are patients, but a competent mother keeps the right to refuse. The nurse counsels, supports her decision, documents, and uses the ethics committee. Beneficence toward the fetus does not override her autonomy, and court orders are almost never justified
Compare combined pills and progestin-only pills for a patient with hypertension.Estrogen can raise blood pressure and clot and stroke risk, so combined pills are avoided with hypertension. Progestin-only pills have no estrogen and are usually the safer pill choice. Their drawbacks are strict timing and irregular bleeding
What is the nurse's primary responsibility for informed consent?Witness the signature and verify understanding. The provider gives the education
What are the three fetal shunts and their purpose?Ductus venosus, ductus arteriosus, and foramen ovale. They let oxygenated blood bypass the fluid-filled lungs and immature liver

🔗 Match Games

Tap a term, then its meaning. Lines connect your matches.

🚦 Priority Decoder

Four clients, one nurse. This is the table that ranks them.

The ranking rule

Do not rank by how abnormal something sounds. Rank by Maslow first: physiological needs before safety and security, then belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. In other words, rank by how fast it can hurt the mother or fetus. Life-threatening bleeding, no fetal movement, and imminent danger come first. An acute change beats a stable abnormal finding. Routine labs and teaching come last.

  • Minutes: heavy bleeding with pain, cord or fetal distress, severe preeclampsia signs, imminent abuse, supine hypotension.
  • Hours: fever with urinary symptoms, decreased fetal movement, dehydration, possible DVT.
  • Days to weeks: routine screening, teaching, expected discomforts.
